Preface

前言

I wrote this book to try to ease two fears that American education seems to inflict on all of us in some form. One is the fear of writing. Most people have to do some kind of writing just to get through the day—a memo, a report, a letter—and would almost rather die than do it. The other is the fear of subjects we don’t think we have an aptitude for. Students with a bent for the humanities are terrified of science and mathematics, and students with an aptitude for science and mathematics are terrified of the humanities—all those subjects like English and philosophy and the arts that can’t be pinned down with numbers or formulas. I now think that these fears are largely unnecessary burdens to lug through life.

我写这本书是为了试图减轻美国教育似乎以某种形式强加在我们每个人身上的两种恐惧。一种是写作的恐惧。大多数人为了应付日常事务，不得不进行某种形式的写作——备忘录、报告、信件——但他们几乎宁愿死也不愿去做。另一种是对我们认为自己没有天赋的科目的恐惧。对人文科学感兴趣的学生害怕科学和数学，而对科学和数学有天赋的学生则害怕人文科学——所有那些无法用数字或公式来衡量的科目，比如英语、哲学和艺术。我现在认为，这些恐惧在很大程度上是不必要的、沉重的人生负担。

This book is a personal journey in which I confronted some of my own fears and lived to tell the tale. What started me on it was my interest in the trend in American schools and colleges called “writing across the curriculum,” whereby writing is no longer the sole possession of the English teacher but is an organic part of how every subject is taught. It’s an idea I like very much. It establishes at an early age the fact that writing is a form of thinking, whatever the subject. It also makes writing more appealing by enabling students to write about subjects that interest them and that they’re good at. The chemistry student who freezes at the mention of Shakespeare or Shelley can write surprisingly well about how oxidation causes rust—or could if anyone asked him to.

这本书是我个人的一段旅程，在这个过程中，我直面了自己的一些恐惧，并最终得以讲述这段故事。促使我写下这本书的，是我对美国中小学和大学中一种名为“跨学科写作”的趋势很感兴趣。在这种趋势下，写作不再是英语老师的专属领域，而是融入到所有学科教学中不可或缺的一部分。我非常赞同这个理念。它让学生从小就认识到，无论主题是什么，写作都是一种思考方式。它也让写作更具吸引力，因为学生可以就自己感兴趣且擅长的领域进行写作。一个一听到莎士比亚或雪莱就语塞的化学系学生，如果有人问他，他或许能写出一篇关于氧化如何导致生锈的精彩文章。

Up to now most teachers haven’t thought of such subjects as being reachable through writing or as having any kind of literature. But every discipline has a literature—a body of good writing that students and teachers can use as a model; writing is learned mainly by imitation. Therefore I decided to look for the literature myself: to collect brief examples of good, accessible writing in a variety of academic disciplines. My hope was to demystify writing for the science types and to demystify science for the humanities types.

迄今为止，大多数教师并未意识到这些学科可以通过写作来教授，或者认为它们本身就存在某种形式的文献。然而，每个学科都有其文献——一系列优秀的写作范例，学生和教师都可以从中汲取灵感；写作主要通过模仿来学习。因此，我决定亲自寻找这些文献：收集各个学科领域中优秀且易于理解的简短范例。我希望能够帮助理科生揭开写作的神秘面纱，也希望能够帮助文科生理解科学的奥秘。

One condition I set was to stick close to the formal discipline. I wouldn’t look for writing, for instance, by journalists, good though it might be. If the discipline was geology I wanted good writing by a geologist. If it was evolution I wanted Darwin, if it was relativity I wanted Einstein, if it was cell biology I wanted Lewis Thomas. 1 wanted to show that it’s not necessary to be a “writer” to write well. Clear writing is the logical arrangement of thought; a scientist who thinks clearly can write as well as the best writer. My book, in short, would be mainly an anthology—a guided tour of good writing in different crannies of the B.A. curriculum.

我设定的一个条件是紧扣学科本身。例如，我不会去寻找记者的作品，即便它们写得再好。如果学科是地质学，我想要地质学家写的优秀文章；如果是进化论，我想要达尔文的作品；如果是相对论，我想要爱因斯坦的作品；如果是细胞生物学，我想要刘易斯·托马斯的作品。我想表明，写好文章并不一定非得是“作家”。清晰的写作是对思想的逻辑梳理；一个思维清晰的科学家也能写出和最优秀的作家一样精彩的文章。简而言之，我的书主要是一部文集——一次对本科课程各个领域优秀写作的导览。

But something happened when I actually started to write. The book took on a life of its own and told me how it wanted to be written. I found myself yanked back to many corners of my past—to long-forgotten people and projects and travels that together taught me much of what I know. I realized that my life had been a broad education and that I couldn’t write a book about learning without saying how much it has meant to me to be a generalist in a land that prefers narrow expertise. The anthology began to look suspiciously like a memoir.

但当我真正开始写作时，一些事情发生了变化。这本书仿佛有了自己的生命，告诉我它想如何被写出来。我发现自己被拉回到了过去的许多角落——那些早已被遗忘的人、事、物，它们共同教会了我许多我所知道的东西。我意识到，我的人生是一次博雅教育，如果我不谈谈在这个崇尚专精的国度里，做一个通才对我来说有多么重要，我就无法写一本关于学习的书。这本选集开始越来越像一部回忆录。

I didn’t fight the current. On the contrary, the writing of the book proved one of its central points: that we write to find out what we know and what we want to say. I thought of how often as a writer I had made clear to myself some subject I had previously known nothing about by just putting one sentence after another—by reasoning my way in sequential steps to its meaning. I thought of how often the act of writing even the simplest document—a letter, for instance—had clarified my half-formed ideas. Writing and thinking and learning were the same process.

我没有逆流而上。相反，写作这本书恰恰印证了它的核心观点之一：我们写作是为了探寻我们已知的事物以及我们想要表达的内容。我回想起自己作为一名写作者，曾多少次通过一句接一句的写作，一步步推演，最终理清了自己原本一无所知的某个主题。我回想起自己写作哪怕是最简单的文件——比如一封信——也常常能帮助我理清那些尚未成形的想法。写作、思考和学习，本质上是同一个过程。

The light bulb that went on over my head at this discovery told me what my book was really about. I saw that “writing across the curriculum” wasn’t just a method of getting students to write who were afraid of writing. It was also a method of getting students to learn who were afraid of learning. I was once such a student, morbidly afraid of the sciences and other disciplines that looked alien and forbidding. Now I began to think that I could have written and thereby reasoned my way into those disciplines—far enough, at least, so that they would have lost their terrors.

这一发现让我恍然大悟，明白了我的书的真正意义所在。我意识到，“跨学科写作”不仅仅是让害怕写作的学生动笔的方法，它也是让害怕学习的学生学习的方法。我曾经就是这样的学生，对科学和其他看起来陌生而令人生畏的学科有着病态的恐惧。现在我开始思考，我本可以通过写作，用理性思考的方式走进这些学科——至少能让我克服对它们的恐惧。

The only thing I didn’t understand was exactly how this would work. How would someone, for instance, write chemistry, or physics, or geology? My journey led me to professors in different parts of the country who told me. Well, then, how about mathematics? Surely that couldn’t be written. Surely it could. Joan Countryman (Chapter 9) cured even my math anxiety. This is a book full of born teachers.

我唯一不明白的是，这究竟是怎么回事。比如说，化学、物理或地质学，这些学科该怎么写呢？我的探索之旅让我拜访了全国各地的教授，他们向我解释了答案。那么，数学呢？数学肯定写不出来。但事实证明，它确实可以写出来。琼·康特里曼（第九章）甚至治好了我的数学焦虑。这本书里全是天生的老师。

But above all it’s a book full of ideas—other people’s ideas—and what I’d like most is for readers to just enjoy those people and those ideas. Nothing about the book is definitive. I’ve left out many disciplines that other writers might have put in; my purpose is to suggest possible approaches, not to touch every base. Similarly, my examples of good writing are just one man’s choices—passages I happened to know about or happened to discover during my trip. One of the pleasures of writing the book, in fact, was not knowing who I would meet.

但最重要的是，这是一本充满各种想法的书——都是别人的想法——我最希望的是读者能够欣赏这些人以及他们的想法。这本书里没有什么是绝对的定论。我省略了许多其他作家可能会涉及的学科；我的目的是提出一些可能的方法，而不是面面俱到。同样，我举出的优秀作品的例子也只是我个人的选择——是我碰巧知道或在旅途中偶然发现的段落。事实上，写作这本书的乐趣之一就在于，我不知道会遇到谁。

Once I met them, however, there was no mistaking the men and women I wanted to have along on the ride. They all had the rare gift of enthusiasm. Again and again I was struck by the exuberance that these writers brought to what they were writing about. Whoever the writer and whatever the subject—the biologist Rachel Carson writing about life on the ocean floor, the anthropologist Clifford Geertz writing about a cockfight in Bali, the art historian A. Hyatt Mayor writing about the lithographs of Toulouse-Lautrec, the zoologist Archie Carr writing about the giant sea turtle, the psychiatrist Robert Coles writing about the gallantry of children under stress, the naturalist John Muir writing about an earthquake in Yosemite Valley, the composer Roger Sessions writing about Beethoven and the mystery of composition—the common thread is a sense of high enjoyment, zest and wonder. Perhaps, both in learning to write and in writing to learn, they are the only ingredients that really matter.

然而，一旦我与他们相遇，我便毫不犹豫地认定了我想要携手同行的这些人。他们都拥有难得的热情。这些作家在写作中流露出的活力一次又一次地深深打动了我。无论作者是谁，无论主题是什么——生物学家蕾切尔·卡森描写海底生物，人类学家克利福德·格尔茨描写巴厘岛的斗鸡，艺术史学家A·海厄特·梅耶尔描写图卢兹-洛特雷克的石版画，动物学家阿奇·卡尔描写巨型海龟，精神病学家罗伯特·科尔斯描写压力下儿童的英勇，博物学家约翰·缪尔描写优胜美地山谷的地震，作曲家罗杰·塞申斯描写贝多芬和作曲的奥秘——贯穿他们写作的共同点是对写作充满热情、活力和好奇。或许，无论是在学习写作的过程中，还是在通过写作学习的过程中，这些才是真正重要的要素。

New York

纽约

April, 1988

1988年4月

1. Hermes and the Periodic Table

1. 赫尔墨斯与元素周期表

As a boy I spent four years at a boarding school in Massachusetts called Deerfield Academy that had two legends attached to it. The first was its headmaster, Frank L. Boyden. When he was a young man just out of college, in 1902, he accepted a position that only a teacher desperate for a first job might have taken: running a moribund academy in the tiny village of Deerfield. The school had so few boys that the new headmaster had to play on the football and baseball teams himself. By the time I got there, in the mid-1930s, Frank Boyden had built Deerfield into one of the best secondary schools in the country, and when he retired, in 1968, his place in American education secure, he had been headmaster for sixty-six years. During all those years he also coached the football, basketball and baseball teams, continuing as an octogenarian to rap out sharp grounders for infield practice before every game. His favorite baseball strategy was the squeeze play—a mark, perhaps, of his Yankee practicality. He was an unusually small man with a plain New England face, slicked-down black hair, and metal-rimmed glasses; nobody would have noticed him in a crowd or picked him out as a leader. But three generations of boys were shaped for life by his values, and I was one of them.

我小时候在马萨诸塞州一所名为迪尔菲尔德学院的寄宿学校待了四年，这所学校有两个传奇人物。第一个是校长弗兰克·L·博伊登。1902年，刚从大学毕业的他接受了一份只有急于找到第一份工作的老师才会接受的职位：管理迪尔菲尔德这个小村庄里一所奄奄一息的学院。学校的学生寥寥无几，以至于这位新校长不得不亲自加入橄榄球队和棒球队。到了20世纪30年代中期我到那里的时候，弗兰克·博伊登已经把迪尔菲尔德学院打造成了全美最好的中学之一。1968年他退休时，在美国教育界的地位稳固，担任校长长达66年。在这66年里，他还担任橄榄球队、篮球队和棒球队的教练，即使到了八十多岁高龄，他仍然坚持在每场比赛前为内场练习击打强劲的滚地球。他最喜欢的棒球战术是触击短打——这或许体现了他务实的“洋基式”作风。他身材矮小，长着一张典型的英格兰新英格兰式的朴素面孔，一头乌黑油亮的头发，戴着一副金属框眼镜；在人群中，没人会注意到他，更没人会把他认作领导者。然而，他的价值观塑造了三代男孩的人生，而我就是其中之一。

The second legend was his wife, Helen Childs Boyden. A tall, bony woman with a face even plainer than her husband’s, she wore her black hair tied in a bun and she peered out at the world through thick glasses, triumphing over eyesight so bad that it would have immobilized a person of weaker will. Helen Childs had also come to Deerfield as a young teacher, fresh out of Smith College with a science degree. She married Frank Boyden in 1907 and for more than sixty years was a strengthening presence in his life and in the life of the school. She was best known, however, for her senior course in chemistry. The legend was that she could teach chemistry to anybody. As it turned out, she couldn’t teach it to me.

第二位传奇人物是他的妻子海伦·查尔兹·博伊登。她身材高挑，骨瘦如柴，相貌比丈夫还要平凡。她把黑发盘成发髻，透过厚厚的眼镜凝视着这个世界，尽管视力很差，意志薄弱的人恐怕早已寸步难行。海伦·查尔兹也曾以年轻教师的身份来到迪尔菲尔德，她刚从史密斯学院毕业，获得了理学学位。1907年，她嫁给了弗兰克·博伊登，此后六十多年来，她一直是丈夫和学校生活中不可或缺的重要力量。然而，她最出名的还是她教授的化学课程。传说她能把化学教给任何人。但事实证明，她教不了我。

The fault was undoubtedly mine. I’m sure I didn’t want to learn chemistry. Probably I had also persuaded myself that I couldn’t learn chemistry, or any of the hard sciences. Those subjects were for all those people who had an aptitude for them—the ones who carried a slide rule and could take a radio apart. I was a liberal arts snob, illiterate about the physical world I lived in, incurious about how things worked. The courses I felt most comfortable with were English and languages, and in my extracurricular hours I indulged my other two loves—playing baseball and writing for the school newspaper. I did what came easiest and avoided what I might not be able to do well.

毫无疑问，错在我。我肯定不想学化学。或许我还说服了自己，我学不会化学，或者说，学不会任何硬科学。那些科目是给那些有天赋的人准备的——那些会用计算尺、能拆收音机的人。我是一个文科生，对现实世界一无所知，对事物运作的原理也毫无兴趣。我最得心应手的课程是英语和语言，课余时间我则沉浸在另外两项爱好中——打棒球和为校报撰稿。我总是做最容易的事，逃避那些我可能做不好的事。

My favorite language was Latin. It transported me back to the classical world, and yet it was anything but dead—thousands of its roots were alive and well in English; in fact, no subject has been more useful to me as a writer and an editor. I took Latin for three years at Deerfield until there were no more courses left to take, finally getting beyond Caesar’s dreary wars and Cicero’s prim orations to Virgil’s Aeneid and Horace’s odes, finally discovering that the wonderful language also had a wonderful literature.

我最喜欢的语言是拉丁语。它带我回到了古典世界，但它绝非死气沉沉——它的数千个词根在英语中依然鲜活；事实上，作为一名作家和编辑，没有哪门学科比拉丁语对我的帮助更大。我在迪尔菲尔德学院学习了三年拉丁语，直到所有课程都已修完，终于从凯撒枯燥乏味的战争史和西塞罗的演说中解脱出来，开始研读维吉尔的《埃涅阿斯纪》和贺拉斯的颂歌，最终发现这门美妙的语言也拥有美妙的文学。

My teacher in that liberating third year was a man so venerable that he seemed to be a schoolmaster from the nineteenth century. Recalling him now, I think of pictures of Darwin as an old man. Charles Huntington Smith had silky white hair, a white mustache and a white goatee, and he wore the black suit and high collar befitting his age and dignity. But his eyes were young, and so were his passions for what he taught. He had turned his classroom into a small corner of ancient Rome. Large framed photographs of the Forum and the Colosseum hung on the walls, and he had also sent away for plaster reproductions of some of the great statues of antiquity. Hermes on tiptoe, beckoning the gods, was on his desk, and the Winged Victory was nearby, still sending her message about beauty and line across the centuries. Mr. Smith was obviously aware of the power exerted by the icons that inhabit the classrooms of our childhood; when I was in Italy during World War II, the first time I got a few days off I hitchhiked to Rome to see the Forum, though the distance was great and the hours I could spend there were short.

我在大学三年级那段自由自在的日子里遇到的老师是一位德高望重的长者，仿佛是从十九世纪穿越而来的教师。如今回想起他，我不禁想起达尔文年老时的照片。查尔斯·亨廷顿·史密斯先生有着丝滑的白发、白色的胡须和山羊胡，身着与他的年龄和尊严相称的黑色西装和高领衬衫。但他的眼神却很年轻，他对教学的热情也同样年轻。他把教室布置成了古罗马的一隅。墙上挂着罗马广场和斗兽场的大幅照片，他还订购了一些古代伟大雕像的石膏复制品。赫尔墨斯踮着脚尖，向众神招手的雕像摆在他的桌子上，而胜利女神像就在附近，几个世纪以来，她依然在传递着关于美和线条的讯息。史密斯先生显然深知，那些在我们童年教室里摆放的偶像具有多么强大的力量；二战期间我在意大利的时候，第一次休假几天，就搭便车去了罗马参观古罗马广场，虽然路途遥远，而且我能在那里待的时间也很短。

In my senior year reality caught up with me: I had to take Mrs. Boyden’s chemistry. I remember her classroom almost as vividly as Mr. Smith’s. I can still smell its acrid smells, alien to my humanist nose. I can still see the retorts and beakers and other strangely shaped vessels designed for measuring whatever they were designed to measure. But the icon that dominates my memory is the huge chart of the periodic table of the elements that hung at the front of the room. Those cryptic letters and numbers, so neatly arranged in their boxes and columns, were the Hermes and Venus of the chemistry class—the gods whose laws and whims would rule our lives. Each box contained its own tremendous story of natural forces working out an ordained pattern. What could that story possibly be? I never found out. The periodic table continues to rebuke me for my indolence.

高三那年，现实终于找上了我：我不得不选修博伊登太太的化学课。我对她的教室记忆犹新，几乎和对史密斯先生的教室一样清晰。我至今还能闻到那刺鼻的气味，对于我这个人文主义者来说，那气味实在太陌生了。我至今还能看到那些烧瓶、烧杯和其他形状奇特的容器，它们被设计用来测量各种各样的东西。但最让我印象深刻的，是挂在教室前面的那张巨大的元素周期表。那些排列整齐的方格和列中的神秘字母和数字，就像化学课上的赫尔墨斯和维纳斯——是主宰我们生活的神祇，它们的法则和运行规律似乎早已注定。每一个方格都蕴藏着一个宏大的故事，讲述着自然力量如何按照既定的模式运行。那究竟是什么故事呢？我始终没有找到答案。元素周期表至今仍在谴责我的懒惰。

Mrs. Boyden had devised a teaching method that I remember as slightly cute but that obviously worked for three generations of boys. It had something to do with one molecule joining hands with another and going off to form a different combination. I must have resisted these little romances, for by about April someone in authority began to think the unthinkable: I would flunk the college entrance exam in chemistry. This would not only ruin my chances of getting into Princeton; it would besmirch Deerfield’s proud record of placing its seniors in America’s best colleges.

博伊登太太设计了一种教学方法，我记得当时觉得有点儿幼稚，但显然对三代男孩都有效。这方法跟一个分子和另一个分子“携手”形成新的组合有关。我当时肯定对这些“浪漫故事”不太感冒，因为到了四月份左右，学校里某个有权势的人开始担心一件不可思议的事情：我会化学考砸大学入学考试。这不仅会断送我进普林斯顿的希望，还会玷污迪尔菲尔德高中引以为傲的、将毕业生送入美国顶尖大学的记录。

The solution was for me to take the Latin exam instead. I was released from Mrs. Boyden’s charge and told to cram for Latin. The decision was easier made than executed; after a year the intricate carpentry of Virgil’s language—the capricious declensions and conjugations, the gerunds and gerundives and the dreaded ablative absolute—had slipped away and had to be hastily stuffed back into my brain. The exam was almost as hard to pass as chemistry would have been. But I was rescued by memory and by an instinct for how languages work and was duly admitted to Princeton.

解决办法是让我去考拉丁语。我摆脱了博伊登太太的管束，被告知要突击复习拉丁语。做决定容易做起来难；一年过去了，维吉尔语言的精妙之处——变格和动词变位、动名词和动名词后缀，以及令人畏惧的独立离格——都已荡然无存，我不得不赶紧把它们重新塞回脑子里。这门考试几乎和化学一样难。但我凭借记忆力和对语言运作方式的直觉，最终顺利通过了考试，被普林斯顿大学录取。

There I continued to skirt the courses that would have made me a more broadly educated man. I satisfied the science requirement by taking biology, which didn’t hold the terrors of chemistry and physics; any boob can dissect a dogfish. Besides, the dogfish and I had many systems in common. Poking about in its innards, I at least knew what I was looking for: heart and lungs and a digestive tract. Unlike the molecule, they could be seen and touched and examined.

在那里，我继续回避那些能让我接受更广泛教育的课程。我选修了生物学来满足科学课的要求，生物学不像化学和物理那样令人畏惧；任何笨蛋都能解剖一条角鲨。再说，我和角鲨有很多共同的系统。在它的内脏里摸索时，我至少知道自己在找什么：心脏、肺和消化道。与分子不同，它们是可以看、可以摸、可以研究的。

On December 7 of my sophomore year, Pearl Harbor ended our reverie of life as an orderly succession of events. Our first impulse was to rush out and enlist, but we were told that “Washington” wanted us to stay in college and get educated for “the war effort.” So began the age of “acceleration” at Princeton. Through the winter, spring and summer of 1942 we took courses that were compressed and elided. Our education had the quality of a speeded-up movie; we became part junior before we finished being sophomores and never knew how many credits we were amassing. The main thing was that we were amassing wisdom, which Washington in its own wisdom would harness to smash the Axis. Meanwhile several gruff men on the gymnastics and physical education staff, whom I had naturally never seen before, labored with ill-concealed contempt to build our muscles. Washington wanted us to be tough.

在我大二那年12月7日，珍珠港事件打破了我们对生活井然有序的憧憬。我们最初的冲动是冲出去应征入伍，但有人告诉我们，“华盛顿”希望我们留在大学，接受教育，为“战争”效力。普林斯顿的“加速”时代就此拉开序幕。1942年的整个冬春夏三季，我们学习的课程都被压缩和省略。我们的教育就像一部快进的电影；我们还没完成大二的学业就已经成了大三的学生，而且根本不知道自己究竟积累了多少学分。最重要的是，我们正在积累智慧，而华盛顿自以为是地利用这些智慧来摧毁轴心国。与此同时，几个我之前从未见过的、脾气暴躁的体操和体育老师，带着毫不掩饰的轻蔑，辛勤地训练我们锻炼肌肉。华盛顿想要我们变得强悍。

By fall the texture of college life began to unravel. So many professors and students had slipped away that nobody knew who was still around. At the end of the term I also left and enlisted in the army. By then I was more senior than junior, my credits badly tangled. But it could all be straightened out when I came back.

到了秋季，大学生活的秩序开始瓦解。许多教授和学生都离开了，以至于没人知道谁还留在那里。学期末，我也离开了学校，应征入伍。那时我已经不是大三学生而是大四学生了，学分也乱成一团。不过，等我回来，一切都会好起来的。

My next three credits I earned just by putting on a uniform. Princeton decided that time spent in the service was time educationally spent, and in my case that was true. My love of remote travel was born on the morning after my troopship landed in Morocco; I awoke to a landscape so startlingly beautiful and exotic—my first glimpse of the Arab world—that I’ve never forgotten the impact of the moment. We were informed of Princeton’s decision about the extra credits in one of the letters that President Dodds periodically wrote to all of us who had gone off to war—letters that caught up with us in places where we had never expected to be. One of them reached me in a sand-blown tent near the Algerian town of Blida, and it enclosed a complete list of Modern Library titles. The university would like to send us three books, President Dodds wrote; we should just check our choices. I did, and my three books reached me six months later in a snow-blown tent near the Italian city of Brindisi.

我接下来的三个学分，仅仅是穿上军装就获得了。普林斯顿大学认为服役时间就是学习时间，而对我来说，的确如此。我对偏远地区旅行的热爱，源于我乘坐的运兵船抵达摩洛哥后的那个早晨；我醒来时，眼前的景色美得令人惊叹，充满异域风情——那是我第一次领略阿拉伯世界的风情——那一刻的震撼至今难忘。普林斯顿大学关于额外学分的决定，是通过多兹校长定期写给我们这些奔赴战场的人的信中得知的——这些信件常常在我们意想不到的地方寄到我们手中。其中一封信寄到了我在阿尔及利亚布利达附近一个被风沙吹得沙尘暴肆虐的帐篷里，信中附有一份完整的现代文库书目清单。多兹校长在信中写道，学校想给我们寄三本书；我们只需确认一下自己的选择即可。我照做了，六个月后，我的三本书寄到了我在意大利布林迪西附近一个被大雪覆盖的帐篷里。

When the war in Europe ended, in May of 1945, the troopships taking men home were assigned to France and England; the Mediterranean theater would have to wait. In July, however, I heard that the army was establishing a college in Florence to keep at least some of its soldiers occupied. Eager for more credits, whatever odd form they might take, I applied and was allowed to attend. Our campus was an aeronautical academy that Mussolini had built in his best Fascist style.

1945年5月，欧洲战事结束，运送士兵回国的运兵船被分配到法国和英国；地中海战区的战事只能暂时搁置。然而到了7月，我听说军队正在佛罗伦萨建立一所学院，以便至少能让一部分士兵有事可做。我渴望获得更多学分，无论这些学分以何种形式出现，于是我申请了这所学院，并获准入学。我们的校园是一所航空学院，由墨索里尼以他最典型的法西斯风格建造而成。

I knew nothing about art, so I decided to take art history courses. It was the ideal time and place—Florence had just begun to bring back the statues and paintings that had been hidden during the war. Crowds of Florentines gathered to watch these installations, as they had when the works were new; it was a re-Renaissance. For me it was the best of summers. On weekends I hitchhiked to other Tuscan towns that were almost as rich: Pisa, Lucca, San Gimignano and my favorite of them all, Siena. When the summer was over I received three certificates saying that I had passed three courses. But only I knew how much they certified.

我对艺术一窍不通，于是决定去上艺术史课程。时机和地点都恰到好处——佛罗伦萨刚刚开始将那些在战争期间被藏匿的雕像和绘画作品重新展出。成群的佛罗伦萨人聚集在一起观看这些展品，就像当年这些作品刚面世时一样；这简直是文艺复兴的复兴。对我来说，那是最美好的夏天。周末，我会搭便车去托斯卡纳其他一些同样富丽堂皇的小镇：比萨、卢卡、圣吉米尼亚诺，还有我最爱的锡耶纳。夏天结束时，我拿到了三张证书，证明我通过了三门课程。但只有我自己知道，这些证书究竟认证了我什么。

In November a huge troopship finally came and took us home. Disgorged into civilian life, I needed to know whether my army credits would give me enough units to graduate. If not, I would have to go back to Princeton for one more term. When I had left I was sure I would want to return. Now I only wanted to be given my degree and to get started on whatever I was going to do next.

十一月，一艘巨大的运兵船终于抵达，接我们回家了。重返平民生活后，我迫切想知道我的军队学分是否足够毕业。如果不够，我就得回普林斯顿再读一个学期。离开时，我确信自己会想回来。现在，我只希望拿到学位，然后开始我接下来要做的事情。

My hopes were not high, however, on the morning when I went to Princeton for an interview with the official who would judge my case. The certificates that I was clutching—the pieces of paper so gratifyingly won in Florence—now looked crude, wholly lacking in academic authority. I went into Nassau Hall and was told that my appointment was with Dean Root. Dean Root! I might as well turn around and go back to New York.

然而，那天早上我去普林斯顿大学面试那位将要审理我案件的官员时，并没有抱太大的希望。我紧紧攥着的那些证书——那些我在佛罗伦萨满怀欣喜地赢得的纸片——现在看起来粗糙不堪，完全缺乏学术权威。我走进拿骚楼，被告知我的面试官是鲁特院长。鲁特院长！我真想掉头回纽约。

Robert K. Root, who was then in his seventies, was dean of the Princeton faculty. I had never met him, but I had taken his sophomore course in English literature and listened week after week to his lectures. They were stern disquisitions, raining on our unappreciative heads the fruits of lifelong scholarship, excavating with dry precision the buried ironies of Swift and the unsuspected jests of Pope, which even then I continued not to suspect. My only other view of Dean Root was at the head of the procession that commenced the service every Sunday morning in Princeton’s chapel. Gray and solemn, bowed under robes representing the highest honors of Academia, he seemed to belong to Oxford or Edinburgh, not to brash young America. Surely such a man, guardian of Princeton’s virtue, would scorn the grab bag of credits I now emptied at his feet.

当时已年过七旬的罗伯特·K·鲁特是普林斯顿大学的教务长。我从未见过他，但我曾选修过他开设的英国文学大二课程，每周都聆听他的讲座。他的讲课严谨而深刻，如同倾盆大雨般将毕生学术的成果倾泻在我们这些懵懂无知的头脑中，以冷静而精准的笔触挖掘出斯威夫特作品中隐藏的讽刺和蒲柏作品中那些我当时仍未察觉的玩笑。我对鲁特院长的唯一其他印象，是每周日早晨普林斯顿教堂礼拜仪式开始时，他总是走在队伍的最前面。他衣着灰白，神情庄重，身着象征着学术最高荣誉的长袍，低头鞠躬，仿佛来自牛津或爱丁堡，而非这群傲慢的年轻美国人。这样一位普林斯顿美德的守护者，想必会鄙视我如今倾倒在他脚下的那堆学分吧。

Dean Root studied my Princeton transcript gravely. Then he studied my certificates and said he had never seen anything like them. Next he began adding up my credits. I could tell that he didn’t know how much weight to give my army learning. I could also tell that he wasn’t optimistic. I remembered that he had a habit of chewing the inside of his cheek, and now his mouth was working rapidly. He shook his head and mumbled that I seemed to be a little short of the necessary total.

鲁特院长认真地查看了我的普林斯顿成绩单。然后他又看了看我的证书，说他从未见过这样的证书。接着他开始计算我的学分。我看得出来，他不知道该如何衡量我在军队的学习经历。我也能感觉到他并不乐观。我记得他有个习惯，喜欢咬腮帮子，现在他的嘴巴正快速地翕动着。他摇了摇头，咕哝着说，我的学分似乎还差一点。

Then, imperceptibly, the arid dean disappeared and I was talking with a person. He asked me what I had done in the army, and where I had gone, and what I had thought about. I could hardly believe that it was the same Dean Root. Was this the face that had cowed three generations of students since he had been hired as a young instructor by an earlier president of Princeton, Woodrow Wilson? I found myself talking to him with enthusiasm, describing my travels in North Africa and my trips to Rome and my Renaissance summer in Florence and my visits to Siena and the other Tuscan towns. By then I was sure that I didn’t have enough credits and that the official part of my interview was over. Not until later did I realize that this was the only part that mattered to Dean Root.

然后，那位冷漠的院长不知不觉地消失了，我和另一个人聊了起来。他问我在军队里都干了些什么，去过哪些地方，又都思考了些什么。我简直不敢相信眼前这个人就是鲁特院长。难道就是这张脸，自从他被普林斯顿大学前任校长伍德罗·威尔逊聘为年轻讲师以来，就一直让三代学生感到畏惧？我发现自己兴致勃勃地和他谈了起来，描述着我在北非的旅行、罗马之行、在佛罗伦萨度过的文艺复兴时期的夏天，以及我游览锡耶纳和其他托斯卡纳小镇的经历。那时，我确信自己的学分不够，面试的正式部分已经结束了。直到后来我才意识到，这才是鲁特院长真正关心的。

At the end a look of sadness came into Dean Root’s eyes and he said, “Tell me—I suppose Siena was mostly destroyed during the war?” I realized that I was the first messenger to come back from Tuscany. Suddenly I understood what Siena would mean to this quintessential humanist; probably Dean Root had first visited Siena as a young man himself. Suddenly it was possible to understand that Dean Root had once been a young man. I told him that Siena hadn’t been touched by the war and that the great striped cathedral was still there.

最后，迪安·鲁特眼中闪过一丝悲伤，他问道：“告诉我——我猜想锡耶纳在战争期间几乎被摧毁殆尽了吧？”我这才意识到，我是第一个从托斯卡纳回来的信使。我突然明白了锡耶纳对这位典型的人文主义者意味着什么；迪安·鲁特年轻时或许也曾到访过锡耶纳。我这才意识到，迪安·鲁特也曾是位年轻人。我告诉他，锡耶纳并未受到战争的波及，那座宏伟的条纹大教堂依然屹立在那里。

Dean Root smiled fleetingly and saw me to the door. He said the university would inform me of its decision soon. Not long afterward he wrote to tell me I had met Princeton’s requirements for a degree and would be given my diploma at a special graduation for returning servicemen early in 1946. I’ve always suspected that he waived one or two credits to make my total come out right. I’ve also thought that if Siena had been destroyed I would have had to go back for another term.

鲁特院长短暂地笑了笑，送我到门口。他说学校很快就会通知我结果。不久之后，他写信告诉我，我已经达到了普林斯顿大学的学位要求，将在1946年初为退伍军人举办的特别毕业典礼上获得毕业证书。我一直怀疑他免除了我一两个学分，好让我的总学分符合要求。我还想过，如果锡耶纳学院被毁，我就得再读一个学期了。

But one thing I’m sure of: My education really began that day in Nassau Hall. Dean Root freed me to get on with my life. Learning, he seemed to be saying, takes a multitude of forms; expect to find them in places where you least expect them to be.

但我确信一件事：我的真正教育始于那一天在拿骚堂的时光。鲁特院长让我得以自由地继续我的生活。他似乎在告诉我，学习的形式多种多样；你会在意想不到的地方发现它们。

In January I rented a cap and gown and received my dubious B.A. and went out into the world. Several months later I got a job with the New York Herald Tribune and began what has turned out to be a career of trying to write clearly and—as an editor and a teacher—to help other people to write clearly. I’ve become a clarity nut. I’ve also become a logic nut. I’m far less preoccupied than I once was with individual words and their picturesque roots and origins and with the various fights over which new ones should be admitted into the language. Those are mere skirmishes at the edge of the battlefield; I will no longer man the ramparts to hurl back such barbarians as “hopefully.”

一月份，我租了一套学士服，领到了那份不太光彩的学士学位，然后踏入了社会。几个月后，我在《纽约先驱论坛报》找到了一份工作，从此开始了我毕生致力于清晰写作的职业生涯——作为一名编辑和教师，我努力帮助其他人也做到清晰写作。我成了个追求清晰表达的狂热分子，也成了个逻辑狂。我不再像以前那样执着于单个词语及其生动的词源和起源，也不再纠结于哪些新词应该被纳入语言体系的各种争论。那些不过是战场边缘的小规模冲突；我再也不会站在城墙上，把“希望如此”之类的野蛮词汇拒之门外了。

What does preoccupy me is the plain declarative sentence. How have we managed to hide it from so much of the population? Far too many Americans are prevented from doing useful work because they never learned to express themselves. Contrary to general belief, writing isn’t something that only “writers” do; writing is a basic skill for getting through life. Yet most American adults are terrified of the prospect—ask a middle-aged engineer to write a report and you’ll see something close to panic. Writing, however, isn’t a special language that belongs to English teachers and a few other sensitive souls who have a “gift for words.” Writing is thinking on paper. Anyone who thinks clearly should be able to write clearly—about any subject at all.

真正让我感到困扰的是平铺直叙的陈述句。我们究竟是如何将它隐藏起来，让如此多的人无法掌握的？太多美国人因为从未学会表达自己而无法从事有用的工作。与普遍认知相反，写作并非只有“作家”才会做；写作是一项基本的生存技能。然而，大多数美国成年人却对写作感到恐惧——如果你让一位中年工程师写报告，你会看到他近乎恐慌的表情。写作并非一种特殊的语言，它不属于英语教师和少数拥有“文字天赋”的敏感之人。写作就是将思考记录在纸上。任何思维清晰的人都应该能够清晰地写作——无论主题是什么。

How, you might ask, do I know that—I who so diligently avoided all the courses I thought I was too dumb to understand or was too lazy to grapple with? I know it because my work has been the education I avoided. Over the years I’ve written or edited hundreds of articles on subjects I had never previously thought about. No other job could have exposed me to so many areas of knowledge. I’ve not only met a wide variety of interesting people doing things that astonished and delighted me. I’ve found that their ideas were never so specialized that I couldn’t grasp them by writing about them or by editing someone else’s writing about them: by breaking the ideas down into logical units, called sentences, and putting one sentence after another. Along the way I’ve also discovered that knowledge is not as compartmented as I thought it was. It’s not a hundred different rooms inhabited by strangers; it’s all one house. Hermes and the periodic table are equally its household gods, and writing is the key that opens the door.

你或许会问，我怎么会知道这些？我可是曾经如此刻意地避开所有我认为自己太笨理解不了或太懒得钻研的课程啊！我知道，因为我的工作正是我曾经逃避的那种教育。这些年来，我撰写或编辑了数百篇关于我以前从未想过的主题的文章。没有任何其他工作能让我接触到如此广泛的知识领域。我不仅结识了形形色色、做着令我惊叹和欣喜的事情的有趣之人，我还发现，他们的想法并非晦涩难懂到我无法理解的地步——只要我把它们写下来，或者编辑别人写出来的东西：把这些想法分解成逻辑单元，也就是句子，然后一个接一个地排列起来。在这个过程中，我还发现，知识并非像我想象的那样泾渭分明。它不是一百个住着陌生人的房间；它其实是一座房子。赫尔墨斯和元素周期表都是这座房子的守护神，而写作就是打开这扇门的钥匙。

That’s what this book is about.

这本书讲的就是这个。

# ↩

2. Writing Across the Curriculum

2. 跨学科写作

One spring day in 1985 I got a telephone call from a professor named Thomas Gover at Gustavus Adolphus College, a small liberal arts college of Lutheran origins in St. Peter, Minnesota. He wanted to tell me about a new program at his college tha he thought would interest me. It did. In fact, it’s what got me thinking about this book.

1985年春天的一天，我接到明尼苏达州圣彼得市古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院一位名叫托马斯·戈弗的教授的电话。这所学院是一所小型文理学院，起源于路德教派。他想跟我介绍他们学院的一个新项目，他觉得我会感兴趣。我的确很感兴趣。事实上，正是这个项目让我萌生了写这本书的想法。

He said that in the fall term Gustavus Adolphus would launch a curriculum in which seventy-five courses, covering the entire spectrum of a baccalaureate education, would be listed with a “W,” meaning that writing would be a required part of the course, that it would be a factor in the student’s grade, and that the teachers would work with the students on the process of organizing, writing and rewriting their papers and reports. Three “W” courses would be required for graduation.

他表示，古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院将于秋季学期推出一项新课程，其中75门涵盖本科教育各个领域的课程都将标注“W”，这意味着写作是课程的必修部分，将计入学生的最终成绩，教师将指导学生组织、撰写和修改论文及报告。学生必须修满三门“W”课程才能毕业。

The call crystallized an idea I realized I felt strongly about: that the teaching of writing should no longer be left just to English teachers but should be made an organic part of every subject. The idea, which goes by the name of “writing across the curriculum,” has been very much in the air among educators for at least a decade. But I had never heard of any school or college actually trying it. (I’ve since heard of many.) That’s why the call from Minnesota excited me. It was a chance to see the idea in action and to find out whether it was as important a trend as I thought it was.

那通电话让我更加清晰地意识到自己一直以来深信不疑的一个想法：写作教学不应再仅仅由英语老师负责，而应该成为所有学科的有机组成部分。这个被称为“跨学科写作”的理念，在教育界已经流行了至少十年。但我从未听说过有哪所学校或大学真正尝试过。（后来我听说了很多。）正因如此，来自明尼苏达州的电话让我兴奋不已。这是一个亲眼见证这一理念付诸实践的机会，也是了解它是否真如我所想的那样重要的机会。

Professor Gover asked if I would like to come out to Gustavus Adolphus and talk to the students about writing. I said I would like to come out and talk to the professors; they were the real heroes of the mission. How were they going to undertake a kind of teaching they had never tried before? How were they going to adapt writing to their discipline? How did they think writing would help their students to learn?

戈弗教授问我是否愿意去古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院和学生们谈谈写作。我说我更愿意去和教授们交流；他们才是这次任务真正的英雄。他们要如何开展一种从未尝试过的教学方式？他们要如何将写作融入到他们的学科中？他们认为写作将如何帮助学生学习？

I asked Thomas Gover how to get to Gustavus Adolphus. He said that if I flew to Minneapolis he would meet me at the airport. I said I’d see him there.

我问托马斯·戈弗如何去古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院。他说如果我飞到明尼阿波利斯，他会在机场接我。我说我会去机场见他。

As baggage I would be taking along a number of strong opinions on why so many Americans don’t learn to write and why they live in so much fear of trying.

作为行李，我将带着一些强烈的观点，这些观点认为，为什么这么多美国人不学习写作，以及为什么他们如此害怕尝试写作。

One of them has to do with English teachers. Under the American system, they are the people who teach our children to write. If they don’t, nobody will. They do it with dedication, and I hope they’ll be rewarded, if not here on earth, at least in heaven, for there’s almost no pedagogical task harder and more tiring than teaching somebody to write. But there are all kinds of reasons why English teachers ought to get some relief. One is that they shouldn’t have to assume the whole responsibility for imparting a skill that’s basic to every area of life. That should be everybody’s job. That’s citizenship.

其中一点与英语教师有关。在美国的教育体系下，他们负责教孩子们写作。如果他们不教，就没人教了。他们兢兢业业地从事这项工作，我希望他们能得到回报，即便不是在人间，至少在天堂也能得到回报，因为几乎没有比教人写作更难、更累的教学任务了。但是，英语教师应该得到一些减轻，原因有很多。其中之一是，他们不应该承担教授这项生活各个领域都至关重要的技能的全部责任。这应该是每个人的责任。这是公民应尽的义务。

Another reason is that it’s not what most English teachers want to do. Their real subject is literature—not how to write, but how to read: how to extract meaning from a written text. That’s what they were primarily hired to teach and what they were trained to teach. Inevitably, much of the writing that English teachers assign is based on literature—on what somebody else has already written—and therefore has little reality And what students in turn write for the English teacher is more florid than what they would write for anybody else. They reach for a “literary” style that they think the teacher wants and that they assume is “good English.” But this style is no part of who they are. Nor is it necessarily good English; much of what academics write and read is fuzzy and verbose. Students should be learning a strong and unpretentious prose that will carry their thoughts about the world they live in.

另一个原因是，这并非大多数英语教师的本意。他们真正的教学对象是文学——不是如何写作，而是如何阅读：如何从文本中提取意义。这才是他们受聘的主要职责，也是他们接受培训的目的。不可避免地，英语教师布置的大部分写作作业都基于文学作品——基于他人已有的文字——因此缺乏真实性。而学生为英语教师写作的文章，往往比他们为其他人写作的文章更加华丽辞藻。他们追求一种他们认为教师想要的、并自认为“标准英语”的“文学”风格。但这种风格并非他们自身的一部分。而且，这种风格也未必是标准英语；学术界人士的写作和阅读也常常晦涩难懂、冗长繁复。学生应该学习一种简洁有力、朴实无华的散文，以此来表达他们对所处世界的思考。

Another powerful element in learning to write is motivation. Motivation is crucial to writing—students will write far more willingly if they write about subjects that interest them and that they have an aptitude for. But they don’t often get that chance; writing tends to be assigned only in subjects like English or history that are identified with writing.

学习写作的另一个重要因素是动机。动机对写作至关重要——如果学生写作的主题是他们感兴趣且擅长的领域，他们会更乐意写作。但他们往往没有这样的机会；写作作业通常只出现在英语或历史等与写作密切相关的学科中。

What also gets imparted in those classes is fear. The fear of writing is planted in countless people at an early age—often, ironically, by English teachers, who make science-minded kids feel stupid for not being “good at words,” just as science teachers make people like me feel stupid for not being good at science. Whichever our type, the loss of confidence stays with us for the rest of our lives.

这些课堂上还会灌输恐惧。无数人从小就被灌输写作恐惧——讽刺的是，这往往是英语老师造成的，他们让那些热爱科学的孩子觉得自己“不擅长文字”，就像科学老师让像我这样的人觉得自己不擅长科学一样。无论我们属于哪一类，这种自信心的丧失都会伴随我们一生。

Much of this fear could be eased if writing became a component of how these subjects are taught. A science-minded student, if he were encouraged to write about a scientific or technological subject, would soon find that he could do it. He would discover that writing is primarily an exercise in logic and that words are just tools designed to do a specific job. Similarly, the sciences could be demystified for liberal arts types like me. We could write our way into at least a partial understanding of many subjects whose language of numbers and symbols has scared us away.

如果写作成为这些学科教学的一部分，许多恐惧就能得到缓解。一个有科学头脑的学生，如果被鼓励去写一篇关于科学或技术主题的文章，很快就会发现自己也能做到。他会发现，写作本质上是一种逻辑练习，文字只是完成特定任务的工具。同样地，像我这样的文科生也能逐渐理解科学的奥秘。我们可以通过写作，至少部分地理解那些曾经让我们望而却步的数字和符号语言。

The hard part, as in swimming, is to take the plunge. The water looks so cold. Can it be warmed up? I think it can. The way to begin is with imitation.

就像游泳一样，最难的是迈出第一步。水看起来好冷啊。能加热吗？我觉得可以。最好的办法就是模仿。

We all need models, whatever art or craft we’re trying to learn. Bach needed a model; Picasso needed a model; they didn’t spring full-blown as Bach and Picasso. This is especially true of writers. Writing is learned by imitation. I learned to write mainly by reading writers who were doing the kind of writing I wanted to do and by trying to figure out how they did it. S. J. Perelman told me that when he was starting out he could have been arrested for imitating Ring Lardner. Woody Allen could have been arrested for imitating S. J. Perelman. And who hasn’t tried to imitate Woody Allen?

无论我们学习什么艺术或技艺，都需要榜样。巴赫需要榜样；毕加索也需要榜样；他们并非一蹴而就，成为巴赫和毕加索。这一点对作家来说尤其如此。写作是通过模仿学习的。我学习写作主要是通过阅读那些创作我理想作品的作家，并努力弄明白他们是如何做到的。S·J·佩雷尔曼告诉我，他刚开始写作时，如果模仿林·拉德纳，他可能会被逮捕。伍迪·艾伦如果模仿S·J·佩雷尔曼，也可能被逮捕。而谁又没尝试过模仿伍迪·艾伦呢？

Students often feel guilty about modeling their writing on someone else’s writing. They think it’s unethical—which is commendable. Or they’re afraid they’ll lose their own identity. The point, however, is that we eventually move beyond our models; we take what we need and then we shed those skins and become who we are supposed to become. But nobody will write well unless he gets into his ear and into his metabolism a sense of how the language works and what it can be made to do. That’s a fundamental premise of this book.

学生们常常会因为模仿他人的写作而感到内疚。他们认为这样做不道德——这种想法值得称赞。或者他们害怕失去自我。然而，关键在于，我们最终会超越模仿的对象；我们汲取所需，然后褪去旧有的外衣，成为我们注定要成为的人。但是，除非一个人真正理解语言的运作方式及其作用，否则他无法写出好文章。这正是本书的基本前提。

Another is that the essence of writing is rewriting. Very few writers say on their first try exactly what they want to say. Recently I got a form letter from my cable TV company saying, “Next month we will upgrade our phones, so it will be difficult to reach us.” A few days later I saw an interoffice memo from a supervisor requesting “a list of all employees broken down by sex.” Meaning is remarkably elusive. After a lifetime of writing I still revise every sentence many times and still worry that I haven’t caught every ambiguity; I don’t want anyone to have to read a sentence of mine twice to find out what it means. If you think you can dash something off and have it come out right, the people you’re trying to reach are almost surely in trouble. H. L. Mencken said that “0.8 percent of the human race is capable of writing something that is instantly understandable.” He may have been a little high. Beware of dashing. “Effortless” articles that look as if they were dashed off are the result of strenuous effort. A piece of writing must be viewed as a constantly evolving organism.

另一个原因是，写作的本质在于修改。很少有作家第一次就能准确地表达出自己想说的话。最近，我收到有线电视公司的一封格式化信函，上面写着：“下个月我们将升级电话，届时可能难以联系到我们。”几天后，我看到一位主管发来的内部备忘录，要求提供“所有员工按性别分类的名单”。意义真是难以捉摸。我写作一生，至今仍然会反复修改每个句子，仍然担心自己没有注意到任何歧义；我不希望任何人需要读两遍我写的句子才能明白它的意思。如果你认为可以随手写写就能写出正确无误的文章，那么你想要传达信息的人几乎肯定会遇到麻烦。H·L·门肯曾说过，“只有0.8%的人类能够写出让人一眼就能看懂的文章。”他可能有点夸张了。要警惕“速成”。那些看似“毫不费力”的文章，其实是付出巨大努力的结果。一篇文字作品必须被视为一个不断演变的有机体。

Curiously, this hasn’t been the prevailing theory in our schools. American children have long been taught to visualize a composition as a finished edifice, its topic sentences all in place, its spelling correct, its appearance tidy. Only lately has there been an important shift. The shift—in the terminology of the trade—is from “product” to “process.” It puts the emphasis where it should have been all along: on the successive rewritings and rethinkings that mold an act of writing into the best possible form. If the process is sound, the product will take care of itself.

奇怪的是，这并非我们学校的主流理论。长期以来，美国儿童被教导将作文想象成一座完工的建筑，主题句到位，拼写正确，外观整洁。直到最近，这种观念才发生了重要的转变。用专业术语来说，这种转变是从“产品”转向“过程”。它将重点放在了原本就应该关注的地方：反复修改和重新思考，最终将写作塑造成最佳形式。如果过程正确，产品自然会水到渠成。

Finally, in the national furor over “why Johnny can’t write,” let’s not forget to ask why Johnny also can’t learn. The two are connected. Writing organizes and clarifies our thoughts. Writing is how we think our way into a subject and make it our own. Writing enables us to find out what we know—and what we don’t know—about whatever we’re trying to learn. Putting an idea into written words is like defrosting the windshield: The idea, so vague out there in the murk, slowly begins to gather itself into a sensible shape. Whatever we write—a memo, a letter, a note to the baby-sitter—all of us know this moment of finding out what we really want to say by trying in writing to say it.

最后，在全国上下热议“为什么约翰尼不会写作”的时候，我们不妨也问问约翰尼为什么学不会。这两者是息息相关的。写作能够组织和理清我们的思路。写作是我们深入思考并形成自己理解的方式。写作使我们能够发现我们对所学内容的已知和未知。将想法诉诸笔端就像给挡风玻璃除霜：原本模糊不清的想法，在文字的引导下，逐渐清晰起来。无论我们写的是什么——备忘录、信件、给保姆的便条——我们都经历过这样的时刻：通过写作，我们最终找到了自己真正想表达的东西。

This was the aspect of “writing across the curriculum” that excited me most of all. It was an idea based on two principles: learning to write and writing to learn.

“跨学科写作”理念中最令我兴奋的一点就是这一点。它基于两个原则：学习写作和通过写作来学习。

St. Peter, Minnesota (pop. 9,000), is two hours south of Minneapolis, near the Iowa border, and Professor Gover drove me through flat and fertile country, its farms farther and farther apart. I wasn’t surprised that I was bound for a college that I had never heard of and that was in such an isolated place. In my travels I’ve found that the teaching of writing is taken more seriously at little-known colleges and universities than at the big and famous ones. Again and again, on campuses in Kentucky and Idaho and Indiana and Missouri and other states far from the Ivy League, I’ve met teachers deeply committed to the task of getting students to write well. The news out there is good.

明尼苏达州圣彼得市（人口9000）位于明尼阿波利斯以南两小时车程处，靠近爱荷华州边界。戈弗教授开车带我穿过平坦肥沃的乡村，农场之间的距离越来越远。我并不惊讶自己要去一所我从未听说过、而且地处偏僻的大学。在我的旅途中，我发现那些名不见经传的大学比那些名牌大学更重视写作教学。在肯塔基州、爱达荷州、印第安纳州、密苏里州以及其他远离常春藤盟校的州的校园里，我一次又一次地遇到那些全身心投入到帮助学生提高写作能力的老师。那里的写作氛围令人欣喜。

Professor Gover explained that he had been chairman of the committee that was putting writing into—and across—the curriculum at Gustavus Adolphus. I asked him how the idea took root.

戈弗教授解释说，他曾担任古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院课程改革委员会的主席，该委员会负责将写作纳入并贯穿整个课程体系。我问他这个想法是如何产生的。

“Over the years,” he said, “our faculty did a lot of good-natured berating of the English department: ‘Why can’t you teach these students to write?’ The English teachers said, ‘They write well for us, but in your classes they don’t have that expectation—students don’t think of writing as being any part of your courses.’ Of course that was true, and what it stemmed from was a lifelong sense of inadequacy on our part. Those of us who teach science and other technical subjects have always felt insecure about writing. It’s not that we felt stupid—we knew that we could deal well with ideas and that we understood our discipline. But somehow when it came to putting words on paper it never came out right, and we heard about it, usually from our grade school or high school English teacher. It’s like the math anxiety you see in people who don’t have a bent for mathematics.

“这些年来，”他说，“我们系的老师们经常善意地批评英语系：‘你们为什么教不好这些学生写作？’英语老师们则说：‘他们在我们这儿写得很好，但在你们的课上，学生们并没有这样的期望——他们根本不把写作当成你们课程的一部分。’当然，这话没错，而这源于我们自身长久以来的写作能力不足感。我们这些教科学和其他技术类学科的老师，总是对写作缺乏自信。倒不是我们觉得自己笨——我们知道自己能很好地处理各种想法，也了解自己的学科。但不知为何，一旦要把文字写在纸上，就总是写不好，而且我们经常听到别人批评我们，通常是来自我们的小学或中学英语老师。这就像那些对数学没有天赋的人会有的数学焦虑一样。”

“What we found developing at Gustavus Adolphus was a sense that we should all be sharing the responsibility for teaching writing. We formed a writing committee that consisted of professors from many different disciplines, and we invited proposals for ‘W’ courses from the entire faculty. The response was instantaneous. As soon as the ownership of writing by the English department was lost, people in other fields said, ‘I’d be willing to give it a try.’ The procedure is that they have to submit a proposal and the writing committee has to approve it. To help them we’re bringing in outside experts to give workshops in how to teach writing. One reason for the high response is that everything is voluntary. If the program had been imposed by the administration I don’t think it would work.”

我们在古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院发现，大家逐渐意识到应该共同承担写作教学的责任。我们成立了一个由不同学科教授组成的写作委员会，并向全体教职工征集“W”课程提案。反响立竿见影。一旦英语系不再垄断写作教学，其他领域的教师纷纷表示：“我愿意尝试一下。” 流程是，他们必须提交提案，并由写作委员会批准。为了帮助他们，我们邀请校外专家举办写作教学研讨会。反响热烈的原因之一是所有活动都是自愿的。如果这个项目是由校方强制推行，我认为它不会成功。

I asked Professor Gover what his own discipline was. He said he was a professor of chemistry. Chemistry! A whiff of sulfur from Mrs. Boyden’s class flew in the car window. Of all subjects, why did that have to be the one he was a professor of? Surely there was no way to write about chemistry. I asked him how he would adapt writing to his subject. He said he was going to teach a course called “Chemical Discoveries That Changed the World” and get his students to write papers about them. I liked the title of the course and the idea of changing the world. I asked him what some of the discoveries were.

我问戈弗教授他自己的专业是什么。他说他是化学教授。化学！博伊登太太班上飘来的硫磺味儿扑面而来，钻进了车窗。那么多科目，为什么偏偏是化学？化学肯定没法写文章。我问他打算怎么把写作融入到他的学科里。他说他要开一门叫“改变世界的化学发现”的课，让学生们写论文。我很喜欢这门课的名字，也喜欢“改变世界”这个理念。我问他有哪些发现。

“One was the synthesizing of urea by a German chemist named Friedrich Wöhler in 1828,” he said. “It was the first time man had made an organic compound, which had always been considered God’s work, and the discovery touched off intense debates about theology and philosophy all across Europe for many years. It shook the foundations of faith.”

“其中一项是德国化学家弗里德里希·维勒于1828年合成尿素，”他说。“这是人类首次合成有机化合物，而有机化合物一直被认为是上帝的杰作。这一发现引发了欧洲各地长达数年的关于神学和哲学的激烈辩论，动摇了信仰的根基。”

Of course I didn’t even know what urea was. Professor Gover told me it was the chief solid component of urine. I also didn’t know that urine had a solid component. But what I did suddenly know was that this was a chemical achievement that went far beyond the chemistry lab.

当然，我当时根本不知道尿素是什么。戈弗教授告诉我，它是尿液的主要固体成分。我也不知道尿液里还有固体成分。但我突然意识到，这是一项意义远超化学实验室范畴的化学成就。

Another discovery that Professor Gover said he would include was the formulation of the periodic table of the elements. I asked him what there was to discover; didn’t the elements already exist? They existed, he said, but there was no organized way of thinking about them or knowing about their affinities to one other. He told me about the Russian chemist D. I. Mendeleyev, who noticed that certain properties of the elements recurred periodically when he arranged them according to their atomic number. From that observation, in 1869, he proposed the periodic law—one of the cornerstones of modern chemistry—and devised the famous chart that puts elements with similar properties in easily identified groups and alignments.

戈弗教授说，他还会介绍另一项发现——元素周期表的制定。我问他，这有什么可发现的？元素不是早就存在了吗？他说，元素确实存在，但当时并没有系统地研究它们或了解它们之间的关系的方法。他给我讲了俄国化学家门捷列夫的故事。门捷列夫注意到，当他按照原子序数排列元素时，某些性质会周期性地重复出现。基于这一观察，他在1869年提出了元素周期律——现代化学的基石之一——并设计了著名的元素周期表，将性质相似的元素归入易于识别的组和排列中。

As Professor Gover described how Mendeleyev juggled the elements into a coherent system, leaving blanks for elements that hadn’t yet been discovered but whose properties he could predict, the periodic table which had intimidated me at Deerfield took on the excitement of a puzzle and a chase. If Mrs. Boyden had asked me to write a paper about Mendeleyev’s search for order in the elemental soup, or about the spiritual agony that Wöhler caused by playing God, I might have been drawn into the history and romance of the subject and lost some of my fear. Now, listening to Thomas Gover’s tales of Wöhler and Mendeleyev and other chemists who journeyed into the unknown, I thought, “What an interesting subject!”—no small thought for someone with chemistry anxiety. Then I thought: Probably every subject is interesting if an avenue into it can be found that has humanity and that an ordinary person can follow. Writing was such an avenue—perhaps, in fact, the main route.

当戈弗教授讲述门捷列夫如何将各种元素巧妙地组合成一个连贯的体系，并预留出空白处来表示那些尚未发现但性质可预测的元素时，曾经令我在迪尔菲尔德感到畏惧的元素周期表，此刻却充满了解谜和探索的乐趣。如果博伊登夫人让我写一篇关于门捷列夫在元素汤中寻找秩序的论文，或者一篇关于沃勒扮演上帝角色所造成的精神折磨的论文，我或许会被这门学科的历史和浪漫情怀所吸引，从而减轻一些恐惧。现在，听着托马斯·戈弗讲述沃勒、门捷列夫以及其他探索未知领域的化学家的故事，我不禁心想：“这真是一个有趣的课题！”——对于一个对化学感到焦虑的人来说，这可不是一件小事。然后我想：或许，只要能找到一条充满人文关怀、普通人也能理解的途径，任何学科都会变得有趣。写作就是这样一条途径——或许，它才是通往这条途径的主要路径。

Actually I was far readier to think this thought than I would have been ten or fifteen years earlier. The difference was that many scientists have recently begun to write about their fields in language that is not only clear but often eloquent. One of them is the biologist Lewis Thomas, whose books, Lives of a Cell and The Medusa and the Snail , vividly proved that a scientist can also be a humanist. Another is the paleontologist Stephen Jay Gould. In his monthly column in Natural History magazine and in books like The Panda’s Thumb I’ve found myself caught up in the riddles of evolution and the miracles of the natural world. Gould never forgets one of nature’s oldest laws: that everybody loves a story. Every month he tells me a remarkable story and then tells me why he thinks it came out the way it did.

事实上，我比十年前或十五年前更容易接受这种观点。不同之处在于，许多科学家近来开始用清晰易懂且往往文笔优美的语言撰写各自领域的研究成果。其中一位是生物学家路易斯·托马斯，他的著作《细胞的生命》和《美杜莎与蜗牛》生动地证明了科学家也可以是人文主义者。另一位是古生物学家斯蒂芬·杰伊·古尔德。在他的《自然历史》杂志月度专栏以及《熊猫的拇指》等著作中，我常常被进化之谜和自然界的奇迹所吸引。古尔德始终铭记自然界最古老的法则之一：人人都爱听故事。每个月他都会给我讲一个精彩的故事，然后解释他认为故事最终呈现出这种面貌的原因。

Another scientist-writer is Paul Davies, author of The Edge of Infinity , whose latest book announced by the boldness of its title, God and the New Physics , that it would jump into spiritual waters where men of science have seldom deigned to go. As Davies says in his introduction, the new physicists have “had to learn to approach their subject in totally unexpected and novel ways that seemed to turn common sense on its head and find closer accord with mysticism than materialism. The fruits of this revolution are only now starting to be plucked by philosophers and theologians [and are] even finding sympathy with psychologists and sociologists, especially those who advocate a holistic approach.” Davies’s book opens almost as many cans of worms for philosophers and theologians as Wöhler did with his synthesized urea.

另一位科学家兼作家是保罗·戴维斯，他是《无限的边缘》一书的作者。他的最新著作《上帝与新物理学》以其大胆的书名宣告，这本书将涉足科学家鲜少涉足的精神领域。正如戴维斯在引言中所说，新物理学家“不得不学习以完全出乎意料的新颖方式来研究他们的课题，这种方式似乎颠覆了常识，并且与神秘主义而非唯物主义更为契合。这场革命的成果如今才开始被哲学家和神学家们采纳，甚至也得到了心理学家和社会学家的认同，尤其是那些倡导整体论方法的人。”戴维斯的这本书给哲学家和神学家们带来的争议，几乎与沃勒合成尿素引发的争议一样多。

Thomas and Gould and Davies belong to a new breed of scientists who don’t consider it demeaning to write for the layman and who will even admit that science doesn’t know all the answers. That this historic gap between science and the humanities was closing I first noticed after I went to work for the Book-of-the-Month Club in 1979—another chapter in my continuing education. At that time the Club’s members were still united in their dread of science; they would only take a science book if it came cloaked in romance (archaeology) or adventure (Thor Heyerdahl’s Kon-Tiki ) or some other humanistic garb. As long as science was disguised as a colorful yarn—grave robbers in the Valley of the Kings, explorers on rafts retracing the Polynesian migrations—readers didn’t have to tax their liberal arts brain.

托马斯、古尔德和戴维斯属于新一代科学家，他们不认为为普通读者写作是一种贬低，甚至会承认科学并非无所不知。我最早注意到科学与人文之间这条历史鸿沟正在缩小，是在1979年加入“每月一书俱乐部”之后——这又是我继续教育生涯中的又一个篇章。当时，俱乐部成员仍然对科学抱有强烈的恐惧；他们只会阅读披着浪漫（考古学）、冒险（索尔·海尔达尔的《康提基号》）或其他人文主义外衣的科学书籍。只要科学被伪装成引人入胜的故事——比如帝王谷的盗墓贼、乘筏探险重走波利尼西亚人迁徙路线的探险家——读者就无需动用他们那文科生的脑力。

But in the early 1980s a new generation of readers came of age who didn’t want to be coddled. Educated by the ecology movement and threatened by nuclear technology, they were eager to know more about chemistry and physics to protect themselves and their habitat. The result is that today there’s hardly a subject so cerebral or abstruse, from quantum mechanics to quarks, that Book-of-the-Month Club members won’t give it a try. One of their favorite writers is Douglas R. Hofstadter, whose ten-year-old Gödel, Escher, Bach shows few signs of fatigue. Several years ago the Club, not even blinking at the title, offered his Metamagical Themas: Questing for the Essence of Mind and Pattern , which ponders such imponderables as the nature of human creativity and the limits of artificial intelligence.

但在20世纪80年代初，新一代读者成长起来，他们不再满足于娇惯。在生态运动的熏陶下，又受到核技术的威胁，他们渴望了解更多化学和物理知识，以保护自身及其栖息地。因此，如今几乎没有哪个学科，从量子力学到夸克，是“每月一书俱乐部”成员不愿尝试的。他们最喜欢的作家之一是道格拉斯·R·霍夫施塔特，他十年前出版的《哥德尔、埃舍尔、巴赫》至今仍经久不衰。几年前，“每月一书俱乐部”甚至对这个书名都毫不犹豫地推荐了他的《元魔法主题：探寻心灵与模式的本质》，这本书探讨了诸如人类创造力的本质和人工智能的局限性等难以捉摸的问题。

Impressed by those brain signals from its science-minded members, the Club sent them a questionnaire in 1986 to find out what their primary field of interest was. It listed twenty fields and asked them to choose only one. They wrote back and said they couldn’t. What they were saying was that although they are scientifically inclined, they are generalists, as interested in astronomy and mathematics and evolution as they are in physics and the genetic code and the processes of life.

俱乐部对这些具有科学思维的成员们所展现出的思维方式印象深刻，于是在1986年向他们寄送了一份问卷，以了解他们的主要兴趣领域。问卷列出了二十个领域，并要求他们从中选择一个。他们回复说无法做出选择。他们的意思是，尽管他们倾向于科学，但他们是通才，对天文学、数学和进化论的兴趣丝毫不亚于物理学、遗传密码和生命过程。

Watching this trend, I realized that people are no longer so imprisoned by the notion that some subjects are “too hard.” Even I was less fearful; because of writers like Lewis Thomas I’ve begun to feel a little less dumb. But it’s also a little late. I would rather have started getting smart earlier, and that’s what I’d like for everybody else—a long acquaintance with the major branches of learning.

观察这种趋势，我意识到人们不再那么执着于“某些科目太难”这种观念。就连我自己也不再那么害怕了；多亏了像路易斯·托马斯这样的作家，我开始觉得自己没那么笨了。但这一切似乎也有些晚了。我宁愿早点开始学习，我也希望其他人都能如此——对各大学科有更深入的了解。

By “major branches” I mean a far broader kaleidoscope than I’ve been talking about here. I’ve singled out the humanities and the sciences because they are regarded as natural opposites, even natural enemies. But this is oversimplifying to make a point. Between English at one end of the spectrum and chemistry at the other are many subjects, like economics, that are a mystery to both camps. Some people would say that economics is also a mystery to the economists. But none of us would deny that economics has a tighter grip on our daily lives than English or chemistry. Shouldn’t we know more about its theories and applications? And how about all those other subjects: anthropology, engineering, mathematics, philosophy, political science, psychology, religion, sociology? What can they tell us about how we behave, build, think, govern ourselves and grope for values to live by?

我所说的“主要分支”远比我在这里讨论的要广泛得多。我之所以单独提及人文科学和自然科学，是因为它们被视为天然的对立面，甚至是天然的敌人。但这只是为了说明一个问题而做的简化。在人文科学和自然科学这两个极端之间，还有许多学科，比如经济学，对这两个群体来说都是一个谜。有些人甚至会说，经济学对经济学家来说也是一个谜。但我们谁也不会否认，经济学对我们日常生活的影响比英语或化学要深远得多。难道我们不应该更多地了解它的理论和应用吗？还有那些其他的学科：人类学、工程学、数学、哲学、政治学、心理学、宗教、社会学等等。它们能告诉我们什么关于我们如何行为、如何建设、如何思考、如何治理自身以及如何寻找人生价值观的信息呢？

They can tell us as much as we want to know. Probably no subject is too hard if people take the trouble to think and write and read clearly. Maybe, in fact, it’s time to redefine the “three R’s”—they should be reading, ’riting and reasoning. Together they add up to learning. It’s by writing about a subject we’re trying to learn that we reason our way to what it means. Reasoning is a lost skill of the children of the TV generation, with their famously short attention span. Writing can help them get it back.

他们能告诉我们所有我们想知道的事情。如果人们愿意认真思考、写作和阅读，或许没有什么科目是太难的。事实上，也许是时候重新定义“三R”了——它们应该是阅读、写作和推理。这三者结合起来才算学习。正是通过写作，我们才能理解我们正在学习的科目，并运用推理能力去理解它的含义。对于电视一代的孩子来说，推理能力已经逐渐丧失，他们的注意力也出了名的短暂。写作可以帮助他们重拾这项技能。

One thing I like about driving into a small college town is that I almost always know where I’ll find the college: on high ground. If the town has a hill of any kind, that’s where the founders chose to build, as if to proclaim through topography that learning is an elevated pursuit. Gustavus Adolphus was a Lutheran version of that ideal. Behind the short and resolutely flat Main Street of St. Peter, with its feed stores and savings associations, the side streets sloped upward for four or five blocks and at the summit I caught a glimpse of the clock tower on what I knew would turn out to be a stately mid-nineteenth-century stone building with a name like Old North. The educational verities were intact.

我喜欢开车去小型大学城的一点是，我几乎总能找到大学的位置：地势较高的地方。如果镇上有任何山丘，那一定是建校者们选择的地方，仿佛要通过地形来宣告学习是一项崇高的事业。古斯塔夫·阿道夫大学就是路德教版的这一理想。圣彼得镇的主街短而平坦，两侧林立着饲料店和储蓄协会，而小街则向上延伸四五个街区，在山顶，我瞥见了钟楼，我知道那将是一座庄严的十九世纪中期石砌建筑，名字大概叫“老北楼”。教育的真谛依然清晰可见。

At the college I spent two days talking with professors who would be teaching “W” courses in the fall. Their disciplines covered the gamut of a liberal education—everything from art history and computer science and engineering to ethics and philosophy and theater. All of them were excited at the prospect of making writing a component of their course. But they still didn’t quite know how they were going to do it. We discussed possible approaches, and I mentioned how strongly I believe that writers learn by imitation. I asked the professors if they knew any examples of what they considered good writing in their field. They all did. A professor of mathematics said she knew of many elegant proofs. Two physics professors said that Einstein’s theory of relativity was a marvel of lucid exposition. Other professors recalled other models they admired.

在大学里，我花了整整两天时间与几位秋季即将开设“W”课程的教授们交流。他们的学科涵盖了博雅教育的各个领域——从艺术史、计算机科学和工程学到伦理学、哲学和戏剧，无所不包。他们都对将写作融入课程感到兴奋不已，但对于如何具体实施写作，他们仍然不太清楚。我们探讨了各种可能的方法，我提到我坚信作家是通过模仿来学习的。我问教授们是否了解各自领域中他们认为优秀的写作范例。他们都给出了答案。一位数学教授说她知道许多优美的证明。两位物理学教授说爱因斯坦的相对论是清晰阐述的典范。其他教授也回忆起他们欣赏的其他模型。

I urged them to make copies of those models for their students. Writing, I reminded them, can’t be taught or learned in a vacuum. We must say to students in every area of knowledge: “This is how other people have written about this subject. Read it; study it; think about it. You can do it too.” In many subjects, students don’t even know that a literature exists—that mathematics, for instance, consists of more than right and wrong answers, that physics consists of more than right or wrong lab reports.

我敦促他们为学生复印这些范例。我提醒他们，写作不能脱离实际环境进行教授或学习。我们必须告诉各个领域的学生：“其他人就是这样写这个主题的。阅读它；研究它；思考它。你们也能做到。”在许多学科中，学生甚至不知道文献的存在——例如，数学不仅仅包含对错答案，物理学也不仅仅包含实验报告的对错。

I wondered if it would be possible to go in search of the literature: to collect models of good, clear writing in different fields and put them in a book. The book would be an informal guided tour for teachers and students required to write about subjects they had never thought of writing about before. At the very least it would take some of the fear out of the writing and learning process. I also thought it would demonstrate that however disparate the fields, the same principles of good writing would apply to them all. Well-written chemistry would be achieved with the same tools as well-written art history.

我当时就在想，是否可以去搜集不同领域的优秀、清晰的写作范例，并将它们汇编成书。这本书将为那些需要撰写他们从未想过要写的主题的教师和学生提供一份非正式的指导。至少，它能减轻他们对写作和学习过程的恐惧。我还认为，这本书能够证明，无论领域多么迥异，优秀的写作原则都是相通的。写出一篇优秀的化学论文和写出一篇优秀的艺术史论文，都需要运用相同的写作技巧。

All that remained was to write my book. I told the professors at Gustavus Adolphus that I would come back at the end of the fall term and see how they had made out.

剩下的就是写我的书了。我告诉古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院的教授们，秋季学期末我会回来看看他们的进展如何。

# ↩

3. A Liberal Education

3. 博雅教育

I didn’t know where my search for the literature would end, but I had no trouble deciding where it should begin. My thoughts went back to the period of my life that had been the most broadly educational of all—the decade I spent at Yale. Two jobs that I held there put me in touch with the community of knowledge at its most liberal.

我不知道我的文献搜寻最终会走向何方，但我毫不犹豫地决定了它的起点。我的思绪回到了我人生中最具教育意义的时期——我在耶鲁大学度过的十年。我在那里从事的两份工作让我接触到了最开放包容的知识社群。

My reason for moving to Yale in 1970 was to teach nonfiction writing. I had never seen Yale before and knew nothing of its traditions except that the bulldog was its mascot and the Whiffenpoofs sang at a place called Mory’s, possibly on the tables. I was a fourth-generation New Yorker and had never lived anywhere else. That’s also where I had had my career: thirteen years as an editor and a writer with the New York Herald Tribune and eleven more as a free-lance writer. Those last eleven years, working alone at home, made me desperate for human contact. Whatever Yale had to offer, I was ready.

1970年我搬到耶鲁是为了教非虚构写作。在此之前，我从未到过耶鲁，对它的传统也一无所知，只知道斗牛犬是它的吉祥物，惠芬普夫合唱团会在一家叫莫里餐厅的地方唱歌，说不定还会在桌子上唱歌。我是土生土长的纽约人，家族在纽约已经生活了四代，从未在其他地方居住过。我的职业生涯也一直在那里：在《纽约先驱论坛报》做了十三年的编辑和撰稿人，之后又做了十一年的自由撰稿人。最后那十一年，独自在家工作，让我渴望与人交往。无论耶鲁能给我带来什么，我都准备好了。

Hardly had I unpacked my bags and my children when I got a call from the chairman of the board of the Yale Alumni Magazine . A sudden domestic crisis, he said, had left the magazine without an editor. He explained that the magazine had a circulation of more than 100,000 and that it went to all the alumni of Yale College and its nine graduate schools, which included schools of art, architecture, divinity, drama, forestry and environmental studies, law, medicine, music and nursing. Would I like to be the editor?

我刚安顿好行李和孩子，就接到了耶鲁校友杂志董事会主席的电话。他说，突如其来的家庭危机导致杂志社没有编辑。他解释说，这份杂志发行量超过十万份，面向耶鲁学院及其九个研究生院的所有校友，这些研究生院包括艺术学院、建筑学院、神学院、戏剧学院、林业与环境研究学院、法学院、医学院、音乐学院和护理学院。他问我是否愿意担任编辑。

At first I thought it was an absurd thing for a middle-aged Princeton man to do. But luckily I had a second thought: What quicker way to get to know a great university? Editors are licensed to be curious. Besides, I enjoyed editing more than writing. I liked thinking of story ideas; I liked working with writers and helping them to present their writing at its strongest, and I especially liked the element of surprise: Every day an editor learns something new. I signed up for the job and did it for seven years.

起初，我觉得一个普林斯顿的中年男人做这件事简直荒谬。但幸运的是，我转念一想：还有什么比这更能快速了解一所伟大的大学呢？编辑的职责就是保持好奇心。而且，我喜欢编辑胜过写作。我喜欢构思故事创意；我喜欢与作者合作，帮助他们以最佳状态呈现作品；我尤其喜欢其中的惊喜元素：编辑每天都能学到新东西。我接受了这份工作，并且做了七年。

I never stopped to ask, “Who is the typical Yale alumnus? Who am I editing for?” One of my principles is that there is no typical anybody; every reader is different. I edit for myself and I write for myself. I assume that if I consider something interesting or funny, a certain number of other people will too. If they don’t, they have two inalienable rights—they can fire the editor and they can stop reading the writer. Meanwhile I draw on two sources of energy that I commend to anyone trying to survive in this vulnerable craft: confidence and ego. If you don’t have confidence in what you’re doing you might as well not do it.

我从未停下来问过自己：“典型的耶鲁校友是什么样的人？我的编辑对象是谁？”我的原则之一是，根本不存在所谓的“典型”人；每个读者都独一无二。我为自己编辑，也为自己写作。我假设，如果我觉得某件事有趣或好笑，那么其他人也会有同样的感受。如果他们不这么认为，他们拥有两项不可剥夺的权利——他们可以解雇编辑，也可以停止阅读这位作者的作品。与此同时，我依靠两种能量来源，我向所有试图在这个充满挑战的行业中生存的人推荐这两种能量来源：自信和自负。如果你对自己所做的事情没有信心，那还不如不做。

As editor of Yale’s magazine I took the whole university as my domain. I wanted to know what was new in every discipline and what scholars were up to in every cranny of the campus. Yale seemed to have no end, for instance, of collections that were unique: silver and textiles, Babylonian tablets and Tibetan sacred texts, Boswell papers and Franklin papers, manuscripts of Charles Lindbergh and Gertrude Stein. In 1972 I noticed that the Western History Association would be holding its annual meeting in New Haven. Why New Haven? It turned out that one of Yale’s professors, Howard R. Lamar, was an eminent Western scholar. I asked him for an article explaining why the Western historians, who had never met east of the Mississippi before, were coming East now.

作为耶鲁大学杂志的编辑，我将整个大学视为我的领地。我渴望了解每个学科的最新进展，以及学者们在校园的每个角落里都在忙些什么。例如，耶鲁大学似乎拥有无穷无尽的独特藏品：银器和纺织品、巴比伦泥板和西藏圣典、博斯韦尔手稿和富兰克林手稿、查尔斯·林白和格特鲁德·斯坦的手稿。1972年，我注意到西部历史协会将在纽黑文举行年会。为什么是纽黑文？原来，耶鲁大学的一位教授霍华德·R·拉马尔是一位杰出的西部历史学者。我请他撰写一篇文章，解释为什么这些此前从未在密西西比河以东地区会面的西部历史学家们现在要齐聚东部。

“In the 1940s Yale filed a claim to much of the history of the trans-Mississippi West,” he wrote, “by acquiring the libraries—books, maps, manuscripts, newspapers and paintings—of six great collectors of Western Americana. Put together under one roof, they have made [Yale’s] Beinecke Library a rendezvous for students of the West and prompted a course on the history of the West that I have been teaching for twenty-one years.” But what most excited Professor Lamar was how “the field of Western history has taken on new dimensions and totally new meanings for the student and the public. The Old West, romantic and heroic, has in two decades become the area that epitomizes the most basic questions facing America today.” His article went on to describe how some of the most entrenched American attitudes—toward Indians, toward Mexican-Americans, toward Western heroes, toward the role of pioneer women and families, toward nature and land and water—had changed almost overnight. That was news to me; my clock was still set to John Wayne and Billy the Kid.

“上世纪40年代，耶鲁大学通过收购六位伟大的西部美国史收藏家的藏书——书籍、地图、手稿、报纸和绘画——从而对密西西比河以西的大部分历史提出了所有权主张，”他写道，“这些藏品汇集于一处，使耶鲁大学的拜内克图书馆成为西部史研究者的聚集地，并促成了我教授了21年的西部史课程。” 但最令拉马尔教授兴奋的是，“西部史领域对学生和公众而言呈现出新的维度和全新的意义。浪漫而英雄主义的旧西部，在短短二十年间，已成为当今美国面临的最基本问题的缩影。” 他的文章继续描述了一些根深蒂固的美国人态度——对印第安人、墨西哥裔美国人、西部英雄、拓荒女性和家庭的角色、以及对自然、土地和水的态度——几乎在一夜之间发生了改变。这对我来说是全新的发现；我的时钟还定在播放《约翰·韦恩和比利小子》的时候。

Or—to go from land to spirit—here’s a piece that originated in the Yale Divinity School. I noticed that the school had on its faculty a Benedictine monk named Aidan Kavanagh, who was a professor of liturgics. Could he explain what a professor of liturgics did? His article met my question head-on in this wonderful paragraph:

或者——从物质层面转向精神层面——这里有一篇源自耶鲁神学院的文章。我注意到该学院有一位名叫艾丹·卡瓦纳的本笃会修士，他是礼仪学教授。他能否解释一下礼仪学教授的工作内容？他的文章中有一个精彩的段落，直接回答了我的问题：

No one can teach wisdom, least of all I. But what I can do in my own field of liturgical scholarship is to engage my students in an environment of facts, method and perspective in which wisdom may be learned by us all. In this regard my peculiar field is rich. What we study, ultimately, is not texts but the ways in which people from time out of mind have regularly come together to express those values that they have found to serve them best in their own struggle to survive. I shall never live forever if I cannot make it through tomorrow morning. The strategic end is born in the tactics with which it is pursued. Little things like salt, smells, oil, bread and wine, singing and seed, dancing, laughter and tears, bodies and babies, and even thoughts and words form the tactical fabric of survival with which a liturgical scholar must deal.

没有人能传授智慧，我更是如此。但我能在我所处的礼仪研究领域，为我的学生营造一个充满事实、方法和视角的环境，在这个环境中，我们所有人都能学习到智慧。就此而言，我所研究的领域十分丰富。我们最终研究的并非文本，而是自古以来人们如何聚集在一起，表达那些在生存斗争中对他们最有益的价值观。如果我无法熬过明天，我就无法永生。战略目标源于实现目标的策略。诸如盐、气味、油、面包和酒、歌唱和种子、舞蹈、欢笑和泪水、身体和婴儿，甚至思想和语言等细微之处，构成了礼仪学者必须面对的生存策略。

On another occasion I arranged for an interview with Bert Waterman, Yale’s highly respected wrestling coach. He mentioned that one of his wrestlers, Michael Poliakoff, was a classics major who was writing his senior thesis on combative sport in the ancient world; during his summer vacation he had toured the museums of England, Italy and Greece to look for classical Greek vase paintings that matched the descriptions of sport he had encountered in his classical reading. How could I get so lucky as an editor? I asked Mike Poliakoff about his search. “I chose this topic,” he said, “because it’s a significant gap in our knowledge of antiquity, though these sports, especially wrestling, permeated every aspect of Greek life.” He showed me some photographs he had taken of vases, cups, coins and sculptures, made between 550 B.C . and 430 B.C ., which depicted wrestlers and referees in positions that haven’t changed since. We made a layout to accompany the interview and he wrote the captions. This was one of them:

另一次，我安排了一次对耶鲁大学备受尊敬的摔跤教练伯特·沃特曼的采访。他提到，他的一名摔跤队员迈克尔·波利亚科夫主修古典学，正在撰写关于古代世界搏击运动的毕业论文；暑假期间，他游历了英国、意大利和希腊的博物馆，寻找与他在古典文献中读到的运动描述相符的古希腊陶瓶绘画。作为一名编辑，我怎么会有这么好的运气？我问迈克·波利亚科夫他的研究方向。“我选择这个主题，”他说，“是因为这是我们对古代了解的一个重大空白，尽管这些运动，尤其是摔跤，渗透到古希腊生活的方方面面。”他给我看了一些他拍摄的陶瓶、杯子、硬币和雕塑的照片，这些器物制作于公元前550年至公元前430年间，上面描绘的摔跤手和裁判的姿势自那时起就未曾改变。我们为采访制作了配图，他负责撰写图注。这是其中一张：

A black-figure neck amphora of the Leagros group of Attic pottery, 520-510 B.C . The triumph of civilization over barbarism is represented as Hercules, with utmost skill and grace, defeats the giant Antaeus while the goddess Athena and the god Hermes oversee the contest. Hercules is using a “front chancery,” a move popular on the Yale wrestling team today.

一件公元前520-510年阿提卡陶器莱阿格罗斯组黑绘颈瓶。瓶身描绘了文明战胜野蛮的场景：赫拉克勒斯以精湛的技艺和优雅的姿态击败巨人安泰俄斯，女神雅典娜和赫尔墨斯在一旁观战。赫拉克勒斯使用的“前手投掷”动作，如今在耶鲁大学摔跤队中十分流行。

Those are just three articles recalled at random from several hundred that popped up in various corners of the university. Most of them were about teaching and learning and research; many were about culture, the arts, libraries and special collections; quite a few were about sports, student attitudes and social change. But all of them delighted me with their unexpectedness and their information. They also taught me a lesson about the integration of knowledge: Separate disciplines are seldom separate. Beyond that, I confirmed what I had always believed about my craft—that there’s no subject that can’t be made accessible in good English with careful writing and editing.

这只是我从大学各个角落偶然发现的数百篇文章中随机挑选出来的三篇。它们大多与教学、学习和研究有关；许多涉及文化、艺术、图书馆和特藏；还有不少是关于体育、学生态度和社会变革的。但所有这些文章都以其出人意料的内容和丰富的信息令我惊喜。它们也让我明白了知识整合的真谛：看似独立的学科之间往往并非泾渭分明。除此之外，我还印证了我一直以来对写作的信念——只要用心写作和编辑，任何主题都能用流畅易懂的英语呈现出来。

My education quickened in 1973 when I was appointed master of Branford College, one of Yale’s twelve undergraduate residential colleges. Every college has a resident master, who presides over its life as an academic and social community. More than a hundred Fellows are also affiliated with each college—professors, deans, research scientists, librarians and other scholars drawn from every discipline and graduate school. One whom I recall with particular affection was the late Aleksis Rannit, an Estonian poet widely honored in Europe. As a postwar emigré in the United States he had become a librarian and was now curator of the Yale’s rich Slavic and East European collections. I once asked him if he would talk at one of the weekly master’s teas that I held to expose students to people I admired whom they wouldn’t ordinarily meet. I wanted him to talk about his past and to read some of his poems.

1973年，我被任命为耶鲁大学十二所本科住宿学院之一——布兰福德学院的院长，我的求学之路也由此加速。每所学院都有一位常驻院长，负责管理学院的学术和社交生活。此外，每所学院还拥有一百多位研究员——他们来自各个学科和研究生院，包括教授、院长、科研人员、图书馆员和其他学者。我尤其怀念已故的爱沙尼亚诗人阿列克西斯·兰尼特，他在欧洲享有盛誉。战后，他移居美国，成为一名图书馆员，并担任耶鲁大学丰富的斯拉夫和东欧藏书的馆长。我曾邀请他参加我每周举办的院长茶话会，旨在让学生们有机会接触到我所敬仰的、他们平时难得一见的人物。我希望他能谈谈自己的过往，并朗诵他的一些诗作。

I still remember that afternoon for three reasons. One was the broad humanistic canvas of his life in prewar Europe. He seemed to have known every artist and writer who was working on some frontier of creativity. (The painter Georges Braque was a typical frontiersman.) I also remember that when I asked him to conclude the afternoon by reading from a volume of his poems, he stood up. Homage to the poem; the rest had been mere reminiscence. But what I remember most was the beauty of the poetry itself. Estonian is a tonal language with an unusual structure of extended beats, and none of us had ever heard it before. But it needed no translating; if Aleksis announced that the next poem was about a lake in winter, we saw the dead leaves on the ice and felt the chill. We were in the presence of a miracle: the ability of poetry to transcend the language it’s written in. The words became music and carried the same kind of emotional weight.

我至今仍记得那个下午，原因有三。其一是他描绘的战前欧洲的人文主义人生画卷。他似乎认识所有在创意前沿领域耕耘的艺术家和作家。（画家乔治·布拉克就是一位典型的先锋人物。）我还记得，当我请他朗诵他的诗集作为下午的总结时，他站了起来。这是对诗歌的致敬；其余的都只是回忆而已。但我印象最深刻的是诗歌本身的美。爱沙尼亚语是一种声调语言，有着独特的延音结构，我们之前从未听过。但它无需翻译；如果阿列克西斯宣布下一首诗是关于冬日的湖泊，我们仿佛看到了冰面上的枯叶，感受到了寒意。我们见证了一个奇迹：诗歌超越语言本身的力量。文字化作音乐，承载着同样的情感分量。

But the Fellow who most nourished me with the inclusiveness of his mind was Willie Ruff, professor of music and of Afro-American studies. A black jazz bassist and French-horn player, Ruff also lived in Branford College and thrived on the ideas that circulated there. One Fellow whose research interested him was Dr. Gilbert H. Glaser, professor of neurology at the Yale School of Medicine and an authority on epilepsy. Ruff had long wanted to know more about rhythm than he knew from the lifelong practice of his art, and he thought Dr. Glaser might lead him to some answers. He proposed that Branford College originate and cosponsor with the Yale School of Medicine and the Yale School of Music a three-day symposium at which “the best minds in other disciplines would talk about how rhythm is at work in what they do.”

但最令我受益匪浅的，是音乐和非裔美国人研究教授威利·拉夫（Willie Ruff）。拉夫是一位黑人爵士贝斯手和法国号演奏家，他也住在布兰福德学院，并深受学院思想氛围的熏陶。他特别关注的一位研究员是耶鲁大学医学院神经病学教授、癫痫权威吉尔伯特·H·格拉泽（Gilbert H. Glaser）博士。拉夫一直渴望了解更多关于节奏的知识，而这些知识远非他毕生从事艺术实践所能涵盖，他认为格拉泽博士或许能为他提供一些答案。他提议布兰福德学院与耶鲁大学医学院和耶鲁大学音乐学院联合举办一个为期三天的研讨会，届时“其他学科的顶尖学者将探讨节奏如何在他们的工作中发挥作用”。

I liked the idea, and so did all the people Ruff invited. (Most of them were from Yale.) Some were artists who knew rhythm through the act of creation and could demonstrate it: the jazz drummer Jo Jones, the dancer Geoffrey Holder, the poet John Hollander, some members of a Javanese gamelan orchestra, the harpsichordist and Bach scholar Ralph Kirkpatrick. But the people who gave the seminar its rigor were from disciplines that had nothing to do with performance. The metallurgist Cyril Smith talked about symmetry and dissymmetry in molecular structure. The geologist John Rodgers talked about the strict numerical repetition in the formation of crystals. The zoologist G. Evelyn Hutchinson talked about the rhythmic movement of lake waters; the art historian Malcolm Cormack talked about rhythm in painting, and Dr. Glaser talked about the role of the brain in the physiology and control of rhythm. For three days the rhythmologists turned each other on, and Ruff has used the format ever since to teach an interdisciplinary seminar on rhythm. He keeps finding new rhythmical affinities between seemingly unrelated areas of life and inducing Yale professors—of architecture, of astronomy, of physics—to talk about them.

我喜欢这个想法，拉夫邀请的所有人都喜欢。（他们大多来自耶鲁大学。）有些人是艺术家，他们通过创作实践了解节奏，并能将其展现出来：爵士鼓手乔·琼斯、舞蹈家杰弗里·霍尔德、诗人约翰·霍兰德、爪哇甘美兰乐团的几位成员、羽管键琴演奏家兼巴赫研究专家拉尔夫·柯克帕特里克。但真正让研讨会严谨起来的，却是那些与表演毫无关系的学科。冶金学家西里尔·史密斯探讨了分子结构的对称性和不对称性；地质学家约翰·罗杰斯谈到了晶体形成过程中严格的数字重复；动物学家G·伊夫林·哈钦森谈到了湖水的韵律运动；艺术史学家马尔科姆·科马克探讨了绘画中的节奏；格拉泽博士则谈到了大脑在节奏的生理和控制中所起的作用。三天里，节奏学家们互相激发灵感，此后拉夫一直沿用这种形式开设跨学科节奏研讨课。他不断在看似毫不相关的领域中发现新的节奏关联，并引导耶鲁大学的教授们——建筑学、天文学、物理学——就此展开讨论。

After I left Yale I kept in touch with Ruff and was rewarded with two of the richest experiences of my life—one in Shanghai, the other in Venice. Not only were they extensions of what I had learned at Yale about the links between widely separated centuries and cultures. They also stretched me as a writer, posing unusually hard problems when I went along on both trips and wrote articles about them that later ran in The New Yorker . One of the underestimated tasks in nonfiction writing is to impose narrative shape on an unwieldy mass of material. That task is so central to this book that I’ll briefly describe what Ruff got me into.

离开耶鲁后，我一直与拉夫保持联系，并因此获得了人生中最宝贵的两次经历——一次在上海，一次在威尼斯。这两次经历不仅拓展了我在耶鲁所学的关于相隔遥远的世纪和文化之间联系的知识，也拓展了我的写作能力。两次旅行都让我遇到了异常棘手的问题，我随后撰写了相关文章，并发表在《纽约客》上。非虚构写作中一项常被低估的任务，就是如何将大量杂乱的素材构建成叙事结构。这项任务对本书至关重要，因此我将简要介绍一下拉夫带我经历的这一切。

The first trip took place in June of 1981. Ruff had spent two years learning Mandarin, his eighth language, in order to introduce jazz to China with the pianist Dwike Mitchell, his longtime partner in the Mitchell-Ruff Duo. The emotional climax of the trip was a concert the two men gave at the Shanghai Conservatory of Music. It began with Ruff explaining in Chinese to three hundred students and professors how jazz originated in the drum languages of West Africa—an oral tradition that was the antithesis of their own tradition—and it ended with Mitchell doing an elegant improvisation on a Chinese piece that one of the students had just performed on the piano. I could hardly believe how many opposite forces were at play in one room. But at the end music was the only force; it had blown every difference away.

第一次中国之行发生在1981年6月。为了与长期搭档、钢琴家德威克·米切尔（Mitchell-Ruff二重奏的成员）一起将爵士乐引入中国，拉夫花了两年时间学习汉语——他的第八门语言。此次旅程的高潮是两人在上海音乐学院举办的一场音乐会。音乐会伊始，拉夫用中文向三百名师生讲解了爵士乐起源于西非的鼓乐语言——这种口头传统与他们自身的传统截然相反——音乐会则以米切尔即兴演奏一首中国乐曲而告终，而这首乐曲正是此前一位学生用钢琴演奏的。我简直难以置信，在一个房间里竟有如此之多的对立力量在交织。但最终，音乐是唯一的力量；它消弭了所有的差异。

Two years later I happened to call Ruff and he mentioned that he was about to go to Venice to play Gregorian chants on his French horn in St. Mark’s cathedral at night when nobody else was there. He said it was a dream that went back thirty years to his student days at Yale, when his professor was the composer Paul Hindemith. Hindemith was obsessed by the relationship between music and science—his hero was the astronomer Johannes Kepler—and he was particularly excited by the music that came out of St. Mark’s basilica in the 1500s and 1600s, when Venice was the center of the musical world. The church’s remarkable acoustics inspired many composers—notably, the Gabrielis, Zarlino and Monteverdi—to create an important new style of polyphonic music.

两年后，我偶然给拉夫打了个电话，他提到他即将前往威尼斯，在夜深人静之时，于圣马可大教堂用法国号演奏格里高利圣咏。他说，这个梦想可以追溯到三十年前他在耶鲁大学求学时期，当时他的教授是作曲家保罗·欣德米特。欣德米特痴迷于音乐与科学之间的关系——他的偶像是天文学家约翰内斯·开普勒——他对16世纪和17世纪威尼斯作为世界音乐中心时，圣马可大教堂所传出的音乐尤为着迷。教堂卓越的音响效果激发了许多作曲家——尤其是加布里埃利兄弟、扎利诺和蒙特威尔第——创造出一种重要的复调音乐新风格。

“Hindemith showed us that that music was a crucial bridge to everything that followed,” Ruff said. “It was also the music that spoke most directly to me. I loved the luxurious sound that the Gabrielis achieved in their polychoral compositions, which were played and sung antiphonally from opposite lofts in St. Mark’s. Ever since then I’ve wanted to know what that sound is like.”

“欣德米特向我们展示了这种音乐是连接之后一切的关键桥梁，”拉夫说道。“它也是对我影响最深的音乐。我非常喜欢加布里埃利兄弟在他们的复调合唱作品中所营造出的那种华丽音响效果，这些作品是在圣马可教堂的两个相对的阁楼上交替演奏和演唱的。从那时起，我就一直想知道那种声音究竟是什么样的。”

As for why he wanted to play Gregorian chants, Ruff said it went back to a concert that the singer Paul Robeson once gave at Carnegie Hall. To show that the folk music of many disparate countries has a common source, Robeson sang an East African tribal chant, a thirteenth-century Slovakian plain chant and an American Negro spiritual that were almost identical. Robeson explained that the Abyssinian church and the church of the Sudan were once part of the Eastern church of Byzantium. Thus African music found its way into the Byzantine liturgy, which later filtered out into Europe and colored the Gregorian chants of the early Roman Catholic Church. “So what I’ll be playing in St. Mark’s,” Ruff told me, “is sacred music that has been played in that church since the Middle Ages.
