And because those chants are also at the core of my spirituals I’m going to play some of them, too.”

至于他为何想演奏格里高利圣咏，拉夫说这要追溯到歌手保罗·罗伯逊曾在卡内基音乐厅举办的一场音乐会。为了证明许多不同国家的民间音乐有着共同的源头，罗伯逊演唱了一首东非部落圣咏、一首十三世纪斯洛伐克素歌和一首美国黑人灵歌，这三首歌几乎完全相同。罗伯逊解释说，阿比西尼亚教会和苏丹教会曾是拜占庭东正教会的一部分。因此，非洲音乐融入了拜占庭礼仪，后来又传入欧洲，并影响了早期罗马天主教的格里高利圣咏。“所以我将在圣马可教堂演奏的，”拉夫告诉我，“是自中世纪以来就在该教堂演奏的圣乐。而且因为这些圣咏也是我创作灵歌的核心，所以我也会演奏一些。”

Such a convergence of ancient streams was something I didn’t want to miss, and I asked Ruff if I could meet him in Venice. He said he didn’t know if he could get the necessary permission; he needed to play when St. Mark’s was empty so that he could test its acoustics and make a tape recording. I said I’d take my chances—betting on Ruff is a no-risk proposition. As it turned out, getting permission was a story in itself—a miniseries of ecclesiastical rebuffs. But finally Ruff persuaded (in Italian) an old monsignor to let him use St. Mark’s for two hours after the last mass adjourned at seven-thirty.

如此古老音乐流派的交汇令我不想错过，于是我问鲁夫能否在威尼斯与他见面。他说他不知道能否获得必要的许可；他需要在圣马可教堂空无一人时演奏，以便测试音响效果并进行录音。我说我愿意冒险一试——押宝鲁夫绝对稳赚不赔。结果，获得许可本身就是一个故事——简直是一连串教会的拒绝。但最终，鲁夫用意大利语说服了一位老主教，允许他在晚上七点半最后一场弥撒结束后使用圣马可教堂两个小时。

Even now I find it hard to believe that those two hours happened to me. In summer, St. Mark’s is visited by twenty-five thousand tourists a day. But on that night, except for the sacristan who let us in, Ruff and I were the only people there. The first note that Ruff blew on his French horn told us that Hindemith had been right—the note seemed to seek out every crevice in the five immense domes and to linger long after it should have died away. Ruff opened a book called the Liber Usualis and began to play some of the oldest chants in the Catholic liturgy: Glorias and Kyries from various masses, a Sanctus, an Agnus Dei, and the beautiful “Pange Lingua.” The sound was extraordinarily pure.

即使现在，我仍然难以置信那两个小时真的发生在我身上。夏天，圣马可大教堂每天接待两万五千名游客。但那天晚上，除了带我们进去的司事之外，只有我和拉夫两个人。拉夫吹响法国号的第一个音符就告诉我们，欣德米特的预言是对的——那音符仿佛探入了五个巨大穹顶的每一个缝隙，久久萦绕，远超它本应消逝的程度。拉夫打开一本名为《常用圣歌集》（Liber Usualis）的书，开始演奏天主教礼仪中最古老的一些圣歌：来自不同弥撒的《荣耀经》和《垂怜经》，《圣哉经》，《羔羊经》，以及优美的《圣体颂》。那声音无比纯净。

I sat in the nave and watched the daylight ebb out of the church. Suddenly the gold mosaics in the domes were drained of color and the interior was dark. The sacristan came and put a candle next to Ruff’s book. Ruff kept playing. He and I were alone with our thoughts—a thousand years had been collapsed into two hours. I was listening to music that had been played in St. Mark’s since it opened in 1067.

我坐在教堂中殿，看着日光渐渐从教堂里消失。突然间，穹顶上的金色马赛克失去了色彩，教堂内部一片昏暗。司事走过来，在拉夫的书旁放了一支蜡烛。拉夫继续演奏。我和他各自沉浸在自己的思绪中——仿佛一千年的时间浓缩成了两个小时。我聆听的音乐，自1067年圣马可教堂开放以来就一直在这里演奏。

Outside in the square, a clock struck nine. Ruff closed his Liber Usualis and stood under the central dome and played “Were You There When They Crucified My Lord?” The great Negro spiritual sounded as majestic as the Gregorian chants. When Ruff finished, the sacristan came hurrying from wherever he had been. “ Bene! Bene! ” he said, clapping his hands, trying to convey his joy, though his face said it all. That the American spiritual moved him more than the chants of his own Catholic liturgy was the final mystery of the night, although, finally, it was no mystery; all the spirituals that Ruff played, including the pentatonic “Go Down, Moses,” were so similar to what he had played earlier that I could hardly tell which was which. Not that I was in any mood to try.

广场外，钟声敲响了九点。拉夫合上他的《常用曲集》，站在中央穹顶下，弹奏起《当他们钉死我的主时，你是否在场？》。这首伟大的黑人灵歌听起来如同格里高利圣咏般庄严雄伟。拉夫弹完后，教堂司事不知从何处匆匆赶来。“好！好！”他拍着手，试图表达喜悦之情，但他的表情已经说明了一切。这首美国灵歌比他自己的天主教礼拜仪式中的圣咏更能打动他，这成了当晚的最后一个谜团，尽管最终，这其实并不神秘；拉夫弹奏的所有灵歌，包括五声音阶的《摩西下山》，都与他之前弹奏的曲目如此相似，以至于我几乎无法分辨。当然，我当时也没心情去尝试。

Back in New York, trying to write my article, I felt overwhelmed (as I had with the Shanghai piece) by the richness of the material. The story had no end of connections between different centuries and civilizations, including a visit to Stravinsky’s grave. Too much had been thrown at me, and I would need to throw quite a lot at the reader. It’s not enough for a nonfiction writer to just write good, clean sentences; he must organize those sentences into a coherent shape, taking the reader on a complicated trip—often with several flashbacks—without losing him or boring him. In this case a reader couldn’t begin to accompany Ruff on his rounds—intellectually or emotionally—without knowing something about Hindemith and the acoustics of St. Mark’s, about the Gabrielis and the Venetian school, about the Byzantine liturgy and the Gregorian chants and the Negro spirituals with which they share a distant ancestry. But too many facts would kill the reader’s enjoyment of the adventure itself, which, beneath all its layers, was just an old-fashioned story of a pilgrim on a quest.

回到纽约，开始撰写文章时，我感到素材之丰富令我应接不暇（就像写上海那篇一样）。故事中不同世纪和文明之间的联系无穷无尽，甚至还包括一次对斯特拉文斯基墓地的探访。我被抛出的信息量太大，而我也需要将同样多的信息传递给读者。对于非虚构作家来说，仅仅写出流畅优美的句子是不够的；他必须将这些句子组织成一个连贯的整体，带领读者踏上一段复杂的旅程——其中往往穿插着多次闪回——同时又不让读者感到迷茫或厌倦。就此而言，如果读者不了解欣德米特和圣马可大教堂的音响效果、加布里埃利兄弟和威尼斯乐派、拜占庭礼仪和格里高利圣咏以及与它们有着遥远渊源的黑人灵歌，就无法真正理解鲁夫的探访——无论是在理智上还是情感上。但过多的事实会扼杀读者对冒险本身的乐趣，而从所有层面来看，这只是一个关于朝圣者踏上征程的古老故事。

Whenever I embark on a story so overloaded with good material I despair of ever getting to the end—of covering all the ground I know I’ll need to cover to tell the story right. In my gloom it helps me to remember two things. One is that writing is linear and sequential. If sentence B logically follows sentence A, and if sentence C logically follows sentence B, I’ll eventually get to sentence Z. I also try to remember that the reader should be given only as much information as he needs and not one word more. Anything else is a self-indulgence. Prior knowledge of the subject, incidentally, isn’t a requirement; only the ability to arrange information in narrative order. Readers may well have thought I was an expert on the Venetian school of music. In fact I had never heard of the Venetian school of music or the Gabrielis until Ruff told me he was going to Venice, and I didn’t learn any other details until I flew there and met him at a café overlooking the Grand Canal. The trip was instant education—sufficient, at least, to enable me to tell my story to other generalists like myself.

每当我开始创作一个素材丰富到令人应接不暇的故事时，我都会绝望地担心自己永远无法完成——担心自己无法涵盖所有必要的细节，从而把故事讲好。在沮丧之余，我会提醒自己两件事。第一，写作是线性的、循序渐进的。如果句子B在逻辑上承接句子A，句子C又在逻辑上承接句子B，那么我最终一定会写到句子Z。第二，我努力记住，应该只提供读者需要的信息，一个字也不要多。任何多余的信息都是自我放纵。顺便一提，事先了解相关主题并非必要条件；关键在于能够将信息按叙事顺序排列。读者或许会认为我是威尼斯音乐学派的专家。事实上，在鲁夫告诉我他要去威尼斯之前，我从未听说过威尼斯音乐学派或加布里埃利家族，直到我飞到威尼斯，在一家俯瞰大运河的咖啡馆里见到他，我才了解到更多细节。这次旅行让我受益匪浅——至少足以让我把我的故事讲述给其他像我一样的普通人。

After that came the hard part: wrestling my new-found education into a narrative that moved logically from A to Z. The only thing I knew at the beginning was how I wanted the article to end: “The sacristan unbolted the door and gave us a warm Italian goodbye and we stepped out into the crowded streets of Venice.” But every preceding sentence was slow labor: the steady accretion of detail and the equally steady removal of whatever I had put in that I realized wasn’t doing necessary work or that the reader could figure out for himself. (I had learned by long travail a far from obvious lesson: Readers must be given room to bring their own emotions to a piece so crammed with emotional content; the writer must tenaciously resist explaining why the material is so moving.) Only when the job was over did I enjoy it. I don’t like to write, but I take great pleasure in having written—in having finally made an arrangement that has a certain inevitability, like the solution to a mathematical problem. Perhaps in no other line of work is delayed gratification so delayed.

接下来才是真正的难点：如何将我新近获得的知识融入一个逻辑清晰、从头到尾流畅的叙事中。一开始，我唯一知道的就是文章的结尾：“教堂司事打开门闩，用热情的意大利式问候和我们道别，我们走入了威尼斯熙熙攘攘的街道。” 但前面的每一句话都像是在缓慢地堆砌细节：一边是不断添加细节，一边是不断删减那些我意识到无关紧要或读者可以自行领悟的内容。（我从漫长的写作过程中领悟到一个并不那么显而易见的道理：对于一篇情感如此丰富的文章，必须给读者留出空间，让他们将自己的情感融入其中；作者必须克制住解释文章为何如此感人的冲动。）只有当写作完成时，我才真正享受其中。我不喜欢写作，但我却很享受写作的过程——终于完成了一件看似理所当然的事情，就像解开了一个数学难题。或许在其他任何行业，都没有像写作这样需要如此长时间的延迟满足感。

So much for the acoustics of St. Mark’s and the carpentry of writing. I’ve told the story because this is a book about process: the process of transmitting information clearly and simply. Only by repeated applications of process—writing and rewriting and pruning and shaping—can we hammer out a clear and simple product.

圣马可教堂的音响效果和写作的技巧就此打住。我之所以讲述这个故事，是因为这本书的主题是过程：清晰简洁地传递信息的过程。只有反复运用这个过程——写作、修改、精简和润色——我们才能最终提炼出清晰简洁的作品。

Now, as I began to think about my book, I thought of my years at Yale and all the teachers there, like Willie Ruff, who took me into their special worlds. I especially remembered Yale professors who cared about good writing even though their subject wasn’t English.

现在，当我开始构思我的书时，我想起了在耶鲁的那些年，以及所有像威利·拉夫这样的老师，他们带我走进了他们独特的世界。我尤其记得那些即使并非英语专业的耶鲁教授们，他们也十分重视优秀的写作。

The first ones who came to mind were the historians; they were the writing stars of the faculty. They understood that writing is the mechanism by which a historian passes his knowledge on to the next generation, and they insisted on good writing in their students’ papers before they considered whether the paper was good history. I also recalled professors in other disciplines who saw clear writing as the corollary of clear thinking—and therefore as a key to learning.

我首先想到的是历史学家们；他们是学院里写作的佼佼者。他们深知写作是历史学家将知识传承给下一代的途径，因此在评判学生论文的历史价值之前，他们首先要确保论文的写作水平过硬。我还想起其他学科的教授们，他们认为清晰的写作是清晰思考的必然结果——因此也是学习的关键。

I made a list of about ten and sent them a letter. I said I was looking for brief examples—around five hundred words—of good writing in their discipline that would be accessible to someone of high school age. Had they written any such passages themselves? (I knew they had.) If not, would they recommend a passage that some other scholar had written? The response was swift and generous. Envelopes containing photocopies of admired passages began to come back in the mail, and the accompanying letters often steered me to writers I hadn’t known about or raised points I hadn’t thought about. Edmund S. Morgan, for instance, my favorite stylist among the history professors, wrote:

我列出了大约十位学者，并给他们寄了信。我在信中说，我正在寻找他们各自学科领域中优秀的短文范例——大约五百字——篇幅要短，适合高中生阅读。他们自己是否写过类似的文章？（我知道他们写过。）如果没有，能否推荐其他学者写的文章？他们的回复迅速而慷慨。我陆续收到了装有他们所欣赏的文章复印件的信封，随信附上的信件也常常让我了解到一些我之前不认识的作家，或者提出了一些我之前没有想到的观点。例如，我最喜欢的历史学教授之一埃德蒙·S·摩根写道：

“I find I am hard put to pick a passage of five hundred words, because the passages I like best usually depend on the preparation of the reader in earlier passages that give resonance to things said later. Indeed the quality I call resonance is what hits me hardest in all writing. And what resounds is not merely things said earlier but common knowledge and experience that everyone can relate to. I’m sending you a few passages from Samuel Eliot Morison (whom I consider the best historical writer, not necessarily the best historian, of this century) and from Perry Miller and George Otto Trevelyan. I’m not sure any of them will be appropriate for you because their principal virtue is their suggestiveness (resonance), not their clarity.”

“我发现很难挑选一段五百字的文字，因为我最喜欢的段落通常都依赖于读者对前面段落的理解，这些理解能使后面的内容产生共鸣。事实上，我称之为共鸣的这种特质，是我在所有写作中最能打动我的。而真正能引起共鸣的，不仅仅是前面提到的内容，更是每个人都能感同身受的常识和经验。我给你发几段文字，分别出自塞缪尔·艾略特·莫里森（我认为他是本世纪最优秀的历史作家，而非最优秀的历史学家）、佩里·米勒和乔治·奥托·特里维廉之手。我不确定这些文字是否适合你，因为它们的主要优点在于其启发性（共鸣），而非清晰度。”

Fair enough: Resonance would have to be factored into the equation. Yet I had no trouble detecting it in the brief passage that Professor Morgan sent me from one of his own books, The Birth of the Republic , which he diffidently included along with Morison, Miller and Trevelyan. I wasn’t surprised to find that I liked it better than anything else in his package:

没错：共鸣效应必须纳入考量。然而，我毫不费力地就从摩根教授寄给我的他自己的著作《共和国的诞生》中的一小段文字中察觉到了这一点。他略显拘谨地将这段文字与莫里森、米勒和特里维廉的作品一同收录在内。不出所料，我最喜欢这段文字，胜过他提供的其他任何内容。

The government of Great Britain had not been designed to cover half the globe, and when Englishmen were not busy extending their possessions still farther, they were apt to regard the problem of turnpikes in Yorkshire as vastly more important than the enforcement of the Navigation Acts in New York. Administration of the colonies was left to the King, who turned it over to his Secretary of State for the Southern Department (whose principal business was England’s relations with southern Europe). The Secretary left it pretty much to the Board of Trade and Plantations, a sort of Chamber of Commerce with purely advisory powers. The Board of Trade told the Secretary what to do; he told the royal governors; the governors told the colonists; and the colonists did what they pleased.

英国政府的设计初衷并非为了统治半个地球，而且当英国人忙于进一步扩张领土时，他们往往认为约克郡的收费公路问题远比在纽约执行《航海条例》重要得多。殖民地的管理权归国王所有，国王又将其交给南方事务大臣（该大臣的主要职责是处理英国与南欧的关系）。大臣几乎完全放任贸易和种植园委员会——一个类似于商会的机构，只有纯粹的咨询权——行事。贸易和种植园委员会告诉大臣该做什么；大臣告诉皇家总督；总督告诉殖民地居民；而殖民地居民则随心所欲。

This system, or lack of system, had at least one virtue: it did no harm, a fact evidenced by the rolling prosperity of mother country and colonies alike. The British Empire, however inefficient in its management, was very much a going concern, and wise men on both sides of the Atlantic believed that its success was intimately connected with the bumbling way in which it was run. They saw both the prosperity and the inefficiency of the empire as results of the freedom that prevailed in it. Freedom, inefficiency, and prosperity are not infrequently found together, and it is seldom easy to distinguish between the first two. The British Empire was inefficient, but its inhabitants were prosperous, and they were free.

这种制度，或者说缺乏制度，至少有一个优点：它没有造成任何损害，这一点从宗主国和殖民地的繁荣昌盛便可见一斑。尽管大英帝国的管理效率低下，但它仍然运转良好，大西洋两岸的智者都认为，它的成功与其笨拙的管理方式密切相关。他们认为，帝国的繁荣和低效都是其内部自由的结果。自由、低效和繁荣常常同时出现，而且前两者之间也很难区分。大英帝国效率低下，但其人民却生活富裕，并且享有自由。

The passage is hard to beat for clarity—and for warmth and humanity and a leavening touch of humor. But surely it also has resonance. If resonance is the product of “common knowledge and experience that everyone can relate to,” there’s nobody who can’t relate to the experience of government-by-bumbling—and no American who can’t relate to the balancing act called American democracy, a marvel of inefficiency that has somehow never quite lost us our prosperity or our freedom.

这段文字清晰易懂，笔触温暖人心，又不失幽默，堪称佳作。它当然也具有很强的共鸣性。如果共鸣源于“人人都能感同身受的常识和经验”，那么没有人能不体会政府的笨拙运作——也没有哪个美国人不能理解美国民主这种看似低效却又奇迹般地维持着繁荣和自由的平衡之道。

Another professor on my list was Dr. David F. Musto, professor of psychiatry and the history of medicine at the Yale School of Medicine, one of whose special interests is the history of drug addiction in America. In 1972 he brought me an eye-opening piece for the Yale Alumni Magazine —at least it opened my eyes—which said that “the use of opiates like heroin and morphine in the United States has been so great, compared with other nations, that some American scientists around World War I called heroin or morphine addiction ‘the American disease.’” Cocaine use was even more common. “From about 1880 to 1900,” Musto wrote, “cocaine was a standard stimulant or tonic, and some of our most popular soda pops had cocaine in them.”

我名单上的另一位教授是耶鲁大学医学院精神病学和医学史教授大卫·F·穆斯托博士，他尤其关注美国毒品成瘾史。1972年，他为《耶鲁校友杂志》撰写了一篇让我大开眼界的文章——至少对我来说是这样——文章指出，“与其他国家相比，美国使用海洛因和吗啡等鸦片类药物的情况非常严重，以至于一战前后一些美国科学家将海洛因或吗啡成瘾称为‘美国病’。”可卡因的使用更为普遍。“从1880年到1900年左右，”穆斯托写道，“可卡因是一种标准的兴奋剂或滋补剂，我们一些最受欢迎的汽水里就含有可卡因。”

To illustrate these startling facts in a layout, Dr. Musto brought me some turn-of-the-century advertisements in which pharmaceutical firms extolled the therapeutic value of their drugs. One, for instance, was for Metcalf’s Coca Wine, whose active ingredient was cocaine. Two other ads proudly introduced heroin as a cough suppressant. One was run by Bayer, who later made aspirin in the same laboratory. The second ad, run by Martin H. Smith & Co., Chemists, declared: “The problem of administering heroin in proper doses in such form as will give the therapeutic virtues of this drug full sway, and will suit the palate of the most exacting adult or the most capricious child, has been solved by the pharmaceutical compound known as GLYCO-HEROIN . The results attained with Glyco-Heroin in the alleviation and cure of cough are attested by numerous clinical studies that have appeared in the medical journals within the past few years.” The adult dosage was one teaspoonful every two hours, with a half-dose suggested for children over ten, and five to ten drops for children of three and older.

为了更直观地说明这些令人震惊的事实，穆斯托博士给我带来了一些世纪之交的广告，其中制药公司极力吹捧其药物的疗效。例如，其中一则广告宣传的是梅特卡夫可卡酒，其活性成分正是可卡因。另外两则广告则自豪地将海洛因作为止咳药推向市场。其中一则广告由拜耳公司投放，该公司后来在同一实验室生产了阿司匹林。另一则广告由马丁·H·史密斯化学公司投放，宣称：“一种名为GLYCO-HEROIN的药物化合物解决了如何以合适的剂量服用海洛因，使其疗效得以充分发挥，并能满足最挑剔的成年人或最任性的儿童的口味这一难题。近年来发表在医学期刊上的众多临床研究证实了GLYCO-HEROIN在缓解和治愈咳嗽方面的疗效。”成人剂量为每两小时服用一茶匙，建议十岁以上儿童服用半剂量，三岁及以上儿童服用五至十滴。

After that I kept track of David Musto’s articles because he seemed to be a vigilante on a dimly lit frontier, where the ignorance of doctors meets the acquiescence of the sick. When I asked him for some examples of his writing, he sent me a recent piece from the Bulletin of the New York Academy of Medicine . It began like this:

之后，我开始关注大卫·穆斯托的文章，因为他就像一位在昏暗的前沿地带挺身而出的义警，那里充斥着医生的无知和病人的默许。当我向他索要一些文章范例时，他发给我一篇最近发表在《纽约医学科学院公报》上的文章。文章开头是这样的：

It is a sad paradox that the healing arts can cause sickness and disease. From witch doctors and early Western medicine, down to the era of William Harvey or Benjamin Rush, the posthumous “Father of American Psychiatry,” we deal with a profession which for centuries routinely inflicted grievous bodily harm without qualm and, further, often at the behest of society. Physicians confidently treated battle wounds with boiling oil and infectious diseases with blistering, vomiting and purging.

令人悲哀的是，医疗手段本身却可能引发疾病。从巫医和早期西方医学，到威廉·哈维或被誉为“美国精神病学之父”的本杰明·拉什的时代，我们所面对的这个行业几个世纪以来都毫不犹豫地对人体造成严重的伤害，而且往往是应社会的要求。医生们自信地用沸油治疗战伤，用泡水、催吐和泻药治疗传染病。

Many of these treatments lasted into our century, among them calomel, or mercurous chloride, perennially popular with physicians and the public and still prescribed in the period between the two world wars. Phlebotomy or bleeding was considered legitimate almost as long. Even Sir William Osler, the most noted physician in the English-speaking world, recommended phlebotomy for selected cases of pneumonia as late as 1909.

许多此类疗法一直沿用至本世纪，其中包括甘汞（氯化亚汞），它长期以来深受医生和公众的青睐，甚至在两次世界大战期间仍被广泛使用。放血疗法也几乎同样长久地被认为是合法的。就连英语世界最著名的医生威廉·奥斯勒爵士，直到1909年仍然建议对某些肺炎病例进行放血治疗。

The medical profession has a long record of treating patients with useless or harmful remedies, often in clinical settings of complete mutual confidence. Iatrogenic diseases, complications and injury have been, in fact, common in the history of medicine. We may look upon addiction to certain dispensed drugs as one variation among the occasional effects of drug therapies.

医学界长期以来一直存在使用无效甚至有害的药物治疗病人的情况，而且往往是在医患双方完全信任的临床环境中。事实上，医源性疾病、并发症和损伤在医学史上屡见不鲜。我们可以将对某些处方药物的成瘾视为药物治疗偶发性副作用的一种表现形式。

“Iatrogenic” means “caused by medical treatment.” It’s a medical term with a precise meaning, and Dr. Musto was writing for a medical journal. Still, his use of the term doesn’t invalidate his article as an example of clear writing for anybody. “Iatrogenic” is easy enough to look up, as I just did. Not only did I enjoy learning a new word; Webster’s definition adds an ironic phrase that makes the rest of Dr. Musto’s piece all the more disturbing: “said esp. of imagined symptoms, ailments or disorders induced by a physician’s words or actions.” Here’s how his story continues:

“医源性”指的是“由医疗行为引起的”。这是一个医学术语，含义明确，而穆斯托医生当时正为医学期刊撰稿。尽管如此，他使用这个词并不影响他的文章作为清晰易懂的写作范例的价值。“医源性”很容易查到，就像我刚才查到的那样。我不仅乐于学习一个新词；韦氏词典的定义还包含一句颇具讽刺意味的话，让穆斯托医生文章的其余部分更加令人不安：“尤指由医生的言语或行为引起的想象中的症状、疾病或紊乱。” 他的故事还在继续：

During the 19th century, with the development of organic chemistry and the manufacturing pharmaceutical industry, the purity of natural substances improved. As the composition of natural substances such as opium and coca leaves was separated into several active ingredients, the potency of drugs increased. Further, modes of application were improved so that these active ingredients, such as morphine, could be more effectively introduced into the body’s physiology. Here the most dramatic step forward was the development of the hypodermic syringe. By the second half of the 19th century several addicting forms of opium were available….

19世纪，随着有机化学和制药工业的发展，天然物质的纯度得到了提高。鸦片和古柯叶等天然物质的成分被分离成多种活性成分，药物的效力也随之增强。此外，给药方式也得到了改进，使得吗啡等活性成分能够更有效地被人体吸收。其中最显著的进步是皮下注射器的发明。到了19世纪下半叶，多种成瘾性鸦片制剂已经问世……

Because of the enormous humanitarian value of reducing pain and fear, [opium] became a pawn in the vigorous competition for patients among health deliverers. There were more people offering health care—homeopaths, regular physicians, natural bone-setters, local wise ones and so on—than communities needed. Confusion over medical theories, the abundance of physicians and a growing objection by patients to the severe treatments meted out by regular physicians—they called it “heroic treatment”—made an opiate a very attractive remedy: it was painless, it worked, it relieved pain and worry and it made tolerable a host of ailments whose cause and proper treatment were completely unknown. Small wonder that the importation of crude opium into the United States started to rise early in the century and grew more rapidly than the population. In 1840, when importation statistics commenced, to the mid-1890s, when the per capita consumption began to level off, the amount of crude opium for each person in the United States grew from 12 grains to 52 grains.

由于鸦片具有减轻疼痛和恐惧的巨大人道主义价值，它成为了医疗服务提供者之间激烈争夺病人的筹码。提供医疗服务的人员——顺势疗法医师、普通医生、自然疗法医师、当地智者等等——远远超过了社区的实际需求。医学理论的混乱、医生数量的激增以及患者对普通医生严厉治疗（他们称之为“英雄式治疗”）日益增长的抵触情绪，使得鸦片成为一种极具吸引力的药物：它无痛、有效，能够缓解疼痛和焦虑，并使许多病因和正确治疗方法完全未知的疾病变得可以忍受。难怪本世纪初，美国粗鸦片的进口量开始上升，并且增长速度超过了人口增长速度。从 1840 年进口统计数据开始，到 19 世纪 90 年代中期人均消费量开始趋于稳定，美国人均粗鸦片量从 12 格令增加到 52 格令。

The article goes on to document the steady march of iatrogenic addiction in this country, noting that “the most important play of America’s greatest playwright,” Eugene O’Neill’s Long Day’s Journey into Night , is “a drama of iatrogenic addiction” and pointing out that the dangers of “physician-induced dependence” have proliferated in our own time with the mass production of tranquilizers and other anxiety-reducing pills. “Great temptations are held out to physicians who are able to relieve symptoms in spite of the dangers inherent in the drugs’ multiple and often addictive effects.”

文章继续记录了美国医源性成瘾的持续蔓延，指出“美国最伟大的剧作家尤金·奥尼尔最重要的剧作”——《长夜漫漫路迢迢》——本身就是一部“医源性成瘾的戏剧”，并指出随着镇静剂和其他抗焦虑药物的大规模生产，“医生诱导依赖”的危险在当今时代日益加剧。“尽管这些药物具有多种且往往具有成瘾性的副作用，但能够缓解症状的医生仍然面临着巨大的诱惑。”

Dr. Musto’s article was just the kind I had hoped to find for my book, bringing a scholar’s knowledge to a complex situation or issue. I wanted to present enough examples from enough fields to suggest that every discipline has an accessible literature waiting to be found by teachers and students. I wanted to eliminate such excuses as “It can’t be done” and “There’s nothing out there.”

穆斯托博士的文章正是我为我的书所希望找到的那种文章，它将学者的知识运用到复杂的情况或问题中。我希望列举足够多的、来自足够多领域的案例，以表明每个学科都有可供教师和学生查阅的文献资料。我希望消除诸如“这不可能”和“根本没有相关资料”之类的借口。

History and writing are of course natural allies, whether it’s colonial history or medical history; one couldn’t live without the other. But what would I get from professors in fields where writing was a more unlikely bedfellow—geology, for instance—or where it had rarely been allowed in bed at all? And what about all those conveniently vague humanities? I remembered that the late Brand Blanshard, professor of philosophy emeritus at Yale, once gave me a small book called On Philosophical Style , in which he explained how to write about that most vaporous of subjects. Such courage doesn’t come along every day. I got out his book and took hope from this early passage:

历史和写作当然是天然的盟友，无论是殖民史还是医学史；二者缺一不可。但是，如果写作与历史关系不那么密切——比如地质学——或者写作几乎从未被允许涉足的领域，我又能从教授那里得到什么呢？还有那些含义模糊的人文学科呢？我记得已故的耶鲁大学哲学荣誉教授布兰德·布兰沙德曾送给我一本名为《论哲学风格》的小册子，他在书中解释了如何撰写关于这个最空灵的主题的文章。这样的勇气并非人人都能遇到。我拿出他的书，从开篇的这段话中看到了希望：

Hard as philosophy is, there have been writers who have actually succeeded in making it intelligible and even exciting, not to the exceptionally gifted alone, but to a wide public. Socrates talked it, and Plato wrote it, in a way that some millions of readers have not been willing to forget. Bergson, without once descending to vulgarity, made it for a time one of the excitements of Paris. The British tradition in philosophy has been exceptionally fertile in writers with the gift of making crooked things straight. So if a philosophical writer cannot be followed, the difficulty of his subject can be pleaded only in mitigation of his offense, not in condonation of it. There are too many expert witnesses on the other side.

哲学固然艰深，但确实有一些作家成功地将其阐释得通俗易懂，甚至引人入胜，不仅吸引了天赋异禀之人，也吸引了广大读者。苏格拉底的论述，柏拉图的著述，都令数百万读者难以忘怀。柏格森的论述从未流于庸俗，却一度使哲学成为巴黎的热门话题。英国的哲学传统孕育了众多才华横溢、善于化繁为简的作家。因此，如果一位哲学作家的作品晦涩难懂，我们只能以他作品的艰涩为由减轻其罪责，而不能为其开脱。因为反对者一方的专家证人众多。

So I began to cast my net for expert witnesses. But what I first needed to know more about was how writing was related to learning. How much do we learn about a subject through writing that we wouldn’t learn in any other way? To find some of the answers I would have to return to Gustavus Adolphus College and see how that first term of writing across the curriculum had gone.

于是我开始四处寻找专家证人。但我首先需要了解的是写作与学习之间的关系。我们通过写作能学到多少其他方式无法学到的知识？为了找到一些答案，我必须回到古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院，看看第一学期将写作融入课程的教学情况如何。

# ↩

4. Writing to Learn

4. 通过写作学习

I regretted my decision to go back to Gustavus Adolphus College in January when the pilot of my plane announced that the temperature in Minneapolis was twenty-five degrees below zero. We were over Lake Michigan and I didn’t see any easy way of turning back. Twenty-five below! I could die if my rented car broke down while I was driving across the frozen tundra of Minnesota. I was a city boy from New York; I didn’t have any of the survival knowledge that Minnesotans are born with, or any of the special equipment they carry in their cars—Sterno stoves and heavy blankets and dried foods—to keep from perishing along the highway. I would just have to take my chances, and I did, hunched against the unbelievable cold, squinting at the snow-blown landscape through the icy windows of my car and guessing at the whereabouts of the road. When I finally got to Gustavus Adolphus the woman who greeted me said, “I hope you at least had a rope in your car. A few years ago six people died not far from here when a sudden blizzard came up and they got out and couldn’t find their way back. You should always have a rope that you can tie to your steering column.”

一月份，飞机飞行员宣布明尼阿波利斯的气温是零下二十五度时，我后悔不已，决定返回古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院。当时我们正飞越密歇根湖，我看不出有什么简单的返航办法。零下二十五度！如果我租的车在穿越明尼苏达州冰封的苔原时抛锚，我可能就没命了。我来自纽约，是个城里孩子；我既没有明尼苏达人与生俱来的生存技能，也没有他们车里常备的特殊装备——固体酒精炉、厚毯子和干粮——来保命。我只能碰碰运气，于是就这么做了。我蜷缩着身子，抵挡着难以置信的严寒，眯着眼睛透过结冰的车窗看着被雪覆盖的景色，猜测着路在哪里。当我终于到达古斯塔夫·阿道夫酒店时，接待我的那位女士说：“我希望你的车里至少备着一根绳子。几年前，离这里不远的地方遭遇了一场突如其来的暴风雪，六个人下车后找不到路，不幸遇难。你应该始终备着一根绳子，可以系在方向盘柱上。”

I had of course been ropeless, but that didn’t matter now. I had survived, and the Gustavus Adolphus faculty quickly warmed me up. For two days professors from every corner of the curriculum came and talked to me. Quite a few were men and women I had met on my previous visit. I asked them how they had taught their “W” courses during the fall term and what they had discovered. Their accounts varied in detail, but on one point they all agreed: Far more learning had been achieved by the addition of a writing requirement.

我当然没有绳子，但这已经不重要了。我活了下来，古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院的教职工很快就让我感到温暖。接下来的两天里，各个学科的教授都来和我交流。其中不少是我上次来访时认识的。我问他们秋季学期是如何教授“W”课程的，以及他们有哪些发现。他们的描述细节不尽相同，但有一点他们都一致认同：增加写作要求后，学生的学习效果显著提升。

Many teachers included themselves among the learners. Barbara Simpson, professor of psychology, said: “I wanted to teach a ‘W’ course because I write very badly myself—in high school I was terrorized by writing. One thing I did last term was to ask students to write a paper in the last five minutes of class, summarizing what I had said in my lecture. It helps them to find out whether they understood what I was talking about. Psychology is a deceptively difficult subject: It sounds like material you’ve known all your life, but actually it’s based on extensive research. And the writing has become far more concrete. In the ’60s psychology was still a probabilistic science, so it developed a hedging language. You can’t get away with that today.”

许多教师也把自己当作学生来学习。心理学教授芭芭拉·辛普森说：“我想开一门写作课，因为我自己的写作水平很差——高中时我非常害怕写作。上学期我做的一件事就是让学生在课的最后五分钟写一篇论文，总结我讲的内容。这有助于他们检验自己是否理解了我的讲解。心理学是一门看似简单实则深奥的学科：它听起来像是你毕生所学的知识，但实际上它建立在大量的研究之上。而且，现在的写作方式也更加具体。在20世纪60年代，心理学还是一门概率论科学，所以它发展出了一种含糊其辞的语言。如今，这种做法已经行不通了。”

Fuzzy thinking turned up repeatedly as the main enemy. “Students don’t know how to be precise,” said Norman Walbek, associate professor of political science. “In my first assignment I asked them to write a paper on ‘What are the most important goals of United States policy?’ It was a values statement—something nobody had ever asked them to write before; usually students are only asked to describe or to analyze: ‘Write an essay on the Declaration of Independence.’ Well, their papers were a disaster. They rambled all over. They couldn’t formulate a goal or a policy except in the most generalized way—‘better communications,’ ‘world peace’—and in almost every case the comment I found myself making was: ‘I don’t understand this.’ As the term went on I tried to get them to use writing to focus their thoughts on specific ideas and issues. I told them I’d be grading their papers for clarity, common sense, logic, plausibility and precision, not for the content of their views. At the end of the term I gave them the same assignment on goals and policies. This time their papers were clear and explicit. Their problems were in thinking, not in the mechanics of writing.”

模糊思维反复出现，被认为是主要问题。“学生们不知道如何做到精确，”政治学副教授诺曼·沃尔贝克说。 “我布置的第一个作业是让他们写一篇关于‘美国政策最重要的目标是什么？’的论文。这是一篇价值观陈述——以前从来没有人要求他们写过这类文章；通常学生只会被要求描述或分析，比如‘写一篇关于《独立宣言》的文章’。结果，他们的论文简直是一场灾难。他们东拉西扯，根本无法提出具体的目标或政策，只能用最笼统的方式概括——‘改善沟通’、‘世界和平’——几乎每次我都会忍不住说：‘我看不懂。’随着学期的进行，我试图引导他们通过写作将思考聚焦于具体的想法和问题。我告诉他们，我会根据论文的清晰度、常识性、逻辑性、合理性和精确性来评分，而不是根据他们观点的具体内容。学期末，我又布置了同样的关于目标和政策的作业。这一次，他们的论文清晰明了。他们的问题出在思考上，而不是写作技巧上。”

Professor Clair McRostie, who teaches International Economics and Management, didn’t wait to discover this dismal fact; he knew it already. The prospectus that he handed out to his students left them in no doubt about his priorities—it said that their three required papers would be graded for “quality of writing, grammar, spelling, organization and content.” His first three lectures, in fact, were devoted entirely to writing and reasoning.

教授克莱尔·麦克罗斯蒂教授教授国际经济与管理，他无需等待便已意识到这一令人沮丧的事实；他早已知晓。他发给学生的课程大纲明确表明了他的教学重点——大纲上写明，学生的三篇必修论文将根据“写作质量、语法、拼写、结构和内容”进行评分。事实上，他的前三节课完全专注于写作和论证。

“Back when some of us were concerned about why Johnny can’t write,” Professor McRostie told me, “a psychologist put it to us that Johnny can’t reason, and I’ve been preoccupied with that thought ever since. The first two books I assigned last term were The Art of Thinking , by Vincent Ruggiero, and Reasoning , by Michael Scriven. This is a generation that has spent fifteen thousand hours watching television, and its attention span is short. I’m challenging my students to find their powers of reasoning. I tell them, ‘If you don’t write reasonably and well on your exam I’ll give you a lower grade. But I’ll also give you extra time if you need it.’ At the end of the term, when they were asked to evaluate the course, they said that the writing component had been an important part of their learning.”

“当初我们有些人还在担心约翰尼为什么不会写作的时候，”麦克罗斯蒂教授告诉我，“一位心理学家告诉我们，约翰尼缺乏推理能力，从那以后，我就一直思考这个问题。上学期我布置的头两本书分别是文森特·鲁杰罗的《思考的艺术》和迈克尔·斯克里文的《推理》。这一代人花了15000个小时看电视，他们的注意力很难集中。我正在挑战我的学生，让他们发掘自己的推理能力。我告诉他们：‘如果你们考试时写得不好，我会给你们低分。但如果你们需要，我也会给你们额外的时间。’学期末，当被问及课程评价时，他们说写作部分是他们学习过程中非常重要的一部分。”

I liked the audacity of a professor devoting his first three lectures to subjects that weren’t the ones he was supposedly there to teach. It was a way of seizing his students’ attention with a radical piece of news: Economics and management are important, but they’re not as important as clear reasoning and writing; without them, all the economic theory in the world won’t take you far. Professor McRostie had me beat as a logic nut, and his credentials were better. I had merely learned by experience that thinking is the foundation of writing. But I had never thought about thinking as a process. How does it work? Why do some people think straighter than others? What are the factors that prevent us from thinking clearly? Can it be taught? I made a note to buy The Art of Thinking when I got back home. I suspected that it would help me to see how so much fuzz gets into the writing machinery and how some of it might be kept out.

我欣赏这位教授的胆识，他竟然用前三节课的时间讲授与他本应教授的内容截然不同的课题。这是一种用一个颠覆性的观点吸引学生注意力的方式：经济学和管理学固然重要，但它们远不及清晰的推理和写作能力重要；没有它们，世界上所有的经济理论都无济于事。麦克罗斯蒂教授的逻辑思维能力远胜于我，而且他的资历也比我更胜一筹。我只是从经验中了解到，思考是写作的基础。但我从未将思考视为一个过程。它是如何运作的？为什么有些人比其他人思路更清晰？是什么因素阻碍了我们清晰地思考？它能被教授吗？我记下回家后要买一本《思考的艺术》。我猜想这本书能帮助我理解写作过程中那些纷繁复杂的因素是如何产生的，以及如何才能避免它们的影响。

“Reading, writing and thinking are all integrated,” said Kevin Byrne, associate professor of history. “An idea can have value in itself, but its usefulness diminishes to the extent that you can’t articulate it to someone else. What the writing program made me realize is that I have to take much more time in class to talk about writing. Teachers have a tremendous tendency to just give writing assignments and let their students sink or swim—which assumes that they’ve learned to write somewhere else. Very often they haven’t. In history we’ve paid great lip service to the need to write, but we haven’t taken the time in our classes to tell students how it’s done. We need to rob time from the study of history to do that. It takes a commitment, and I found it very painful because the term is too short anyway to cover all the historical issues I’d like to discuss.”

“阅读、写作和思考是密不可分的，”历史学副教授凯文·伯恩说道。“一个想法本身可能很有价值，但如果你无法将其清晰地表达给别人，它的价值就会大打折扣。写作课程让我意识到，我必须在课堂上花更多的时间来讲解写作。教师们常常只是布置写作作业，然后就放任学生自生自灭——这种做法的前提是学生已经从其他地方学会了写作。但很多时候，他们并没有。在历史学领域，我们口头上很重视写作的必要性，但却从未在课堂上花时间告诉学生如何写作。我们需要从历史学习中挤出时间来做这件事。这需要投入大量精力，而我发现这非常痛苦，因为学期本来就很短，根本无法涵盖所有我想讨论的历史议题。”

Early in the term Professor Byrne told his students to bring in a historical passage that they considered well written and to explain why. “It forces them to think about the elements that go into good writing,” he said, “and it shows them that there are many different kinds of good writing, not just one. I was amazed at what happened when students questioned each other about the writing in a historical account. Their ideas became much more focused when the whole class discussed a passage in terms of how it was written.”

学期伊始，伯恩教授就要求学生们带来一篇他们认为写得好的历史文章，并解释原因。“这迫使他们思考优秀文章的构成要素，”他说，“也让他们明白，优秀的文章有很多种，并非只有一种。当学生们就历史文章的写作手法互相提问时，我惊讶地发现，全班同学一起讨论文章的写作方式时，他们的想法变得更加清晰。”

In all these accounts I heard a pleasant sense of discovery: Writing could get into corners that other teaching tools couldn’t reach. But it was a professor of chemistry, Lawrence W. Potts, who took me to the heart of what I had come to find out. During the fall, he said, he had taught a “W” course called “Instrumental Methods of Analysis” for juniors and seniors who hoped to go into chemistry as a profession.

在所有这些叙述中，我都感受到了一种令人愉悦的发现感：写作能够触及其他教学工具无法企及的领域。但真正让我领悟到我所发现的真谛的，是一位名叫劳伦斯·W·波茨的化学教授。他说，秋季学期，他为那些希望从事化学专业的大学三年级和四年级学生开设了一门名为“仪器分析方法”的W课程。

“I’ve been grading my students’ lab reports both for their scientific merit,” Professor Potts said, “and for the language in which they tell me what they did, what their results were and how they interpret those results. If they don’t write well they lose a full grade. Like all writing, it’s an exercise in thinking. The easy way for a chemistry professor to evaluate lab work is just to have students turn in index cards with the numbers they got. But students don’t get much out of that—there’s an important link they miss.

“我给学生的实验报告评分时，既看其科学价值，”波茨教授说，“也看他们如何用语言描述实验过程、结果以及如何解读这些结果。如果写作不好，就会被扣一分。写作和所有写作一样，都是一次思考的练习。化学教授评估实验结果最简单的方法就是让学生交上写着实验数据的索引卡片。但学生从中得不到太多——他们忽略了一个重要的环节。”

“I want them to go first to the literature, so they know how the experiment has been done before and what to expect in the lab and how to plan their work. Having to plan their work helps them to write it up as they go along, so that writing becomes woven through the entire class and lab experience. If they fall into a pitfall they can explain how they got there, and that’s education. The process also enables me to see how their mind worked. By having them describe how they arrived at a result I can comment on it, and they can make use of my comment when they go back to the experiment. There’s a feedback that isn’t possible when the teacher just grades from numerical answers. Revising helps the students to rethink.”

“我希望他们先查阅文献，了解之前的实验是如何进行的，在实验室里会遇到什么情况，以及如何规划自己的实验。规划实验有助于他们边做边记录，让写作贯穿整个课堂和实验过程。如果他们遇到问题，可以解释自己是如何陷入困境的，这本身就是一种学习。这个过程也让我能够了解他们的思维方式。通过让他们描述得出结论的过程，我可以进行点评，而他们也可以在重新进行实验时参考我的点评。如果老师只是根据分数打分，就无法提供这种反馈。修改实验有助于学生重新思考。”

I don’t remember whether I cried “Eureka!” when I heard that. Not being Greek, I probably didn’t. But I do remember thinking I would probably never get a more concise statement of what writing across the curriculum is all about, or a better illustration of how the act of writing gives the teacher a window into the brain of his student. See Johnny reason! Watch him make a wrong turn! Follow his cogitations as he wonders what to do next!

我不记得听到这句话时是否惊呼“找到了！”。我不是希腊人，大概没有。但我记得当时我想，我可能再也听不到比这更简洁明了的跨学科写作阐述了，也再也听不到比这更生动的例证了写作如何让老师窥探学生的内心世界。瞧瞧约翰尼的思考！看他走错了路！听听他琢磨下一步该怎么做！

I thought of all the subjects where the teacher never gets this inside look, where students are graded solely on the basis of a right or a wrong answer. I don’t only mean hard sciences, like physics, that deal in numerical answers. The humanities and the social sciences also rely heavily on tests that measure a student’s learning by what he knows, not by how he got to know it: multiple-choice exams and “short-answer questions.” Economics, for example, is a discipline that rests finally on numbers and projections and probabilities—“answers,” as they might be loosely called. But the future economist should be as accountable as the future chemist for describing the steps that took him to his numerical result, and the economics teacher should be no less eager to read about the trip.

我想到了许多学科，在这些学科中，老师永远无法深入了解学生的学习过程，学生的成绩仅仅取决于答案的对错。我指的不仅仅是像物理这样以数值答案为主的硬科学。人文和社会科学也严重依赖于考试，这些考试衡量的是学生掌握了多少知识，而不是他们是如何获得这些知识的：选择题和“简答题”。例如，经济学最终也是建立在数字、预测和概率之上的——这些或许可以粗略地称为“答案”。但是，未来的经济学家应该像未来的化学家一样，有责任描述他们得出数值结果的步骤，而经济学老师也应该同样渴望了解学生的解题过程。

Eagerness to read and correct student writing, however, is not a commodity that grows on trees; it’s far easier to just check right and wrong answers. Unfortunately, there’s no quick and easy way to teach writing. When I first did it I assumed that a good part of the job could be accomplished by explaining in class the elements that constitute good writing. Surely if I assailed my students with my sacred principles of clarity and simplicity and brevity, if I exhorted them to use active verbs and short words and short sentences, if I pointed out the pitfalls that await the writer of a travel piece or a sports piece or an interview, they would go and do what I had told them to do.

然而，乐于阅读和批改学生作文并非易事；检查答案的对错显然要容易得多。遗憾的是，教授写作并没有什么捷径可走。我最初教写作时，以为只要在课堂上讲解优秀写作的要素，就能完成大部分工作。我当时的想法是，如果我向学生灌输清晰、简洁、精炼的写作原则，如果我鼓励他们使用主动语态、短词和短句，如果我指出游记、体育报道或采访稿写作中可能遇到的陷阱，他们肯定会照我说的去做。

No such transfer takes place. Writing teachers are lucky if 10 percent of what they said in class is remembered and applied. The bad habits are just too habitual. They can be cured only by that most painful of surgical procedures: operating on what the writer has actually written. Only there, where a writer is at his most vulnerable, having put some part of himself on paper, does he make the connection between principle and practice. The operation is almost as hard on the teacher. Like the parent who tells the spanked child that “this hurts me more than it hurts you,” the writing teacher wants nothing so much as a paper that’s well written—one that won’t mire him in endless repairs and emotional debris. I sometimes find myself emitting small moans as I start to read a paper and realize the magnitude of the problems ahead.

这种转化根本不会发生。写作老师如果课堂上讲的内容能被学生记住并运用，就算很幸运了。坏习惯根深蒂固，只能通过最痛苦的手术来纠正：对作者实际写出来的东西进行“手术”。只有在作者最脆弱、最脆弱的时候，当他把自己的一部分写在纸上时，他才能将理论与实践联系起来。这种“手术”对老师来说几乎同样痛苦。就像父母对被打的孩子说“我比你更疼”一样，写作老师最渴望的莫过于一篇写得好的文章——一篇不会让他陷入无休止的修改和情绪困扰的文章。有时，当我开始阅读一篇作文，意识到即将面临的问题有多么严重时，我也会忍不住发出低低的呻吟。

Why, then, would anyone in his right mind want to be a writing teacher? The answer is that writing teachers aren’t altogether in their right mind. They are in one of the caring professions, no more sane in the allotment of their time and energy than the social worker or the day care worker or the nurse. Whenever I hear them talk about their work, I feel that few forms of teaching are so sacramental; the writing teacher’s ministry is not just to the words but to the person who wrote the words. One of my hopes for writing across the curriculum is that teachers in many fields will discover this transaction. Through the writing of our students we are reminded of their individuality. We are reminded, whatever subject we are charged with teaching, that our ultimate charge is to produce broadly educated men and women with a sense of stewardship for the world they live in.

那么，究竟是什么人会想当写作老师呢？答案是，写作老师本身就不是完全理智的人。他们从事的是一种需要关怀的职业，在时间和精力的分配上，他们并不比社工、托儿所工作人员或护士更理智。每当我听到他们谈论自己的工作时，我都觉得很少有教学形式像写作老师那样具有神圣的意义；写作老师的职责不仅在于指导文字本身，更在于指导书写文字的人。我希望跨学科写作教学能够让各个领域的教师都体会到这种意义。通过学生的写作，我们能够感受到他们的独特性。无论我们教授什么科目，我们都会意识到，我们最终的使命是培养具有博学多才、对所处世界负有责任感的男女。

A funny thing happened on the way to that ideal when the first space satellite was launched by the Soviet Union in 1957. Overnight, Sputnik turned us into a nation obsessed by technology and determined to produce a bumper crop of technicians every year. Pure science has been an American deity ever since. Many science professors say that their discipline is now taught without any reference to its past traditions or to its present or future impact on society.

在通往理想的道路上，一件有趣的事情发生了：1957年苏联发射了第一颗人造卫星。一夜之间，人造卫星“斯普特尼克”使我们这个国家痴迷于科技，并决心每年培养出大批技术人才。自此以后，纯粹科学就成了美国人奉为圭臬。许多科学教授表示，如今的科学教学完全忽略了其历史传统，也忽视了其对社会的现在和未来影响。

“I was a Sputnik student,” Professor Potts told me. “I graduated from Oberlin in 1967, and the chemistry I was taught was all hard-core science. The only time you talked about values was over coffee. As a result, my generation of chemistry teachers has been afraid to get into the background of the subject because we were never exposed to it ourselves. But now colleges like ours are paying more attention to the history and the ethics of science. We’re also trying harder to reach the non-science student. This term, for instance, I’m teaching a course on hazardous wastes called ‘Chemical Time Bombs,’ and I’ve asked for a paper summing up the legal and ethical issues of Love Canal. That course wouldn’t have been taught ten years ago.”

“我曾是‘人造卫星’时代的学生，”波茨教授告诉我。“我1967年毕业于奥柏林学院，当时学的化学全是纯粹的硬科学。只有在喝咖啡的时候才会谈到价值观。因此，我们这代化学老师不敢深入探讨这门学科的背景，因为我们自己从未接触过。但现在像我们这样的大学越来越重视科学史和科学伦理。我们也在努力吸引非理科专业的学生。比如这学期，我开设了一门关于危险废物的课程，叫做‘化学定时炸弹’，我还要求学生写一篇论文，总结拉夫运河事件的法律和伦理问题。这门课在十年前是根本不可能开设的。”

If such values aren’t imparted in the classroom they will probably never get imparted; college students who are praised and coddled for acquiring technical knowledge aren’t likely to have an onset of ethics when they get out in the world of profit and loss. Yet moral dilemmas have never been woven so bewilderingly through American life. Every day we are assaulted by scientific or biomedical questions that we don’t even know how to think about, from toxic wastes and “Star Wars” and nuclear energy to acid rain and gene splicing and surrogate motherhood. Many of them are the legacy of scientists who now admit that they didn’t understand how their decisions would affect the quality of life, or life itself. Too many sick chickens have come home to roost. Too many lakes and rivers have died, too many fish and birds, too many people in states like Utah who had the bad luck to live downwind from the scientists. Too many names that we had never heard before—Bhopal, Chernobyl, Three Mile Island—have become instant synonyms for technology gone wrong.

如果课堂上不传授这些价值观，它们可能永远也无法传授；那些因掌握技术知识而受到赞扬和娇惯的大学生们，在步入充满盈亏的社会后，不太可能具备任何道德意识。然而，道德困境从未像现在这样令人困惑地交织在美国人的生活中。我们每天都受到各种科学或生物医学问题的冲击，这些问题我们甚至不知道该如何思考，从有毒废物、“星球大战”计划、核能到酸雨、基因拼接和代孕。其中许多问题都是一些科学家的遗留产物，他们现在承认，自己当初并不理解他们的决定会如何影响生活质量，甚至影响生命本身。太多恶果最终自食其果。太多湖泊河流干涸，太多鱼类和鸟类死亡，太多像犹他州这样不幸地住在科学家下风口的人们也深受其害。太多我们以前从未听说过的名字——博帕尔、切尔诺贝利、三里岛——瞬间成为了技术失控的代名词。

That’s why I liked the two trends that Professor Potts mentioned: educating future scientists to be more attuned to the impact of their work, and educating the rest of us to be more scientifically literate. It does us no good to just feel a growing sense of jeopardy over what the scientists are “up to.” As citizens we’re responsible for what we know and what we don’t know.

这就是我喜欢波茨教授提到的两个趋势的原因：一是培养未来的科学家，让他们更关注自身工作的影响；二是提升我们所有人的科学素养。仅仅对科学家们的“所作所为”感到日益增长的担忧对我们毫无益处。作为公民，我们有责任了解我们所知道的和我们所不知道的。

Where does writing figure in all this? Writing is a tool that enables people in every discipline to wrestle with facts and ideas. It’s a physical activity, unlike reading. Writing requires us to operate some kind of mechanism—pencil, pen, typewriter, word processor—for getting our thoughts on paper. It compels us by the repeated effort of language to go after those thoughts and to organize them and present them clearly. It forces us to keep asking, “Am I saying what I want to say?” Very often the answer is “No.” It’s a useful piece of information.

写作在这一切中扮演着怎样的角色？写作是一种工具，它使各个领域的人们都能与事实和思想进行对话。与阅读不同，写作是一种体力活动。它要求我们操作某种工具——铅笔、钢笔、打字机、文字处理软件——将我们的想法记录在纸上。它通过语言的反复运用，促使我们去追寻这些想法，并将它们组织起来，清晰地呈现出来。它迫使我们不断地问自己：“我表达清楚了吗？”很多时候，答案是“否”。而这本身就是一条有用的信息。

One of the most striking things I heard at Gustavus Adolphus came from a professor of philosophy, Deane Curtin. He said, “Many of my ‘A’ papers last term were ‘failures.’ A great paper in philosophy is often one that tells me why the student couldn’t get where he wanted to go. That’s progress. It’s better than deluding yourself that something was proved that really hadn’t been.”

我在古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院听到的最令人印象深刻的话之一，来自哲学教授迪恩·柯廷。他说：“上学期我批下来的很多‘A’级论文其实都是‘不及格’的。一篇优秀的哲学论文往往能告诉我，学生为什么没能达到他想要的目标。这才是进步。这比自欺欺人地认为某些实际上并未被证明的东西得到了证明要好得多。”

I liked the example because I’ve always believed that failure is one of the great teachers, every bit as instructive as success. It’s not, however, a point that Americans want to hear. Winning is the national creed. Forget the pursuit of happiness—is the kid an “achiever”? How we love the student who “tests” high. How we hate the football team that loses. Reading the letters in the Princeton Alumni Weekly , year after year, I marvel at how bothered this highly educated segment of the populace is by the fact that their alma mater can’t field a winning football team. There is no end of ululation in the letters column.

我喜欢这个例子，因为我一直认为失败是最好的老师之一，其教益丝毫不亚于成功。然而，美国人并不想听到这一点。胜利是他们的国民信条。别提追求幸福了——这孩子是不是个“成功者”？我们多么喜欢那些考试成绩高的学生，又多么痛恨那些输球的橄榄球队。每年读着《普林斯顿校友周刊》上的来信，我都会惊叹于这群受过高等教育的人竟然如此在意他们的母校无法组建一支常胜的橄榄球队。来信栏里充斥着无休止的抱怨。

But failure isn’t the end of the world, in football or anywhere else. In writing—and therefore in learning—it’s often the beginning of wisdom. The point came up again when a professor of religion, Garrett E. Paul, told me about his course in “Ethics in Business and Economics.” Early in the term he assigned his students a paper that would be read aloud in class.

但失败并非世界末日，无论是在足球场上还是其他任何领域。在写作中——因此在学习中——失败往往是智慧的开端。这一点在我听一位宗教学教授加勒特·E·保罗讲述他开设的“商业与经济伦理”课程时再次得到印证。学期伊始，他就布置了一篇论文，需要在课堂上朗读。

“It gets them to write for their peers and not for the teacher,” he told me, “and what they learned was a revelation to them. They learned by the presence or absence of response to what they had written. The good paper raised all the right questions, and on those days the paper would teach the class. The poor paper was instantly noticeable. There wouldn’t be much in it to discuss—there’d be no place to start, or it was so unclear that we’d have to go back over it and try to figure out what it was about. It made everybody in the class realize that a piece of writing is a piece of thinking. By the end of the term all the students said how much better they understood a subject by having to write about it.”

“这让他们为同伴而不是为老师写作，”他告诉我，“他们从中得到的收获对他们来说简直是醍醐灌顶。他们通过观察自己文章的反响来学习。好的文章会提出所有正确的问题，在那些日子里，文章本身就能启发全班。而差的文章则一眼就能看出来。这类文章没什么可讨论的——要么无从下手，要么晦涩难懂，我们不得不反复阅读，试图弄明白它到底在讲什么。这让班上的每个人都意识到，写作也是一种思考。学期结束时，所有学生都说，通过写作，他们对所学内容的理解有了显著的提高。”

Like his colleagues, Professor Paul had found many models of good writing in his discipline. One of his favorite assignments dealt with the issue of morality in advertising. Students were told to read a chapter on the “dependence effect” from John Kenneth Galbraith’s The Affluent Society and then to read a rebuttal by Friedrich von Hayek, called “The Non-Sequitur of the Dependence Effect.” (Both are in an anthology called Ethical Theory in Business .) “What I particularly pointed out,” Professor Paul said, “was the elegance of von Hayek’s argument. It’s elegant in the sense of a geometric argument: Everything that needs to be there is there, and the essay has nothing in it that doesn’t support the argument. I also emphasized to the students how short von Hayek’s answer is. I’m paying much more attention now to the quality of the writing that we discuss in class.”

和他的同事们一样，保罗教授在他的学科领域里也发现了许多优秀的写作范例。他最喜欢的一项作业是关于广告中的道德问题。他要求学生们阅读约翰·肯尼斯·加尔布雷思的《富裕社会》中关于“依赖效应”的章节，然后再阅读弗里德里希·冯·哈耶克的反驳文章《依赖效应的非逻辑推理》（两篇文章都收录在《商业伦理理论》一书中）。保罗教授说：“我特别强调的是冯·哈耶克论证的精妙之处。这种精妙体现在几何论证上：所有必要的要素都包含在内，文章中没有任何内容与论点相悖。我还向学生们强调了冯·哈耶克的回答有多么简洁。现在，我更加关注课堂上讨论的写作质量。”

So my two days at Gustavus Adolphus gave me a glimpse of most of the courses that might be encountered in a liberal education and of the role that writing could play in learning them. Some of the disciplines caught me unaware of how they had changed. A professor of geography, for instance, Robert B. Douglas, said that he now insists on writing as a major component of his classes. “I keep in touch with my recent graduates,” he told me, “and they all say that what they really needed in college were writing courses, because they now have jobs in fields like urban planning or retail store location, or in agencies for economic development or rural land use planning, and they have to write a great many reports, which have to be clear.”

在古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院的两天让我得以一窥博雅教育中可能遇到的大部分课程，以及写作在学习这些课程中所扮演的角色。有些学科的变化让我始料未及。例如，地理学教授罗伯特·B·道格拉斯告诉我，他现在坚持将写作作为课堂教学的重要组成部分。“我一直和最近的毕业生保持联系，”他告诉我，“他们都说，他们在大学里真正需要的是写作课程，因为他们现在从事城市规划、零售店选址、经济发展机构或农村土地利用规划等领域的工作，需要撰写大量清晰易懂的报告。”

To give his students due reverence for the mother tongue, Professor Douglas sends them to the books of his literary hero, J. B. Jackson—books such as The Necessity of Ruins and The Vernacular Landscape . “Every review of a new book by J. B. Jackson,” he said, “begins by calling attention to the clarity of his language, the brevity of his prose and the beauty of his style. I use him in two ways. I might tell a student, ‘Let’s see what Jackson has to say about the character of small towns in the Midwest, or about the grid plan of city streets.’ Later I get them to critique the writing style itself. Why is it so effective?”

为了让学生们对母语保持应有的尊重，道格拉斯教授让他们阅读他文学偶像J·B·杰克逊的作品，例如《废墟的必然性》和《乡土景观》。他说：“我对J·B·杰克逊新书的每一篇评论，都以强调他语言的清晰、散文的简洁和文风的优美为开篇。我运用他的作品有两种方式。我会告诉学生，‘我们来看看杰克逊是如何描述中西部小镇的风貌，或者城市街道的网格状布局的。’之后，我会让他们分析杰克逊的写作风格本身。为什么他的写作风格如此有效？”

Hearing from so many academic provinces, I occasionally wondered: What does the English department think of all this? I got my answer from Claude C. Brew, associate professor of English.

听取了这么多学术界的意见后，我偶尔会想：英语系对这一切有何看法？我从英语系副教授克劳德·C·布鲁那里得到了答案。

“Writing across the curriculum reinforces what we do,” he said, “and of course it gives writing a much broader base. That’s a healthy direction. In this country the English major has always been defined almost entirely in terms of literature and literary analysis, and therefore English department writing has a strong literary bias. In fact, the teaching of writing has only recently been incorporated in graduate English programs. Our education as English teachers never prepared us to do that.

“跨学科写作强化了我们的教学内容，”他说，“当然，它也为写作提供了更广泛的基础。这是一个健康的趋势。在这个国家，英语专业几乎完全以文学和文学分析为核心，因此英语系的写作带有浓厚的文学倾向。事实上，写作教学直到最近才被纳入英语研究生课程。我们作为英语教师所接受的教育从未让我们做好这方面的准备。”

“I was lucky in coming to Gustavus Adolphus because the college has a tradition that everybody in the English department teaches composition. I taught one course for five years in writing about science, which opened me to criticism from my department colleagues. But I learned something important: I got horribly literary papers from my students, because they thought that’s what an English teacher would want. They wrote things in those papers that they would never say. I tried to show them that science has a fine literature of its own. I got them reading the essays of Victor Weisskopf and books like Loren Eiseley’s The Immense Journey , Stephen Jay Gould’s Ever Since Darwin and Thomas Kuhn’s The Structure of Scientific Revolutions .”

“我很幸运能来到古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院，因为这所学院有个传统，英语系的每个人都要教写作。我教了一门关于科学写作的课程，教了五年，这让我受到了系里同事的批评。但我从中吸取了一个重要的教训：我收到的学生论文文笔糟糕透顶，因为他们觉得英语老师就应该写这种水平的论文。他们在论文里写的东西，他们平时根本不会说。我努力让他们明白，科学本身也有其独特的文学性。我让他们阅读维克多·魏斯科普夫的论文，以及洛伦·艾斯利的《漫长的旅程》、斯蒂芬·杰伊·古尔德的《自达尔文以来》和托马斯·库恩的《科学革命的结构》等书籍。”

I asked Professor Brew what he thought of the “comp/lit” double grade that many English departments use to distinguish between how a paper is written and what it says.

我问布鲁教授，他对许多英语系用来区分论文写作方式和论文内容的“写作/文学”双等级评分有何看法。

“I don’t approve of it,” he told me, “because it emphasizes the split. Writing is not divisible.” I was greatly cheered to hear this truth affirmed by a professor of English. Professors of English are by no means unanimously delighted to see “their” subject—writing—parceled out to teachers beyond the tribal walls. Chemistry teachers! Geography teachers! Many English teachers would rather hold on to the keys. Why, they ask, can’t they correct a chemistry paper for its writing and let the chemistry teacher correct it for its chemistry? The answer, of course, is that an act of writing is an act of thinking—an organic compound, as the chemists would say. There’s little point in having a teacher clean up the messy syntax in a chemistry paper if he can’t also clean up the messy chemistry. The indivisibility of language is what gives writing its authority and its majesty. Lewis Thomas writes eloquently about cell biology because in his bones he is a cell biologist. That he also happens to be a good writer is a bonus.

“我不赞成这样做，”他告诉我，“因为它强调了这种分裂。写作是不可分割的。”听到一位英语教授肯定了这一真理，我感到非常欣慰。英语教授们并非都乐于见到“他们”的学科——写作——被分配给其他学科的老师。化学老师！地理老师！许多英语老师宁愿自己掌握话语权。他们会问，为什么他们不能负责批改化学论文的写作部分，而让化学老师负责批改化学部分呢？答案当然是，写作本身就是一种思考——正如化学家所说，它是一种有机化合物。如果老师不能同时纠正化学论文中混乱的化学内容，那么让他去纠正化学论文中混乱的语法又有什么意义呢？语言的不可分割性赋予了写作权威和魅力。路易斯·托马斯之所以能以优美的文笔描写细胞生物学，是因为他骨子里就是一位细胞生物学家。他恰好也是一位优秀的作家，这无疑是锦上添花。

My last visitors at Gustavus Adolphus were two professors of nursing, Ann Garwick and Marilee Miller. Their appearance at the end of a long parade of academics took me by surprise. I was secure in my knowledge that nurses are primarily technicians and that most of them work in hospitals. What would technicians want with reading or writing or a baccalaureate education?

我在古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院的最后两位访客是护理学教授，安·加维克和玛丽莉·米勒。她们出现在一长串学者队伍的末尾，这让我感到很意外。我一直很确信，护士本质上是技术人员，而且她们大多数都在医院工作。技术人员要识字、写作或者接受本科教育有什么用呢？

The two women quickly set me straight. High technology has taken over many nursing tasks in hospitals, they said, and far more nurses are now out in the world of health care, keeping watch on some of our most important frontiers. “The value of a baccalaureate education for nurses today,” said Professor Miller, “is that it helps them to become leaders and decision-makers and advocates. The caring role is critical, and often nurses are the only people in a community who are in a position to see what’s happening to a family when something goes wrong—for instance, when the child of two working parents gets sick—and to find a solution.

两位女士很快纠正了我的误解。她们说，高科技已经取代了医院里许多护理工作，现在有更多的护士活跃在医疗保健领域，守护着我们一些最重要的前沿阵地。“如今，护士接受本科教育的价值在于，”米勒教授说，“它能帮助她们成为领导者、决策者和倡导者。护理工作至关重要，而且通常情况下，当家庭出现问题时——例如，双职工家庭的孩子生病了——护士是社区里唯一能够了解情况并找到解决方案的人。”

“We push our nurses to be agents of change on health issues: everything from seat belts to day care to the right of employees to know about hazardous substances in their work environment. We’re trying to make our nurses more socially aware and more politically astute. One course we require them to take is ‘American Minorities.’ It’s a sociology course that helps them to understand how to work with different cultural groups. There’s a big Southeast Asian population in Minneapolis, where many of them will be based.”

“我们鼓励护士们成为健康议题上的变革推动者：从安全带的使用、日托服务到员工了解工作环境中危险物质的权利，无所不包。我们努力提升护士们的社会意识和政治敏锐度。我们要求她们修读一门名为‘美国少数族裔’的课程。这是一门社会学课程，旨在帮助她们了解如何与不同的文化群体合作。明尼阿波利斯拥有庞大的东南亚裔人口，许多护士将在那里工作。”

Both professors make their students do extensive reading and writing. “We’re pushing them into the literature,” Professor Garwick said. “Among other things, we ask them to make a search of the pertinent journals and then to choose one article that particularly interests them and to write an annotated summary of it. Writing helps them to organize their plan of health care. It also expands their thinking and raises further questions that they ought to be asking. It’s exciting to work with our students on their successive drafts. A wonderful thing happens when they realize they don’t have to write in isolation—that they have a colleague who will go over their work with them—and when a section that had been giving them trouble just falls into place on the next draft.”

两位教授都要求学生进行大量的阅读和写作。“我们引导他们深入文献，”加维克教授说。“我们要求他们检索相关的期刊，然后选择一篇自己特别感兴趣的文章，并撰写一份带注释的摘要。写作有助于他们组织医疗保健计划，拓展思维，并提出他们应该思考的更多问题。与学生们一起修改他们的论文草稿是一件令人兴奋的事情。当他们意识到自己不必孤军奋战，有同学会和他们一起审阅论文时，那种感觉真是太棒了——之前让他们感到棘手的部分在下一稿中迎刃而解。”

Listening to the two women, caught up in their enjoyment of what they were teaching, I suddenly thought it was the most natural thing in the world that they had made reading and writing an integral part of their nursing courses. How else will we get the kind of nurses we need to make a difference in a society groping for decent health care? I had known all along that I liked the idea of writing across the curriculum. But nobody had told me how far across the curriculum it could reach.

听着两位女士兴致勃勃地讲解，我突然意识到，她们把阅读和写作融入护理课程是多么自然而然的事情。不然，我们又如何才能培养出真正能改变社会现状、为社会提供体面医疗保健的优秀护士呢？我一直都很喜欢跨学科写作的想法，但没人告诉我它的影响范围竟然如此之广。

# ↩

5. Crotchets and Convictions

5. 怪癖与信念

The artist Paul Klee once told his students that “art is exactitude winged by intuition.” I like that equally as a definition of good writing. One of the things I enjoy about Klee is his willingness to be surprised during the creative process by an antic idea. Paintings that might have been cold because of their exactitude are animated by humor, nonsense and whim. Klee’s humanity keeps jumping out of his material; I feel connected not only to the artist but to the man, especially because so much of the nonsense makes sense.

艺术家保罗·克利曾对他的学生说：“艺术是精准与直觉的完美结合。” 我觉得这句话同样适用于对优秀写作的定义。我欣赏克利的一点是，他乐于在创作过程中接受那些奇思妙想。那些原本可能因为过于精准而显得冷峻的画作，却因幽默、荒诞和奇思妙想而焕发生机。克利作品中的人性光辉不断涌现；我不仅与这位艺术家产生了共鸣，也与他本人产生了共鸣，尤其因为他作品中许多看似荒诞的元素都蕴含着深刻的意义。

As a writer I’m no less grateful than Klee presumably was for unexpected visitors from the subconscious mind. In this book, memory has already taken me down many roads where I hadn’t expected to go. I was startled, for instance, to find that I had forgotten all about the Latin teacher who so influenced me at Deerfield; the name Charles Huntington Smith and the silky white goatee jumped out at me in their full Victorian splendor. Once again I was struck by one of the miracles of the cognitive process—that the act of writing will summon from the buried past exactly what we need exactly when we need it. Memory and intuition and chance associations will always generate a certain percentage of what any writer writes. The remainder is generated by reason.

作为一名作家，我对潜意识中那些意想不到的访客的感激之情，丝毫不亚于克利。在这本书里，记忆已经引领我走过许多意想不到的道路。例如，我惊讶地发现，我竟然完全忘记了在迪尔菲尔德对我影响至深的拉丁语老师；查尔斯·亨廷顿·史密斯这个名字，以及他那丝滑的白色山羊胡，仿佛维多利亚时代的辉煌跃然纸上。我再次被认知过程的奇迹所震撼——写作能够从尘封的过去中，在我们需要的时候，精准地召唤出我们所需的一切。记忆、直觉和偶然的联想总会构成任何作家作品的一部分，而其余部分则源于理性。

Therefore, for the purposes of this book, I’ll generalize outrageously and state that there are two kinds of writing. One is explanatory writing: writing that transmits existing information or ideas. Call it Type A writing. The other is exploratory writing: writing that enables us to discover what we want to say. Call it Type B. They are equally valid and useful.

因此，为了本书的目的，我将大胆概括，指出写作有两种类型。一种是说明性写作：传递现有信息或观点的写作，我们称之为A类写作。另一种是探索性写作：帮助我们发现想要表达的内容的写作，我们称之为B类写作。这两种写作类型同样有效且实用。

As a teacher I’ve concentrated on Type A writing because it’s so badly needed. We are a society paralyzed by the inability to convey routine information—the inability of the executive to explain company policy in a memo to the staff, of the employee to explain his new idea in a proposal to the boss, of the bank to explain its “simplified” new bank statement to the customer, of the manufacturer to explain in a consumer manual how its product works, of the health and insurance professions to explain in a brochure how to get reimbursed for being sick, of the educator to explain in a letter how the school is educating our children, of the Internal Revenue Service to explain on its new tax form how to fill it out. Type A writing is what most people need to get through the day, both as writers and as readers. Its sole purpose is to inform; it has no deeper content that the writer will discover in the act of writing.

作为一名教师，我专注于A型写作，因为它的需求实在太迫切了。我们这个社会因为无法有效传递日常信息而陷入瘫痪——高管无法在备忘录中向员工解释公司政策，员工无法在提案中向老板阐述自己的新想法，银行无法向客户解释其“简化版”新银行对账单，制造商无法在消费者手册中解释产品工作原理，医疗和保险从业人员无法在宣传册中解释如何报销病假费用，教育工作者无法在信中解释学校如何教育我们的孩子，美国国税局无法在其新税表上解释如何填写。A型写作是大多数人日常生活中必不可少的，无论作为写作者还是读者。它的唯一目的是传递信息；它本身并不包含写作者在写作过程中能够发现的更深层次的内容。

My advice to Type A writers begins with one word: Think! Ask yourself, “What do I want to say?” Then try to say it. Then ask yourself, “Have I said it?” Put yourself in the reader’s mind: Is your sentence absolutely clear to someone who knows nothing about the subject? If not, think about how to make it clear. Then rewrite it. Then think: “What do I need to say next? Will it lead logically out of what I’ve just written? Will it also lead logically toward where I want to go?” If it will, write the sentence. Then ask yourself, “Did it do the job I wanted it to do, with no ambiguity?” If it did, think: “ Now what does the reader need to know?” Keep thinking and writing and rewriting. If you force yourself to think clearly you will write clearly. It’s as simple as that. The hard part isn’t the writing; the hard part is the thinking.

我对A型性格写作者的建议始于一个词：思考！问问自己：“我想表达什么？”然后试着表达出来。再问问自己：“我表达清楚了吗？”设身处地地站在读者的角度思考：对于一个对这个主题一无所知的人来说，你的句子是否完全清晰易懂？如果不是，想想如何才能让它清晰明了。然后重写。接着思考：“接下来我需要表达什么？它是否能合乎逻辑地衔接我刚才写的内容？它是否也能合乎逻辑地引出我想要表达的方向？”如果可以，就把这句话写下来。然后问问自己：“它是否达到了我想要的效果，没有丝毫歧义？”如果达到了，就思考：“现在读者还需要知道什么？”不断地思考、写作、修改。如果你强迫自己清晰地思考，你就能写出清晰的文章。就这么简单。难的不是写作，而是思考。

Type B writing—exploratory writing—requires no such cogitation, no prior decisions about which road to take; the road will reveal itself. Today many of America’s best writing teachers believe that this is the only kind of writing worth teaching, especially to young children. Unlike Type A writing, which they consider mainly a technical skill, Type B writing is a voyage of discovery into the self. Only by going into uncharted territory, they feel, can a writer find his potential and his voice and his meaning. Meaning, in fact, doesn’t exist until a writer goes looking for it.

B型写作——探索性写作——无需深思熟虑，无需预先决定该走哪条路；道路会自然而然地显现。如今，许多美国顶尖的写作教师认为，这才是唯一值得教授的写作类型，尤其对低龄儿童而言。与他们主要视为技巧的A型写作不同，B型写作是一次自我发现之旅。他们认为，只有踏入未知的领域，作家才能找到自己的潜能、表达自我、找到意义。事实上，意义只有在作家去寻找它时才会出现。

I don’t entirely buy that theory because I think both types of writing are necessary for survival and fulfillment. But I like the humanism behind it—the idea that writing is a means of growth and that it should never be without elements of joy and wonder. Nor do I think Type B writers are exempt from the laws of grammar and order. However subconsciously they may stumble on what they want to say, they are finally as obligated as every other writer to make themselves understood. “Free writing” is a search mechanism, not a license to let it all hang out.

我并不完全认同这种理论，因为我认为两种类型的写作对于生存和自我实现都至关重要。但我欣赏它背后的人文主义理念——写作是一种成长的途径，它应该始终充满乐趣和惊奇。我也不认为B型写作者可以凌驾于语法和秩序的规则之上。无论他们潜意识里多么磕磕绊绊地表达自己的想法，最终他们和其他所有写作者一样，都有义务让读者理解他们。“自由写作”是一种探索机制，而不是放任自流的通行证。

Such theorizing, however, is too vague to be useful here. It’s time to get down to fundamentals. What makes good writing good and bad writing bad? Here are some notions that are important to me.

然而，这种理论过于笼统，在这里并不适用。是时候回归本质了。好的写作和坏的写作，究竟是什么决定了它们的优劣？以下是我认为很重要的一些观点。

F ICTION AND N ONFICTION . This book has nothing to do with fiction. I’m dealing only with nonfiction, or factual writing, by which I mean all the kinds of writing that harness the world we live in and are therefore accountable to the truth. By contrast, the fiction writer—the writer of novels and short stories—is accountable only to his art. His gift is that he can take us into interior worlds where the fact-bound writer can’t go: worlds of imagination, rumination and fantasy. In return we enter into a more forgiving contract with him, allowing him to come at his subject slowly, discursively, obliquely, elliptically or just plain densely if that’s his vision. Density, in fact, is one of the qualities that William Faulkner’s fans most like about him.

虚构与非虚构。这本书与虚构无关。我只探讨非虚构作品，或者说纪实写作，我指的是所有那些反映我们所处世界、因而对真相负责的写作类型。相比之下，小说家——长篇小说和短篇小说的作者——只对其艺术负责。他的天赋在于，他能带领我们进入那些受制于事实的作家无法触及的内心世界：想象、沉思和幻想的世界。作为回报，我们与他达成了一种更为宽容的契约，允许他以缓慢、漫谈、迂回、省略，或者干脆晦涩的方式来阐述他的主题，如果这正是他的创作理念。事实上，晦涩正是威廉·福克纳的粉丝们最欣赏他的特质之一。

I’m not into density; I’d make a lousy editor for Henry James—I’d cut out all the elements that make him Henry James. But I respect every novelist’s right to do things his own way. I like Catch-22, Gravity’s Rainbow and Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance , for instance, because the authors of those three surrealistic novels—Joseph Heller, Thomas Pynchon and Robert Pirsig—invented their own rules, knowing that the old ones wouldn’t do the job they had in mind. Probably many people dislike those novels as much as I dislike Faulkner. But as readers of fiction we have no right to say that the author’s method was “wrong.” We can only say it didn’t work for us.

我并不喜欢晦涩难懂的风格；我肯定做不了亨利·詹姆斯的编辑——我会把所有构成他独特风格的元素都删掉。但我尊重每位小说家按照自己的方式来创作的权利。比如，我喜欢《第二十二条军规》、《万有引力之虹》和《禅与摩托车维修艺术》，因为这三部超现实主义小说的作者——约瑟夫·海勒、托马斯·品钦和罗伯特·皮尔西格——都创造了自己的规则，因为他们知道旧的规则无法满足他们的需求。或许很多人像我讨厌福克纳一样讨厌这些小说。但作为小说读者，我们无权断言作者的创作手法是“错误的”。我们只能说，这种手法对我们来说并不奏效。

No such immunity is granted the nonfiction writer. He can do all kinds of things wrong. He is endlessly accountable: to the facts, to the people he is writing about, to his “quotes,” to the mood, to the ethical nuances of the story. He is also accountable to his readers. They won’t put up with being delayed, lost, confused, bored or taken down unnecessary trails by failures of craft. Fiction may still be worshiped on the slopes of Parnassus as the higher form. But writing good nonfiction is in many ways harder and more exacting work.

非虚构作家没有这样的豁免权。他可能会犯各种各样的错误。他要对事实、对笔下的人物、对引用的内容、对故事的氛围、对故事中伦理的细微差别负责。他还要对读者负责。读者不会容忍因为写作技巧的缺陷而耽误时间、迷失方向、感到困惑、感到无聊，或者被引入不必要的歧途。小说或许仍然被奉为帕纳索斯山上的文学圣品，但写好非虚构作品在很多方面都更加艰难，也更加严谨。

I NFORMATION AND N OISE . One of the most helpful books I’ve read recently is Grammatical Man: Information, Entropy, Language, and Life , by Jeremy Campbell. It’s the story of “information theory,” a science that wasn’t born until World War II but whose laws have governed us since the first grunt. I bought Grammatical Man because I had begun to think of writing across the curriculum as a vast information system, and I remembered the stir the book caused at the Book-of-the-Month Club when it was published in 1982. We offered it because several of our editors were crazy about it—which is the best possible reason.

信息与噪声。我最近读过的最有帮助的书之一是杰里米·坎贝尔的《语法人：信息、熵、语言与生活》。这本书讲述了“信息论”的故事。信息论是一门二战后才诞生的科学，但它的规律却从人类文明的开端就一直影响着我们。我买这本书是因为我开始把跨学科写作看作一个庞大的信息系统，而且我还记得这本书在1982年出版时，在我们每月读书俱乐部引起的轰动。我们之所以推荐这本书，是因为我们的几位编辑都对它赞不绝口——这无疑是最好的理由。

The book is not only interesting; it’s a model of linear writing, leading the reader across rocky new terrain in steps of clarity and logic. Jeremy Campbell never fails to ask: “What would a novice need to know next? How can I explain it in the way that would be easiest to grasp?”

这本书不仅引人入胜，而且堪称线性写作的典范，它以清晰严谨的逻辑，一步步引导读者穿越崎岖的新领域。杰里米·坎贝尔始终不忘提问：“新手接下来需要了解什么？我该如何用最容易理解的方式解释呢？”

Here’s how he first tells his readers about the trip they are about to set out on, one that will take them through mechanisms of sending and receiving information as diverse as language, memory, dreams, artificial intelligence, probability theory, radar, electronics and the DNA code:

他首先向读者们讲述了他们即将踏上的旅程，这段旅程将带领他们了解发送和接收信息的机制，这些机制涵盖了语言、记忆、梦境、人工智能、概率论、雷达、电子学和 DNA 代码等诸多领域：

It was not until the 1940s that information was defined as a new scientific term, and this definition was quite new, unlike any in the standard dictionaries. Yet the concept of information, by being described precisely enough to satisfy mathematicians and telecommunications engineers, became increasingly fascinating for nonscientists. The word began to recapture some of its other meanings which had fallen into disuse. The view arose of information as an active agent, something that does not just sit there passively but “informs” the material world, much as the messages of the genes instruct the machinery of the cell to build an organism, or the signals from a radio transmitter guide the intricate path of a vehicle on its journey through space.

直到20世纪40年代，“信息”才被定义为一个新的科学术语，而且这个定义相当新颖，与标准词典中的任何定义都截然不同。然而，信息的概念由于其精确的描述足以满足数学家和电信工程师的需求，也开始吸引非科学家的目光。这个词开始重新唤起一些此前已被弃用的其他含义。人们逐渐认识到，信息是一种主动的媒介，它并非被动地存在，而是像基因的信息指导细胞机制构建生物体，或者无线电发射器的信号引导飞行器在太空中复杂的路径一样，影响着物质世界。

Thus information emerged as a universal principle at work in the world, giving shape to the shapeless, specifying the peculiar character of living forms and even helping to determine, by means of special codes, the patterns of human thought. In this way, information spans the disparate fields of space-age computers and classical physics, molecular biology and human communication, the evolution of language and the evolution of man.

因此，信息作为一种普遍原则在世界中发挥作用，它赋予无形之物以形态，阐明了生命形式的独特特征，甚至通过特殊的编码方式帮助确定了人类的思维模式。如此一来，信息便跨越了太空时代的计算机与经典物理学、分子生物学与人类交流、语言的演化与人类的演化等截然不同的领域。

Evidently nature can no longer be seen as matter and energy alone. Nor can all her secrets be unlocked with the keys of chemistry and physics, brilliantly successful as these two branches of science have been in our century. A third component is needed for any explanation of the world that claims to be complete. To the powerful theories of chemistry and physics must be added a late arrival: a theory of information. Nature must be interpreted as matter, energy, and information.

显然，我们不能再仅仅将自然视为物质和能量。化学和物理学这两门学科虽然在本世纪取得了辉煌的成就，但它们也无法解开自然的所有奥秘。任何声称能够完整解释世界的理论都需要第三个要素。除了强大的化学和物理学理论之外，我们还必须加入一个后来者：信息理论。自然必须被解释为物质、能量和信息的组合。

One of the recurring themes of Grammatical Man is the need to protect the integrity of the message. In information parlance, the enemy is “noise”—a perfect word for all the random interferences with what man or nature is trying to say. Noise is the typographical error and the poorly designed page and the caption that doesn’t quite explain what’s happening in the picture. Noise is handwriting that’s hard to read. Noise is distortion on the TV screen. Noise is the lapse of memory, the slip of the tongue, the wrong neuron fired by the brain—anything that brings disorder to the intended order of a message. So pervasive is noise, disorder being such a strong natural force, that nature has evolved an infinite number of backup systems for getting messages to their destination “more or less in the original form,” as Campbell puts it. “In nearly all forms of communication, more messages are sent than are strictly necessary to convey the information intended by the sender.”

《语法人》一书反复强调的主题之一是保护信息的完整性。在信息领域，敌人是“噪音”——这个词完美地概括了所有干扰人类或自然试图传达信息的随机因素。噪音包括排版错误、设计糟糕的页面、以及未能充分解释图片内容的说明文字。噪音包括难以辨认的字迹、电视屏幕上的失真、记忆失误、口误、大脑错误激活的神经元——任何会扰乱信息预期顺序的因素。噪音如此普遍，混乱又是如此强大的自然力量，以至于自然界进化出了无数的备用系统，以确保信息能够“或多或少地以原始形式”到达目的地，正如坎贝尔所说。“在几乎所有形式的交流中，发送的信息量都远远超过了发送者实际需要的信息量。”

Certainly writing is one of the main endeavors where disorder is more common than order. Murphy’s Law, which says that if something can go wrong it will, applies to the average sentence almost as inexorably as a law of physics. If you want a law of physics, I can commend (thanks to Grammatical Man ) the Second Law of Thermodynamics, which states that the tendency of energy is to decay in usefulness—a change for the worse known as entropy. I found it consoling after all these years to learn that writers are up against nothing less than the fundamental anarchy of the universe; entropy, prince of disorder, is sprinkling noise on everything we write. Ambiguity is noise. Redundancy is noise. Misuse of words is noise. Vagueness is noise. Jargon is noise. Pomposity is noise. Clutter is noise: all those unnecessary adjectives (“ongoing progress”), all those unnecessary adverbs (“successfully avoided”), all those unnecessary prepositions draped onto verbs (“order up”), all those unnecessary phrases (“in a very real sense”).

写作无疑是混乱远比秩序更为常见的领域之一。墨菲定律——凡事皆有可能出错——几乎像物理定律一样无情地适用于普通句子。如果你想找个物理定律，我可以推荐（感谢“语法先生”）热力学第二定律，它指出能量的有用性会衰减——这种向坏的方向变化被称为熵。多年后，我终于明白，作家们面对的正是宇宙的根本无序；熵，混乱之王，正将噪音洒向我们写的一切。歧义是噪音。冗余是噪音。用词不当是噪音。含糊不清是噪音。行话是噪音。自命不凡是噪音。冗余就是噪音：所有那些不必要的形容词（“持续进展”），所有那些不必要的副词（“成功避免”），所有那些附加在动词上的不必要的介词（“排序”），所有那些不必要的短语（“在某种意义上”）。

Information is your sacred product, and noise is its pollutant. Guard the message with your life.

信息是你的神圣产品，噪音是它的污染物。用生命守护信息。

O BSCURITY . Obscurity being one of the deadly sins, anyone might suppose that serious people would labor mightily to avoid it in their writing. But to suppose this is to overlook another force of nature that almost equals entropy as a drag on life’s momentum. That force is snobbery. Yes, gentle reader (as the Victorian novelists put it when they had to deal with the darker traits), it pains me to say that there are writers who actually want to be obscure. Their principal habitat is Academia, though they can be spotted without the aid of binoculars wherever intellectuals flock. Not for them the short words and active verbs and concrete details of ordinary speech; they believe that a simple style is the sign of a simple mind. Actually a simple style is the result of harder thinking and harder work than they are willing or able to do.

晦涩难懂。晦涩难懂是七宗罪之一，任何人都可能认为严肃的作家会竭尽全力避免在写作中陷入这种窠臼。但这种想法忽略了另一种自然力量，它几乎与熵一样，会阻碍人生的前进。这种力量就是势利眼。是的，亲爱的读者（正如维多利亚时代的作家在不得不面对这些阴暗面时所说的那样），我不得不遗憾地告诉您，确实有一些作家想要晦涩难懂。他们的主要栖身之地是学术界，不过无论知识分子聚集在哪里，不用望远镜也能一眼认出他们。他们不屑于使用日常口语中常见的简短词汇、生动的动词和具体的细节；他们认为简洁的文风是头脑简单的标志。事实上，简洁的文风恰恰是他们愿意或能够付出的更艰辛的思考和努力的结果。

The thought of a writer being deliberately unclear stirs such hostile vibrations in my breast that I’m going to let Sir Peter Medawar make the case for me; I can trust him not to foam at the mouth. Medawar was an English biologist who won the Nobel Prize for medicine in 1960. I had never heard of him until I began asking people for examples of good science writing and his name kept bobbing up in their replies. That struck me as a good omen, and I bought a book of his called Pluto’s Republic . The book takes its piquant title from a remark made by one of Sir Peter’s neighbors, who, knowing of his interest in philosophy, said, “Don’t you just adore Pluto’s Republic? ” It seemed to him an apt name for the “intellectual underworld”—various misconceptions about science—that his book explores. One of its essays, “Science and Literature,” has this to say about obscurity:

一想到作者故意晦涩难懂，我就感到一阵强烈的反感，所以我决定让彼得·梅达沃爵士来替我解释；我相信他不会气得跳脚。梅达沃是一位英国生物学家，1960年荣获诺贝尔生理学或医学奖。在此之前，我从未听说过他，直到我开始向人们征求优秀的科学写作范例，他的名字才频频出现在他们的回复中。这让我觉得是个好兆头，于是我买了一本他的书，名为《冥王星共和国》。这本书的书名颇具讽刺意味，源于梅达沃爵士的一位邻居的一句玩笑话。这位邻居知道梅达沃爵士对哲学感兴趣，便问道：“你难道不觉得《冥王星共和国》这本书很棒吗？” 在他看来，这个名字恰如其分地描述了梅达沃爵士在书中探讨的“知识分子地下世界”——各种关于科学的误解。书中一篇题为《科学与文学》的文章，对晦涩难懂的现象有如下论述：

In the eighteenth century obscurity was regarded as a disfigurement not merely of philosophic and scientific but also of theological prose. To conceal meaning (it was reasoned) is equally to conceal lack of meaning…. But even in those enlightened days the appeal of obscurity was clearly recognized. Of Dryden, Johnson said that “he delighted to tread upon the brink of meaning, where light and darkness begin to mingle.” Don’t we all, up to a point? We all recognize a voluptuary element in the higher forms of incomprehension and a sense of deprivation when matters which have hitherto been mysterious are now made clear.

在十八世纪，晦涩难懂不仅被视为哲学和科学散文的缺陷，也被视为神学散文的缺陷。人们认为，掩盖意义就等于掩盖意义的缺失……但即便在那个启蒙时代，晦涩难懂的魅力也显而易见。约翰逊曾评价德莱顿说：“他乐于涉足意义的边缘，那里光明与黑暗开始交融。”我们难道不都如此吗？在某种程度上，我们都能在更高层次的晦涩中感受到一种愉悦，也能在那些曾经神秘莫测的事物变得清晰明了时，感受到一种失落感。

The rhetorical use of obscurity, however, is a vice…. If the text is made hard to follow because of non sequiturs, digressions, paradoxes, impressive-sounding references to Gödel, Wittgenstein and topology, “in” jokes and a general determination to keep all vulgar sensibilities at bay, then we shall have great difficulty in finding out what the author intends us to understand. We shall have to reason it out therefore, much as we reasoned out a passage in some language we didn’t fully understand. In both texts some pretty strenuous reasoning may be interposed between the author’s conceptions and our understanding of them, and it is strangely easy to forget that in one case the reasoning was the author’s but in the other case our own. We have thus been the victims of a confidence trick.

然而，修辞上运用晦涩难懂却是一种弊端……如果文本因为不合逻辑的论述、离题的离题、悖论、故弄玄虚地引用哥德尔、维特根斯坦和拓扑学、内部笑话以及刻意回避一切庸俗情感而变得难以理解，那么我们就很难弄清作者究竟想让我们理解什么。因此，我们不得不像理解一段我们并不完全理解的语言文字那样，进行推理。在这两种情况下，作者的构想和我们对它们的理解之间都可能存在相当费力的推理，而我们却很容易忘记，在一种情况下，推理是作者的，而在另一种情况下，推理是我们自己的。就这样，我们成了骗局的受害者。

In all territories of thought which science or philosophy can lay claim to, including those upon which literature has also a proper claim, no one who has something original or important to say will willingly run the risk of being misunderstood; people who write obscurely are either unskilled in writing or up to mischief.

在科学或哲学可以涉足的所有思想领域，包括文学也可以涉足的领域，任何有原创性或重要观点要表达的人都不会甘愿冒被误解的风险；写作晦涩难懂的人要么写作技巧拙劣，要么居心叵测。

Medawar’s own style is worth noticing before we move on. The sentences are somewhat long, but they move persuasively and also with a certain grandeur. We’re in the company of a mind that has urbanity and wit and that is likable for its dislike of humbug.

在继续讨论之前，我们不妨先来了解一下梅达沃的个人风格。他的句子虽然略长，但行文流畅有力，又不失气势恢宏。我们仿佛置身于一位既有都市风范又充满智慧的作家之中，他厌恶虚伪做作，令人喜爱。

Probably the most engaging advice on obscurity comes from E. B. White, in Strunk and White’s The Elements of Style , a book every writer should read once a year. “Although there is no substitute for merit in writing,” White says, “clarity comes closest to being one. Even to a writer who is being intentionally obscure or wild of tongue we can say, ‘Be obscure clearly! Be wild of tongue in a way we can understand!’”

关于晦涩难懂的写作技巧，最引人入胜的建议或许要数E·B·怀特在斯特伦克和怀特合著的《风格的要素》一书中提出的，这本书每个作家都应该每年读一遍。怀特说：“虽然写作中没有任何东西可以替代才华，但清晰易懂是最接近才华的。即使对于故意晦涩难懂或辞藻华丽的作家，我们也可以说：‘晦涩难懂也要清晰！辞藻华丽也要用我们能理解的方式！’”

V OICE AND T ONE . Not long after reading Pluto’s Republic I bought a book by another Nobel Prize winner: Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman! by Richard N. Feynman, as told to Ralph Leighton.
