The island would generally be considered as very uninteresting; but to any one accustomed only to an English landscape, the novel aspect of an utterly sterile land possesses a grandeur which any more vegetation might spoil. A single green leaf can scarcely be discovered over wide tracts of the lava plains; yet flocks of goats, together with a few cows, contrive to exist.

从海上眺望，波尔图普拉亚附近地区呈现出一片荒凉景象。远古火山的烈焰和热带烈日的炙烤，使得大部分地区的土壤不再适宜植物生长。地势呈阶梯状起伏，间或点缀着一些截锥形的小山丘，地平线尽头是连绵起伏的巍峨群山。在这种气候下，透过朦胧的空气，眼前的景色别有一番趣味；当然，前提是，一个刚从海上归来，第一次漫步于椰子树林的人，除了自身的幸福感之外，还能对什么做出评判。这座岛屿通常会被认为乏味无趣；但对于一个只习惯了英国风景的人来说，这片完全荒芜的土地所展现出的新奇景象，却蕴含着一种独特的壮丽，任何植被的繁茂都可能破坏这种壮丽。在广袤的熔岩平原上，几乎找不到一片绿叶；然而，成群的山羊和几头牛却设法生存了下来。

So unendingly rich is The Voyage of the Beagle in its accounts of animals, birds and the whole panoply of natural life that I could quote from any of its five hundred pages. I’ve chosen the following episode because it takes place in the Galapagos archipelago, which was of course the expedition’s pivotal landfall, enabling Darwin, because of the long isolation of those islands from nature’s chain, to study animal forms that didn’t exist anywhere else and thus to glimpse his theory of the origin of species and the survival of the fittest.

《贝格尔号航行记》对动物、鸟类以及整个自然界的描述如此丰富，我可以从五百页中的任何一页引述。我之所以选择以下这段，是因为它发生在加拉帕戈斯群岛，而加拉帕戈斯群岛正是这次探险的关键登陆点。由于这些岛屿长期与世隔绝，达尔文得以研究其他任何地方都不存在的动物形态，从而初步了解了他的物种起源和适者生存理论。

It is now the fall of 1835; the Beagle has been at sea for almost four years. But Darwin has lost none of his reportorial zest as he describes a lizard that even he seems to regard as one of evolution’s oddballs:

现在是1835年秋天；“贝格尔号”已经在海上航行了近四年。但达尔文仍然保持着他作为记者的热情，他描述着一种蜥蜴，就连他自己似乎也认为这种蜥蜴是进化论中的一个怪胎：

The Amblyrhynchus, a remarkable genus of lizards, is confined to this archipelago. There are two species, resembling each other in general form, one being terrestrial and the other aquatic. The latter species (A. cristatus) was first characterized by Mr. Bell, who well foresaw from its short, broad head, and strong claws of equal length, that its habits of life would turn out very peculiar, and different from those of its nearest ally, the Iguana. It is extremely common on all the islands throughout the group, and lives exclusively on the rocky sea-beaches, being never found, at least I never saw one, even ten yards in-shore. It is a hideous-looking creature, of a dirty black color, stupid, and sluggish in its movements. The usual length of a full-grown one is about a yard, but there are some even four feet long; a large one weighed twenty pounds.

钝吻蜥属（Amblyrhynchus）是一种奇特的蜥蜴，仅分布于此群岛。该属有两个物种，外形大致相似，一个是陆生的，另一个是水生的。后者（A. cristatus）最早由贝尔先生描述，他从其短而宽的头部和等长的强壮爪子上，敏锐地预见到它的生活习性会非常独特，与它最近的近亲鬣蜥截然不同。这种蜥蜴在整个群岛的各个岛屿上都非常常见，它们只生活在岩石海滩上，至少我从未见过它们靠近海岸十码远的地方。这种蜥蜴外形丑陋，通体脏黑，行动迟缓愚钝。成年钝吻蜥的体长通常约为一码，但也有一些长达四英尺；一只体型较大的钝吻蜥重达二十磅。

Their tails are flattened sideways, and all four feet partially webbed. They are occasionally seen some hundred yards from shore, swimming about…. This lizard swims with perfect ease and quickness, by a serpentine movement of its body and flattened tail—the legs being motionless and closely collapsed on its sides. A seaman on board sank one, with a heavy weight attached to it, thinking thus to kill it directly; but when, an hour afterwards, he drew up the line, it was quite active. Their limbs and strong claws are admirably adapted for crawling over the rugged and fissured masses of lava, which everywhere form the coast. In such situations, a group of six or seven of these hideous reptiles may oftentimes be seen on the black rocks, a few feet above the surf, basking in the sun with outstretched legs.

它们的尾巴扁平向两侧，四肢部分蹼状。偶尔会在离岸几百码的地方看到它们游来游去……这种蜥蜴游得轻松自如，速度极快，身体和扁平的尾巴像蛇一样蜿蜒摆动——四肢则一动不动地紧贴身体两侧。船上的一名水手曾用重物吊起一只蜥蜴，想直接杀死它；但一个小时后，当他收起绳索时，发现它依然活动自如。它们的四肢和强壮的爪子非常适合在崎岖不平、裂缝纵横的熔岩上爬行，这些熔岩遍布海岸线。在这种情况下，人们常常可以看到六七只这种丑陋的爬行动物聚集在离海浪几英尺高的黑色岩石上，伸展着四肢晒太阳。

I opened the stomachs of several and found them distended with minced sea-weed (Ulvae), which grows in thin foliaceous expansions of bright green or a dull red color. I do not recollect having observed this sea-weed in any quantity on the tidal rocks; and I have reason to believe it grows at the bottom of the sea, at some little distance from the coast. If such be the case, the object of these animals occasionally going out to sea is explained. The stomach contained nothing but the sea-weed. Mr. Bynoe, however, found a piece of a crab in one; but this might have got in accidentally, in the same manner as I have seen a caterpillar, in the midst of some lichen, in the paunch of a tortoise.

我剖开了几只动物的胃，发现里面塞满了切碎的海藻（浒苔），这种海藻呈薄片状，颜色有亮绿色和暗红色。我不记得在潮间带的岩石上见过这种海藻，而且我有理由相信它生长在离海岸不远的海底。如果真是这样，就能解释这些动物偶尔出海的原因了。胃里除了海藻什么也没有。不过，拜诺先生在一只动物的胃里发现了一块螃蟹肉；但这可能是偶然混进去的，就像我曾经在乌龟的肚子里，在某种地衣丛中看到过毛虫一样。

Notice how welcome it is to hear about human activity in the midst of so much scientific activity. Darwin keeps reminding us that this is an expedition and that science is done by people, usually in collaboration. The references to Mr. Bell, who first surmised that the lizard would turn out very peculiar; to Mr. Bynoe, who evidently was just as inquisitive as Darwin about the contents of its stomach, and to the seaman who found the lizard “quite active” after sinking it for an hour with a weight—these vignettes give us a sense of being along on the Beagle’s voyage. We get a feeling for the dailiness of scientific research: the steady accretion of facts about the lizards basking on the beach but not venturing ten yards inland (“at least I never saw one”). Caught up in the general curiosity, we’re eager to learn what else Darwin found out about this unlovely specimen.

在如此密集的科学活动中，听到人类活动的描述是多么令人欣喜。达尔文不断提醒我们，这是一次探险，科学是由人完成的，而且通常是合作完成的。文中提到贝尔先生，他最先推测这种蜥蜴会非常奇特；提到拜诺先生，他显然和达尔文一样对蜥蜴的胃内容物充满好奇；还提到那位水手，他用重物将蜥蜴沉入水中一小时后发现它“非常活跃”——这些小故事让我们仿佛置身于贝格尔号的航行之中。我们感受到科学研究的日常性：不断积累着关于蜥蜴的发现，它们在沙滩上晒太阳，却不敢冒险进入内陆十码（“至少我从未见过一只”）。我们被这种普遍的好奇心所吸引，渴望了解达尔文对这个并不讨喜的标本还有哪些发现。

The intestines were large, as in other herbivorous animals. The nature of this lizard’s food, as well as the structure of its tail and feet, and the fact of its having been seen voluntarily swimming out at sea, absolutely prove its aquatic habits; yet there is in this respect one strange anomaly, namely, that when frightened it will not enter the water. Hence it is easy to drive these lizards down to any little point overhanging the sea, where they will sooner allow a person to catch hold of their tails than jump into the water. They do not seem to have any notion of biting; but when much frightened they squirt a drop of fluid from each nostril. I threw one several times as far as I could, into a deep pool left by the retiring tide; but it invariably returned in a direct line to the spot where I stood. It swam near the bottom, with a very graceful and rapid movement, and occasionally aided itself over the uneven ground with its feet. As soon as it arrived near the edge, but still being under water, it tried to conceal itself in the tufts of sea-weed, or it entered some crevice. As soon as it thought the danger was past, it crawled out on the dry rocks and shuffled away as quickly as it could.

与其他草食动物一样，这种蜥蜴的肠道很大。它的食物种类、尾巴和脚的结构，以及人们曾目睹它主动游向大海的事实，都充分证明了它的水生习性；然而，在这方面却有一个奇怪的例外，那就是它受到惊吓时不会下水。因此，很容易就能把这些蜥蜴赶到任何露出海面的小岬角，在那里，它们宁愿让人抓住它们的尾巴，也不愿跳进水里。它们似乎没有咬人的本能；但当极度惊恐时，它们会从每个鼻孔喷出一滴液体。我曾多次将一只蜥蜴扔到退潮后留下的深水潭里，力道之远，但它总是径直游回我站立的地方。它在水底附近游动，动作非常优美而迅速，偶尔会用脚在不平坦的海底滑行。它一靠近边缘，但仍在水下，就试图把自己藏在海藻丛中，或者钻进某个缝隙里。一旦觉得危险过去，它就爬到干燥的岩石上，尽快溜走了。

I several times caught this same lizard, by driving it down to a point, and though possessed of such perfect powers of diving and swimming, nothing would induce it to enter the water; and as often as I threw it in, it returned in the manner above described. Perhaps this singular piece of apparent stupidity may be accounted for by the circumstance that this reptile has no enemy whatever on shore, whereas at sea it must often fall a prey to the numerous sharks. Hence, probably, urged by a fixed and hereditary instinct that the shore is its place of safety, whatever the emergency may be, it there takes refuge….

我曾多次捕捉到这只蜥蜴，把它赶到一处岬角，尽管它拥有高超的潜水和游泳技巧，却怎么也不肯下水；每次我把它扔进水里，它都会像上面描述的那样爬回来。或许这种奇特的愚蠢行为可以解释为：这种爬行动物在陆地上没有任何天敌，而在海里却经常成为众多鲨鱼的猎物。因此，很可能是出于一种根深蒂固的本能，认为海岸是它的避难所，无论遇到什么紧急情况，它都会躲在那里……

I asked several of the inhabitants if they knew where it laid its eggs; they said that they knew nothing of its propagation, although well acquainted with the eggs of the land kind—a fact, considering how very common this lizard is, not a little extraordinary.

我问了几位居民是否知道它在哪里产卵；他们说他们对这种蜥蜴的繁殖一无所知，尽管他们对陆生蜥蜴的卵很熟悉——考虑到这种蜥蜴非常常见，这确实有点不寻常。

That’s the writing of a scientist totally committed to his subject. But Darwin never forgets that the purpose of his writing is to transmit information. The Voyage of the Beagle is above all supremely useful—which is its supreme strength. Nonfiction writing should always have a point: It should leave the reader with a set of facts, or an idea, or a point of view, that he didn’t have before he started reading. Writers may write for any number of good personal reasons—ego, therapy, recollection, validation of their lives. But what they produce will have a validity of its own to the extent that it’s useful to somebody else.

这是出自一位全身心投入研究领域的科学家之手。但达尔文始终铭记，他写作的目的是传递信息。《贝格尔号航行记》最重要的价值在于其极高的实用性——这正是它最大的优势。非虚构类作品必须始终具有意义：它应该让读者在阅读之前获得一些新的事实、想法或观点。作家写作的理由可能多种多样，出于各种正当的个人原因——满足虚荣心、寻求精神慰藉、回忆往事、肯定人生价值等等。但他们的作品只有在对他人有用时，才具有其自身的价值。

It’s not necessary to be Darwin, however, to write helpfully about the natural world. There’s plenty of important writing to be done about the animals, fish and birds in our own increasingly crowded habitat. I’m a fan, for instance, of a magazine called Missouri Conservationist , which performs the genial tightrope act of telling the people of Missouri both how to enjoy their state and how to take care of it. Its articles aren’t shrill or punitive; they never say: “Don’t hunt and don’t fish.” What they do say is: “Be informed. Know the facts.” The following passage is from an article by Tom R. Johnson, a herpetologist, which tries to allay the “needless anxiety and fear” associated with water snakes:

然而，要写出有益于自然界的文章，并不需要成为达尔文。在我们日益拥挤的栖息地中，关于动物、鱼类和鸟类，有很多重要的文章值得撰写。例如，我非常喜欢一本名为《密苏里州自然保护主义者》（Missouri Conservationist）的杂志，它巧妙地平衡了如何既享受密苏里州的自然风光，又保护它的重要性。它的文章既不尖锐也不带有惩罚性；它们从不说：“不要打猎，不要钓鱼。”它们说的是：“要了解情况，要知道事实。”以下段落摘自爬虫学家汤姆·R·约翰逊（Tom R. Johnson）的一篇文章，这篇文章试图消除人们对水蛇的“不必要的焦虑和恐惧”：

Water snakes are often classed as “pugnacious” by people who have tried to capture them. As with many forms of wild-life, these snakes will not hesitate to defend themselves. If grabbed by a person, a water snake will thrash about violently, reach around and bite, and also smear a foul-smelling musk from glands in the base of the tail. Contrary to popular belief, water snakes can and do bite while underwater, either to defend themselves or to catch prey. In all cases, however, the bite caused by a water snake produces mild scratches and nothing more.

水蛇常被试图捕捉它们的人描述为“好斗”。和许多野生动物一样，这些蛇会毫不犹豫地进行自卫。如果被人抓住，水蛇会剧烈挣扎，伸出触手咬人，还会从尾巴根部的腺体分泌出一种难闻的麝香。与人们普遍的认知相反，水蛇在水下也会咬人，可能是为了自卫或捕食。但无论如何，水蛇的咬伤通常只会造成轻微的擦伤，不会造成更严重的伤害。

What do water snakes eat? I wish more people would ask this question before killing water snakes. Many people have the mistaken idea that these animals eat too many fish and are not good for anything. Some people who fish look upon water snakes as competitors for game fish and try to kill every snake they see. Just the opposite is true. Water snakes predominantly eat nongame fish—especially diseased or injured ones. A number of studies have shown that water snakes pose no threat to fish populations or to our sport fisheries. They add to the aquatic environment both as predator and prey. Besides fish, water snakes eat frogs and tadpoles, salamanders and crayfish. Young water snakes are food for bass, pickerel, goggle-eye, bullfrogs, mink, otter and herons.

水蛇吃什么？我希望更多人在杀死水蛇之前能问问这个问题。许多人误以为这些动物吃太多鱼，对环境毫无益处。一些钓鱼爱好者把水蛇视为垂钓的竞争对手，看到蛇就想杀。事实恰恰相反。水蛇主要以非垂钓鱼类为食，尤其是患病或受伤的鱼类。许多研究表明，水蛇对鱼类种群或我们的垂钓活动不构成威胁。它们作为捕食者和猎物，对水生环境都有益。除了鱼类，水蛇还吃青蛙和蝌蚪、蝾螈和螯虾。幼蛇是鲈鱼、梭鲈、大眼鲷、牛蛙、水貂、水獭和苍鹭的食物。

Another reason why people who fish do not enjoy seeing water snakes is that they think these snakes are aggressive. I have had people tell me about snakes that “came right after them” or that “tried to get into their boat.” This does actually happen, but not because of aggression. Water snakes locate their prey—diseased or injured fish—by smell. An injured fish gives off an odor that is quickly picked up by a water snake’s tongue. A successful fisherman, surrounded by the odor of injured fish, may find himself in the company of a hungry snake with one thing on its mind: “Where’s the fish?” This is not aggression; it is a reaction to a possible food source. The snake is just doing its job as predator or scavenger and is not after the person fishing.

钓鱼爱好者不喜欢看到水蛇的另一个原因是他们认为这些蛇具有攻击性。我曾听人说过，蛇“直接追着他们跑”或者“试图爬进他们的船里”。这种情况确实会发生，但并非出于攻击性。水蛇通过嗅觉寻找猎物——生病或受伤的鱼。受伤的鱼会散发出一种气味，水蛇的舌头能迅速捕捉到这种气味。一个钓鱼成功的渔夫，周围弥漫着受伤鱼的气味，可能会发现自己身边有一条饥饿的水蛇，它脑子里只有一个念头：“鱼在哪儿？” 这并非攻击性行为，而是对潜在食物来源的反应。水蛇只是在履行其作为捕食者或食腐动物的职责，并非针对钓鱼的人。

But (I hear you saying) can’t we please have some ordinary animals? Cows, maybe. Or pigs. Fair enough—most of us get through our allotted span without running into a water snake, a giant sea turtle or an Amblyrhynchus cristatus. So I’ll conclude with two forms of natural life that there’s no getting away from: insects and birds.

但是（我仿佛听到你们在说），难道我们就不能说说一些普通的动物吗？比如牛，或者猪。好吧——我们大多数人一生中都不会遇到水蛇、巨型海龟或者凤头钝吻蝠。所以，最后我想说说两种我们无法回避的自然生物：昆虫和鸟类。

In the literature of insects one name towers over all others: the French entomologist J. Henri Fabre. That’s my main reason for including him here—it’s always a pleasure to see giants at work. But I have two further reasons. One has to do with translation. Because Fabre was French, his work raises the question of what qualities enable writing to cross over into another language. My other reason has to do with drive. Because of the astonishing curve of Fabre’s career he should be the patron saint of all those people who say they’d “like to try a little writing sometime” when they retire from the boring job they’re doing now.

在昆虫学文献中，有一个名字鹤立鸡群：法国昆虫学家让·亨利·法布尔。这正是我把他列入此书的主要原因——欣赏巨匠的杰作总是令人欣喜。但我还有两个原因。其一与翻译有关。由于法布尔是法国人，他的作品引发了一个问题：究竟是什么特质使得文字能够跨越语言的界限，被翻译成另一种语言？我的另一个原因则与动力有关。鉴于法布尔惊人的学术成就，他应该成为所有那些退休后想“尝试写作”的人们的守护神。

Born in 1823, the son of peasants in Provence, Fabre spent the bulk of his life in poverty, piecing together academic odd jobs—teaching and writing instructional science books—that barely supported him and his family. On Thursday afternoons, the traditional half-day of French education, and on summer holidays he studied the insect world. Not until he was fifty-five had he saved enough money to buy his first piece of land—an arid tract outside the village of Serignan, which was unfit for grazing or agriculture but ideal for wasps, wild bees and other insects that he wanted to study and write about for the remainder of his days. Thus began his monumental work, Souvenirs Entomologiques , which would take him twenty-eight years to complete. Its ten volumes attracted so little attention as they periodically came off the press that nobody could have foreseen how the long saga would finally end.

法布尔1823年出生于普罗旺斯的一个农民家庭，一生大部分时间都在贫困中度过，靠着教书、写科普书籍等零工勉强糊口。每周四下午，也就是法国传统的半天课时，以及暑假期间，他都会潜心研究昆虫世界。直到55岁，他才攒够钱买下第一块地——塞里尼昂村外的一片干旱土地。这块地不适合放牧或耕种，但却是黄蜂、野生蜜蜂和其他他想研究和记录的昆虫的理想栖息地，他希望用余生来研究和记录这些昆虫。就这样，他开始了鸿篇巨著《昆虫学回忆录》（Souvenirs Entomologiques）的创作，这部著作耗费了他28年的时间才完成。这部十卷本的著作断断续续地出版，却鲜有人问津，以至于没有人能够预料到这部漫长的史诗最终会以怎样的结局收尾。

As Edwin Way Teale tells the story in the introduction to his anthology The Insect World of J. Henri Fabre: “His long years of neglect, his decades of painstaking labor, ended in five exhausting years of fame. Fabre was eighty-four when the last of the ten volumes of his magnum opus appeared. Soon afterwards, he was suddenly discovered by such eminent literary figures as Maurice Maeterlinck, Edmond Rostand and Romain Rolland. A jubilee in his honor was held at Sérignan in 1910. Government officials and representatives of scientific institutions and societies did him homage. A statue was erected in the village. People who had never heard of the ‘Insect’s Homer’ began reading his books at home and abroad. Scientific societies in London, Brussels, Stockholm, Geneva and St. Petersburg elected him to membership. The government bestowed upon him an annual pension of $400. The president of France journeyed to Sérignan to meet its first citizen. After the long years of poverty, of labor, of niggardly recognition, Fabre, nearing his ninetieth year, saw with his failing eyesight the sunshine of brilliant acclaim.”

正如埃德温·韦·蒂尔在其文集《J·亨利·法布尔的昆虫世界》的引言中所述：“他多年来的默默无闻，以及数十年的辛勤耕耘，最终成就了他五年令人筋疲力竭的辉煌。法布尔八十四岁时，他的十卷巨著的最后一卷问世。不久之后，他突然被莫里斯·梅特林克、埃德蒙·罗斯丹和罗曼·罗兰等著名文学家所发现。1910年，塞里尼昂为他举行了纪念活动。政府官员、科研机构和学会的代表纷纷向他致敬。村里竖立了一座他的雕像。那些从未听说过这位‘昆虫界的荷马’的人们开始在国内外阅读他的作品。伦敦、布鲁塞尔、斯德哥尔摩、日内瓦和圣彼得堡的科学学会都选举他为会员。政府授予他每年400美元的养老金。法国总统专程前往塞里尼昂会见这位杰出的公民。漫长的岁月之后……”经历了贫困、辛劳和吝啬的认可之后，年近九十的法布尔用他日渐衰退的视力看到了辉煌赞誉的阳光。

That his writing could make friends in so many countries, surviving the usual perils of translation, was no accident. “I have always thought that the quality of being readily rendered into a foreign tongue is a test of good writing,” said the translator of Fabre’s works into English, Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. “It is the tortured, labored, fantastic, would-be ‘original’ style that hampers the translator. Fabre’s style is invariably straightforward.”

他的作品能在如此多的国家广受欢迎，并经受住了翻译过程中常见的种种考验，绝非偶然。“我一直认为，作品能否被轻易翻译成外语是衡量其好坏的标准，”法布尔作品的英文译者亚历山大·特谢拉·德·马托斯说道，“那些矫揉造作、故作姿态、故弄玄虚、试图保持‘原汁原味’的风格才是阻碍译者发挥的。法布尔的风格总是直白易懂。”

What had formed the straightforward style was the discipline of cranking out textbooks that popularized science by presenting it to students in prose that was both simple and interesting. It was writing that paid the bills and taught Fabre a craft. Later, when he could at last turn to the work that had been in his heart all along, he added the priceless gift of enthusiasm—an ingredient mentioned in this book with shameless frequency. He also brought the gift of his personality, one that took me by surprise with its warmth and humor; somehow I had never connected the words “charm” and “entomologist.” My interest in insects has been always minimal and often adversarial—the mosquito and the hornet and the cockroach have seen to that. But my interest in Fabre’s interest in insects is high. The transaction between a writer and his subject is the central relationship in nonfiction.

这种直白的写作风格源于他日复一日地撰写科普教科书的习惯，他用简洁有趣的散文向学生普及科学知识。写作不仅让他维持生计，也让他掌握了一门技艺。后来，当他终于可以从事自己一直以来真正热爱的工作时，他又增添了一份无价的热情——本书中对此毫不掩饰地反复提及。他还带来了他独特的人格魅力，这种魅力和幽默让我感到惊喜；我之前从未将“魅力”和“昆虫学家”这两个词联系起来。我对昆虫的兴趣一直很淡薄，甚至常常带有敌意——蚊子、黄蜂和蟑螂就足以证明这一点。但我对法布尔对昆虫的兴趣却非常感兴趣。在非虚构作品中，作家与写作对象之间的互动是核心所在。

Here’s how one of Fabre’s chapters begins:

以下是法布尔其中一章的开头：

Among the treasures of my laboratory I place in the first rank an ant-hill of Polyergus rufescens , the celebrated Red Ant, the slave-hunting Amazon. Unable to rear her family, incapable of seeking her food, of taking it even when it is within her reach, she needs servants who feed her and undertake the duties of housekeeping. The Red Ants make a practice of stealing children to wait on the community. They ransack the neighboring ant-hills, the home of a different species; they carry away nymphs, which soon attain maturity in the strange house and become willing and industrious servants.

在我实验室的众多珍宝中，最珍贵的莫过于红蚁（Polyergus rufescens）的蚁丘，这种蚂蚁被誉为著名的红蚁，如同奴隶贩卖的亚马逊女战士。它无法养育后代，也无法觅食，即便食物近在咫尺，它也无力取用。因此，它需要仆人来喂养它，并承担家务。红蚁们惯于偷走幼蚁来服侍蚁群。它们会洗劫邻近的蚁丘——那是另一种蚂蚁的家园；它们掳走幼蚁，这些幼蚁很快便会在陌生的巢穴中长大，成为勤劳而心甘情愿的仆人。

When the hot weather of June and July sets in, I often see the Amazons leave their barracks of an afternoon and start on an expedition. The column measures five or six yards in length. If nothing worthy of attention be met upon the road, the ranks are fairly well maintained; but, at the first suspicion of an ant-hill, the vanguard halts and deploys in a swarming throng. Scouts are sent out; the Amazons recognize that they are on a wrong track; and the column forms again. It resumes its march, crosses the garden paths, disappears from sight in the grass, reappears farther on, threads its way through the heaps of dead leaves, comes out again and continues its search. At last, a nest of Black Ants is discovered. The Red Ants hasten down to the dormitories where the nymphs lie and soon emerge with their booty. Then we have, at the gates of the underground city, a bewildering scrimmage between the defending blacks and the attacking reds. The struggle is too unequal to remain indecisive. Victory falls to the reds, who race back to their abode, each with her prize, a swaddled nymph, dangling from her mandibles.

六七月份天气炎热时，我常常看到亚马逊女战士们在午后离开营房，开始远征。队伍绵延五六码长。如果路上没有发现什么值得注意的东西，队伍就能保持整齐；但只要一发现蚁丘的迹象，先锋队就会立刻停下，四散开来。侦察兵被派出去；亚马逊女战士们意识到她们走错了路；队伍重新集结。她们继续行进，穿过花园小径，消失在草丛中，又在更远的地方出现，穿过成堆的落叶，再次出现，继续搜索。最终，她们发现了一个黑蚁巢穴。红蚁们迅速赶到蚁后们的宿舍，很快就带着战利品出来了。然后，在地下城的城门前，我们看到了一场混乱的混战，防守的黑蚁和进攻的红蚁之间爆发了激烈的冲突。这场斗争实力悬殊，无法继续犹豫不决。最终胜利属于红色阵营，她们争先恐后地返回巢穴，每人嘴里都叼着自己的战利品——一个裹在襁褓中的仙女。

Obviously Fabre has been well served by his translator, De Mattos, a man sensitive to language and rhythm and to the nuance that prefers a particular word to its near neighbor. But even a poor translator couldn’t kill a style that moves with such narrative certainty. Fabre is telling us the story of a raid; he could be talking about the Comanches swooping down on Fort Dodge. The return trip is no less vivid:

显然，法布尔的译者德·马托斯功不可没，他是一位对语言、韵律以及细微差别都非常敏感的译者，能够精准地把握用词的精髓，甚至会选择某个特定的词语而非其相邻的词语。但即便译者水平不高，也无法掩盖法布尔叙事中那种酣畅淋漓的风格。法布尔讲述的是一次突袭的故事；他也可以描绘科曼奇人突袭道奇堡的场景。而返程的描写同样生动传神：

The route taken [on the raid] is a matter of indifference to the marching column. Bare ground, thick grass, a heap of dead leaves or stone, brickwork, a clump of shrubs: all are crossed without any marked preference for one sort of road rather than another. What is rigidly fixed is the path home, which follows the outward track in all its windings and all its crossings, however difficult. Laden with their plunder, the Red Ants return to the nest by the same road, often an exceedingly complicated one, which the exigencies of the chase compelled them to take originally. They repass each spot which they passed at first; and this is to them a matter of such imperative necessity that no additional fatigue nor even the gravest danger can make them alter the track.

对于行进的队伍来说，行军路线无关紧要。裸露的地面、茂密的草地、成堆的落叶或石块、砖墙、灌木丛：它们都毫不偏袒地穿过，没有明显的偏好。唯一不变的是归途，它沿着来时的路线蜿蜒而行，无论多么艰难。满载战利品的红蚁沿着原路返回巢穴，这条路往往极其复杂，也是它们最初因追逐而被迫选择的。它们会重新经过最初经过的每一个地方；对它们来说，这是至关重要的，任何额外的疲惫，甚至最严重的危险，都无法让它们改变路线。

“Can you give us an example?” we think at this point. A good writer always knows what his readers are thinking and what they want to be told next. Fabre nails down the general principle with a specific case:

“你能举个例子吗？”我们这时会想。一位优秀的作家总是知道读者在想什么，以及他们接下来想读到什么。法布尔用一个具体的例子阐明了这一普遍原则：

Let us suppose that they have crossed a thick heap of dead leaves, representing to them a path beset with yawning gulfs, where every moment some one falls, where many are exhausted as they struggle out of the hollows and reach the heights by means of swaying bridges, emerging at last from the labyrinth of lanes. No matter: on their return they will not fail, though weighed down with their burden, once more to struggle through that weary maze. To avoid all this fatigue, they would have but to swerve slightly from the original path, for the good, smooth road is there, hardly a step away. This little deviation never occurs to them.

假设他们已经穿过了一大堆枯叶，这堆枯叶在他们眼中象征着一条布满深渊的小路，每时每刻都有人跌倒，许多人筋疲力尽地挣扎着爬出洼地，借助摇晃的桥梁到达高处，最终走出迷宫般的小路。然而，即便如此，他们返回时，即使负重前行，也一定会再次艰难地穿过那令人疲惫的迷宫。为了避免这一切疲惫，他们只需稍微偏离原路，因为平坦宽阔的道路就在不远处。然而，他们却从未想到这一点。

I came upon them one day when they were on one of their raids. They were marching along the inner edge of the stone-work of the garden pond, where I have replaced the old batrachians [frogs and toads] by a colony of goldfish. The wind was blowing very hard from the north and, taking the column in flank, sent whole rows of the ants flying into the water. The fish hurried up; they watched the performance and gobbled up the drowning insects. It was a difficult bit; and the column was decimated before it had passed. I expected to see the return journey made by another road, which would wind round and avoid the fatal cliff. Not at all. The nymph-laden band resumed the parlous path and the goldfish received a double windfall: the ants and their prizes. Rather than alter its track, the column was decimated a second time.

有一天，我偶然撞见了它们，当时它们正在进行一次突袭。它们沿着花园池塘石砌边缘的内缘行进，我把池塘里原先的蛙类换成了一群金鱼。北风呼啸，从侧翼袭来，把蚂蚁吹得成排成排地落入水中。金鱼们迅速游过来，观看这场“表演”，然后吞食那些溺水的昆虫。这可不是闹着玩的，蚂蚁队伍还没走完就被消灭殆尽。我原以为它们会绕道而行，避开那致命的悬崖。然而并没有。这群满载着若虫的蚂蚁又回到了那条危险的小路上，金鱼们则意外地收获了双份：蚂蚁和它们的战利品。蚂蚁队伍非但没有改变路线，反而再次遭到了灭顶之灾。

I can’t leave Fabre without turning him loose briefly on the firefly, or glow-worm, that blithe diversion of our summer nights. How does a mere insect do something so ingratiating? Here’s how Fabre introduces him:

我不能就此放过法布尔，让他简单介绍一下萤火虫，或者说发光虫，这种夏夜里令人愉悦的消遣。一只小小的昆虫，究竟是如何做到如此讨人喜欢的呢？以下是法布尔对它的介绍：

Few insects vie in popular fame with the glow-worm, that curious little animal which, to celebrate the little joys of life, kindles a beacon at its tail-end. Who does not know it, at least by name? Who has not seen it roam amid the grass, like a spark fallen from the moon at its full? The Greeks of old called it , meaning the bright-tailed. Science employs the same term: it calls the lantern-bearer Lampyris noctiluca . In this case, the common name is inferior to the scientific phrase, which, when translated, becomes both expressive and accurate.

很少有昆虫能像萤火虫那样广为人知。这种奇特的小动物，为了庆祝生命中的点滴喜悦，会在尾部点燃一盏明灯。谁不认识它，至少听说过它的名字？谁没见过它在草丛中漫步，宛如满月时坠落的火花？古希腊人称它为“亮尾萤火虫”（ ），意为“亮尾萤火虫”。科学界也采用了同样的术语：它将这种提灯小虫命名为Lampyris noctiluca。在这种情况下，俗名不如科学名称来得贴切，后者翻译过来既生动又准确。

In fact, we might easily cavil at the word “worm.” The Lampyris is not a worm at all, not even in general appearance. He has six short legs, which he well knows how to use; he is a gad-about, a trot-about. In the adult state, the male is corectly garbed in wing-cases, like the true Beetle that he is. The female is an ill-favored thing who knows naught of the delights of flying: all her life long she retains the larval shape. [But] even in this initial stage, the word “worm” is out of place. We French have the expression “naked as a worm,” to point to the lack of any defensive covering. Now the Lampyris is clothed, that is to say, he wears an epidermis of some consistency; moreover, he is rather richly colored: his body is dark brown all over, set off with pale pink on the thorax, especially on the lower surface. Finally, each segment is decked at the hinder edge with two spots of a fairly bright red. A costume like this was never worn by a worm.

事实上，我们很容易对“虫”这个词提出异议。灯蛾根本不像虫子，即使从外形上看也截然不同。它有六条短腿，而且非常善于运用；它四处游荡，轻快地走来走去。成虫阶段，雄性灯蛾像真正的甲虫一样，被鞘翅包裹着。雌性灯蛾则相貌丑陋，对飞行的乐趣一无所知：它终生保持着幼虫的形态。[但是]即使在幼虫阶段，“虫”这个词也显得不恰当。我们法语里有“像虫子一样赤裸”的表达，用来形容它缺乏任何防御性的保护。而灯蛾是有“衣服”的，也就是说，它有一层有一定的表皮；此外，它的颜色也相当鲜艳：全身呈深棕色，胸部，尤其是腹面，则带有淡淡的粉红色。最后，每个节段的后缘都点缀着两个鲜红色的斑点。这样的装扮可不是蚯蚓会穿的。

Having rescued the glow-worm from wormdom, Fabre invokes the words of his compatriot, the gastronome Henri Brillat-Savarin, who said, “Show me what you eat and I will tell you what you are.” A similar question, Fabre says, “should be addressed to every insect whose habits we propose to study, for, from the least to the greatest in the zoological progression, the stomach sways the world; the data supplied by food are the chief of all the documents of life.” He proceeds to tell us that the seemingly docile firefly is in fact “a hunter of game [who] follows his calling with rare villainy. His regular prey is the snail. Before he begins to feast, the glow-worm administers an anesthetic: he chloroforms his victim, rivaling in the process the wonders of our modern surgery.”

法布尔将萤火虫从虫群中解救出来后，引用了他的同胞、美食家亨利·布里亚-萨瓦兰的话：“告诉我你吃什么，我就能告诉你你是什么样的人。”法布尔说，类似的问题“应该问我们打算研究的每一种昆虫，因为在动物进化过程中，从最小的到最大的，胃都左右着世界；食物提供的信息是所有生命记录中最主要的。”他接着告诉我们，看似温顺的萤火虫实际上是“一个猎手，它以一种罕见的邪恶方式履行着自己的使命。它的主要猎物是蜗牛。在开始享用美食之前，萤火虫会给猎物注射麻醉剂：它用氯仿迷晕猎物，其手法堪比我们现代外科手术的奇迹。”

Six pages later Fabre has taken us through two bizarre procedures: an intricate feat of anesthesia and an act of gastronomy so fastidious that it wouldn’t be out of place at Brillat-Savarin’s table, concluding with “a wash and brush-up,” which the glowworm performs “point by point, from one end of the body to the other, with a scrupulous persistency that proves the great interest which he takes in the operation. What is his object in thus sponging himself, in dusting and polishing himself so carefully? It is a question, apparently, of removing a few atoms of dust or else some traces of viscidity that remain from the evil contact with the snail.”

六页之后，法布尔向我们展示了两个奇异的程序：一项复杂的麻醉术和一项极其讲究的美食仪式，其精细程度堪比布里亚-萨瓦兰的餐桌佳肴。仪式最后以“清洗和梳洗”结束，萤火虫“从身体的一端到另一端，一丝不苟地进行着，这种一丝不苟的坚持证明了他对这项操作的极大兴趣。他如此仔细地擦拭自己、掸去灰尘、打磨自己究竟是为了什么呢？显然，是为了去除一些灰尘，或者说是与蜗牛接触后残留的粘液痕迹。”

Only then does Fabre get around to explaining what most of us thought was the firefly’s real parlor trick:

直到这时，法布尔才开始解释我们大多数人认为萤火虫真正的把戏：

If the glow-worm possessed no other talent than that of chloroforming his prey by means of a few tweaks resembling kisses, he would be unknown to the vulgar herd. But he also knows how to light himself like a beacon; he shines, which is an excellent manner of achieving fame….

如果萤火虫除了用几下类似亲吻的轻柔触碰来迷惑猎物之外别无其他才能，那么它就不会为庸俗之辈所知。但它也懂得如何像灯塔一样照亮自己；它闪闪发光，这是一种极佳的成名方式……

Surely, we might think, nobody would ever write so well about the insect world again. But in our own time one writer, Vladimir Nabokov, has matched Fabre for elegance. Nabokov’s obsession, which began when he was a child in Russia, touched only one small corner of Fabre’s universe: butterflies and moths. But the intensity with which it bobs up in his writing is proof of how it consumed him.

我们或许会想，恐怕再也不会有人能把昆虫世界描绘得如此精彩了。然而，在我们这个时代，弗拉基米尔·纳博科夫这位作家，其文笔之优美足以与法布尔比肩。纳博科夫对昆虫的痴迷始于他在俄罗斯的童年时期，虽然他笔下的昆虫世界只触及了法布尔世界的一小部分：蝴蝶和飞蛾。但纳博科夫的作品中，这种对昆虫的描绘如此浓烈，足以证明他对昆虫的痴迷程度。

English was Nabokov’s fourth language, but no native-born writer of my native language dazzles me more with the precision of his imagery. Though the hilarious Lolita is a work of fiction, it’s one of the most minutely observed travel books ever written about America and its tacky landscape of motels and burger huts. Nabokov’s exactitude reaches its purest refinement in Speak, Memory , that most stylish of memoirs. In the following excerpt he recalls how his “ardent adolescent interest” led him to ponder “the links between butterflies and the central problems of nature.”

英语是纳博科夫的第四语言，但没有哪个以我的母语写作的作家能像他那样，以如此精准的意象令我叹为观止。尽管滑稽的《洛丽塔》是一部虚构作品，但它却是对美国及其充斥着汽车旅馆和汉堡店的俗艳景象观察最为细致入微的游记之一。纳博科夫的精准在《说吧，记忆》这部极具风格的回忆录中达到了极致。在以下节选中，他回忆起自己“青少年时期的浓厚兴趣”如何引导他思考“蝴蝶与自然界核心问题之间的联系”。

The mysteries of mimicry had a special attraction for me. Its phenomena showed an artistic perfection usually associated with man-wrought things. Such was the imitation of oozing poison by bubble-like macules on a wing (complete with pseudo-refraction) or by glossy yellow knobs on a chrysalis (“Don’t eat me—I have already been squashed, sampled and rejected”). When a certain moth resembled a certain wasp in shape and color, it also walked and moved its antennae in a waspish, un-mothlike manner. When a butterfly had to look like a leaf, not only were all the details of a leaf beautifully rendered but markings mimicking grub-bored holes were generously thrown in. “Natural selection,” in the Darwinian sense, could not explain the miraculous coincidence of imitative aspect and imitative behavior, nor could one appeal to the theory of “the struggle for life” when a protective device was carried to a point of mimetic subtlety, exuberance and luxury far in excess of a predator’s power of appreciation. I discovered in nature the non-utilitarian delights that I sought in art. Both were a form of magic, both were a game of intricate enchantment and deception.

拟态的奥秘对我有着特殊的吸引力。它的种种表现展现出一种通常只有人造物才具备的艺术完美。例如，翅膀上气泡状的斑点（甚至带有伪折射效果）可以模仿渗出的毒液，蛹上闪亮的黄色小疙瘩则仿佛在说：“别吃我——我已经被碾碎、品尝过，然后被抛弃了。”当某种蛾子在形状和颜色上酷似某种黄蜂时，它的行走方式和触角摆动也如同黄蜂一般，而非蛾子。当蝴蝶必须伪装成一片叶子时，不仅叶子的所有细节都被精雕细琢，就连模仿虫蛀孔的纹路也毫不吝啬地添加上去。达尔文意义上的“自然选择”无法解释这种模仿外形与模仿行为的奇妙巧合，也无法用“生存斗争”理论来解释，当一种保护机制发展到如此精妙绝伦、极尽奢华，远远超出捕食者的鉴赏能力时。我在自然中发现了我在艺术中苦苦追寻的非实用性乐趣。两者都是一种魔法，都是一场错综复杂的魔法与欺骗的游戏。

Finally, birds. Though nobody has ever confused me with Roger Tory Peterson, I often marvel at certain prodigies of bird behavior—flight, song, nest-building, migration—that seem to me beyond explaining. At such times I turn to a book called Birds and Their Attributes , by Glover Morrill Allen. The book was published in 1925, but I doubt if anyone knows more about birds today than Professor Allen knew then—typical chapters are “Feathers,” “Birds’ Colors and Their Uses” and “Bills, Feet, Wings, and Bones”—or can write about their habits with such clarity and vigor. Here’s how he explains the attribute of birds that man has envied and tried to emulate since Icarus flew too near the sun:

最后，说说鸟类。虽然没人把我跟罗杰·托里·彼得森（Roger Tory Peterson）搞混，但我常常惊叹于鸟类某些行为的奇妙之处——飞行、鸣唱、筑巢、迁徙——在我看来，这些都难以解释。每当这时，我就会翻阅格洛弗·莫里尔·艾伦（Glover Morrill Allen）的著作《鸟类及其属性》（Birds and Their Attributes）。这本书出版于1925年，但我怀疑如今是否有人比艾伦教授当年更了解鸟类——书中典型的章节包括“羽毛”、“鸟类的颜色及其用途”以及“喙、脚、翅膀和骨骼”——或者能像他那样清晰生动地描述鸟类的习性。以下是他对鸟类一项特质的解释，这项特质自伊卡洛斯飞得太靠近太阳以来，就一直令人类羡慕不已，并试图效仿：

We do not know how birds first became fliers, but it is supposed that their early ancestors ran on their hind legs, leaving their fore limbs free to develop as wings or as sails by the aid of which they glided from bough to bough or from tree to tree. In this the wings were probably held outstretched and the legs were extended behind. In many bats additional support is gained by the growth of a membrane which stretches between the extended toes and the tip of the tail. This is called a “patagium.”

我们并不清楚鸟类最初是如何学会飞行的，但据推测，它们的早期祖先用后腿奔跑，使前肢得以自由发育，最终形成翅膀或帆状结构，借助翅膀或帆状结构在树枝间或树木间滑翔。在这种情况下，它们的翅膀可能完全展开，双腿向后伸展。许多蝙蝠通过生长一层膜状结构来获得额外的支撑，这层膜状结构连接着伸展的脚趾和尾尖，被称为“翼膜”。

With “patagium” Professor Allen throws a technical term at us from his discipline of zoology. That’s the prerogative of any writer writing about a special field, and as educated readers we should be glad to know about such strangers and to make them our own. I’m delighted to meet “patagium.” But a writer also has an obligation to make us comfortable with these terms, not to use them unnecessarily or just to show off or to exclude everyone who isn’t a member of the lodge. Here Professor Allen takes the time to explain why the word is important to the point he is making:

艾伦教授用“翼膜”这个词向我们抛出了一个来自他所研究的动物学领域的专业术语。这是任何一位撰写某一特定领域文章的作者的特权，而作为受过教育的读者，我们应该乐于了解这些陌生的词汇，并将它们内化为己有。我很高兴认识了“翼膜”这个词。但是，作者也有义务让我们能够轻松理解这些术语，而不是滥用它们，或者仅仅为了炫耀，或者将非专业人士拒之门外。在这里，艾伦教授花时间解释了为什么这个词对于他所要表达的观点至关重要：

It has been argued that if the ancestors of birds had learned to glide before their feathery covering had become evolved, they would probably have had a thin membrane of skin stretching between the fingers and from the sides of the tail to the feet, just as there is in bats and in the extinct flying lizards or pterodactyls. Since, however, this “patagium” is lacking, it is believed that some of the feathers on the hand had already become large enough to sustain the bird in the air.

有人认为，如果鸟类的祖先在羽毛覆盖进化之前就学会了滑翔，那么它们很可能像蝙蝠和已灭绝的飞蜥（翼龙）一样，在手指之间以及尾部两侧延伸到脚部，形成一层薄膜状的皮肤。然而，由于这种“翼膜”并不存在，人们认为当时鸟类手部的一些羽毛已经足够大，足以支撑它们在空中飞行。

That ancient birds extended the legs behind in flight is rendered probable not only from analogy with bats, but also because most of the primitive birds still do so. For example, ducks, loons, herons, cranes, sandpipers, gulls, as well as grouse, hens, hawks, owls, pigeons and the cuckoos all fly with the legs out behind when under way, in contrast to many of the more specialized or perching birds which fly with the feet drawn up in front ready to grasp a branch on alighting; such are the crows, sparrows, warblers, thrushes….

古代鸟类飞行时会向后伸展双腿，这不仅可以类比蝙蝠，而且大多数原始鸟类至今仍然如此，因此这种现象也很有可能存在。例如，鸭子、潜鸟、苍鹭、鹤、鹬、海鸥，以及松鸡、母鸡、鹰、猫头鹰、鸽子和杜鹃等，飞行时双腿都向后伸展，这与许多更特化的鸟类或栖息鸟类形成鲜明对比，后者飞行时双脚收拢在前，以便落地时抓住树枝；例如乌鸦、麻雀、莺、画眉……

After the gliding stage, flight was perhaps acquired by a laborious process of alternate flapping and sailing, much as we see in the Sharp-shinned Hawk when not in direct flight. The primitive flying birds were probably small species and by gradually increasing the rapidity of their wing beats they developed swifter flight. Observations made in Europe on birds harnessed to automatic registers showed in the pigeon about 480 wing beats to the minute, in a duck 540, and in the sparrow 780…

滑翔阶段之后，飞行或许是通过交替拍打翅膀和滑翔的艰苦过程获得的，就像我们看到的锐尾鹰在非直接飞行时那样。原始的飞行鸟类可能体型较小，它们通过逐渐加快翅膀拍动的频率，发展出了更快的飞行能力。在欧洲，对佩戴自动记录仪的鸟类进行的观察显示，鸽子每分钟大约拍动翅膀480次，鸭子540次，麻雀780次……

Once the art of sustaining the body in air was acquired, we may suppose the more expert forms of flight followed, such as soaring, or poising with delicate adjustment on air currents. Such a form of poising is seen in the Rough-legged Hawks, which have learned to hang in the air nearly motionless by balancing on an upward current coming over the brow of a hill….

一旦掌握了在空中保持身体平衡的技巧，我们就可以推测，更高级的飞行方式也随之而来，例如翱翔，或者通过巧妙地调整气流来保持平衡。毛腿鹰就展现了这种平衡能力，它们学会了利用山顶上升的气流保持平衡，几乎静止地悬停在空中……

Professor Allen is on a roll here that any sportswriter might envy. One of the hardest kinds of writing is to describe motion in a way that the reader can picture. Dance critics also know the problem. Specific detail, as always, helps:

艾伦教授的文笔真是炉火纯青，任何体育记者都会羡慕不已。写作最难的部分之一就是用生动形象的方式描述动作，让读者身临其境。舞蹈评论家也深知这一点。一如既往，具体的细节描写至关重要：

Passengers on steamers have often admired the beautiful flight of gulls which, taking advantage of the wave of air forced upward by the advance of the vessel against the wind, are able to poise on motionless wings in this current and yet keep pace with the steamer as it advances. Once outside a certain zone, however, the force of the air current falls and they cannot maintain their position except by flapping. These two cases indicate a very delicate adjustment of forces in the poising bird.

轮船上的乘客常常赞叹海鸥优美的飞行姿态。它们利用轮船逆风航行时产生的上升气流，能够保持翅膀静止不动，却依然能与轮船并肩前行。然而，一旦离开某个特定区域，气流就会减弱，它们就只能通过拍打翅膀来维持姿态。这两种情况都表明，这种保持姿态的鸟类需要非常精细地调节自身的力量。

But even this feat of equilibrium is not the most glorious of the flying arts, as Professor Allen, leading us from the simple to the intricate, as good teachers and nonfiction writers should, goes on to explain:

但即便如此，这种保持平衡的壮举也并非飞行艺术中最辉煌的部分，正如艾伦教授（他像优秀的教师和非虚构作家那样，带领我们从简单走向复杂）继续解释的那样：

The most complex and interesting type of flight is true soaring, by which is meant the ability to glide through the air, to rise or descend, to increase or check speed, to circle or go straight away, all without flapping the wings or greatly varying the general outstretched position….

最复杂、最有趣的飞行类型是真正的滑翔，这意味着能够在空中滑翔、上升或下降、增加或减少速度、盘旋或直线飞行，所有这些都不需要拍打翅膀或大幅改变整体伸展姿势……

In calm air there is very little drift down wind, but instead the successive circles overlap. There may be circling without gain in height—or “ease-circling.” With an increase of wind the circles may overlap less and less, making loops to leeward, and there often comes a sudden increase of speed at the commencement of the down-wind glide, following a slight adjustment of the wings.

在无风条件下，飞机几乎没有顺风漂移，而是连续的盘旋轨迹相互重叠。有时甚至会出现盘旋但高度没有增加的情况，即所谓的“轻松盘旋”。随着风力增强，盘旋轨迹的重叠部分会越来越少，飞机开始向背风侧盘旋，并且在顺风滑翔开始时，由于机翼的轻微调整，速度往往会突然增加。

In “ease-circling” without gain of height the wings are held straight out from the shoulder. In gliding straight ahead, however, there is a slight bend at the wrist which advances the primary feathers of the wings nearly to the level of the beak. This gives greater speed and is called “flex-gliding.”

在不增加高度的“轻松盘旋”中，翅膀从肩部笔直伸展。然而，在直线滑翔时，手腕略微弯曲，使翅膀的初级飞羽几乎与喙齐平。这能带来更大的速度，被称为“屈伸滑翔”。

Soaring flight does not occur at any or all times. On the contrary, in calm air, soaring flight may not be possible in early morning or late afternoon, but as morning advances its occurrence depends upon the presence of upward currents of air due to the heating of the lowermost layers of the atmosphere. In other words, the air becomes “soarable” at a more or less particular time, and this “soarability” gradually increases, as proved by the fact that the lighter birds first start circling and the heavier ones follow in the order of their weight.

翱翔飞行并非随时都会发生。相反，在平静的空气中，清晨或傍晚可能无法翱翔飞行，但随着时间推移，由于大气层底层受热而产生的上升气流，翱翔飞行便会发生。换句话说，空气会在某个或多或少特定的时间变得“适宜翱翔”，而且这种“适宜翱翔”的状态会逐渐增强，正如较轻的鸟类首先开始盘旋，较重的鸟类随后也开始盘旋这一现象所证明的那样。

Professor Allen isn’t bad at soarability himself.

艾伦教授本人也具备一定的滑翔能力。

# ↩

9. Writing Mathematics

9. 数学写作

One day I got a letter from a woman named Joan Countryman, who is head of the mathematics department at Germantown Friends School in Philadelphia. She had heard about my interest in writing across the curriculum.

有一天，我收到了一封来自一位名叫琼·康特里曼的女士的信，她是费城日耳曼敦友谊学校数学系的主任。她听说了我对跨学科写作的兴趣。

“For many years,” she said, “I’ve been asking my students to write about mathematics as they learned it, with predictably wonderful results. Writing seems to free them of the idea that math is a collection of right answers owned by the teacher—a body of knowledge that she will dispense in chunks and that they have to swallow and digest. That’s how most non-mathematicians perceive it. But what makes mathematics really interesting is not the right answer but where it came from and where it leads.”

“多年来，”她说，“我一直要求学生们写下他们学习数学的过程，结果不出所料地好极了。写作似乎让他们摆脱了这样一种观念：数学是老师掌握的一系列正确答案——老师会把这些知识分块灌输给他们，而他们必须吞咽消化。大多数非数学专业人士就是这样看待数学的。但真正让数学有趣的不是正确答案，而是答案的由来和它指向何方。”

The letter grabbed my attention. Surely mathematics was a world of numbers. Could it also be penetrated with words? Could a person actually write sentences that would lead him through a mathematical problem and suggest further questions—different questions from the ones the teacher might raise? It had never occurred to me that the teacher wasn’t the sole custodian of mathematical truth, and it certainly never occurred to E. Grant Spicer, my elementary school math teacher, who so cowed me with his ownership of the right answer that I’ve had math anxiety ever since. To this day I consider it a lucky month when I balance my checkbook, and the task is always accompanied by a slight pounding in my chest that I would otherwise take to be the onset of a heart attack. I still resent having to subtract a larger number from a smaller one by “borrowing” from the adjacent column. I resent it not only because I’m never sure I’ve done it right; I also seem to have to borrow more often than anyone else does. Why me?

这封信引起了我的注意。数学当然是一个数字的世界。难道文字也能渗透其中吗？一个人真的能写出引导自己解开数学难题并提出更多问题——与老师提出的问题不同的问题吗？我从未想过老师并非数学真理的唯一守护者，我的小学数学老师E·格兰特·斯派塞肯定也从未想过这一点。他总是用自己掌握正确答案的权威性让我感到畏惧，以至于我从此对数学产生了焦虑。直到今天，我仍然觉得每个月能平衡收支都是幸运的，因为每次平衡收支时，我的胸口都会微微怦怦直跳，平时我甚至会以为这是心脏病发作的征兆。我仍然很讨厌用相邻的数列“借位”来计算小数减大数。我讨厌它不仅是因为我永远不确定自己算得对不对，还因为我似乎比任何人都更频繁地需要借位。为什么是我？

Such self-pity would have been despised by Mr. Spicer; emotions have no place in mathematics. He was one of those people who have “a head for figures,” instantly certain that twelve times nine is—well, whatever it is. Confronted with a student who was unable to produce the right answer, he would begin to turn red, a man betrayed by his vascular system, until his round face and bald head were crimson with disbelief that such dim-wittedness was at large in the next generation. After my years under his baleful gaze I took as little math as possible, banishing it along with chemistry to the limbo of subjects I didn’t think I had an aptitude for.

这种自怜自艾的情绪，斯派塞先生一定会嗤之以鼻；在数学中，情感毫无立足之地。他属于那种“数字控”，总能立刻断定十二乘以九等于——嗯，不管等于多少。一旦遇到答不上来的学生，他就会开始涨红脸，仿佛被自己的血管出卖了一般，直到他那张圆脸和光秃秃的脑袋都因难以置信而涨得通红，难以置信这种愚钝之辈竟然还存在于下一代之中。在他那充满敌意的目光注视下度过了几年之后，我尽可能少地选修数学，把它和化学一起扫进了我自认为没有天赋的学科的垃圾堆。

Yet here in the morning mail was a teacher who got her math students to write—a humanist in the world of fractions and cosines. Joan Countryman explained that she was one of a small but growing number of pioneers in her discipline, frequently invited to give workshops to introduce teachers to the idea of writing mathematics. I called her and asked if she would introduce the idea to me. My palms were so sweaty that I could hardly hold the phone—a condition that AT&T’s long lines obviously transmitted. The woman I was calling could tell she had a mathophobe on her hands. “I know I can help you,” she said.

然而，就在这早晨的邮件里，我看到了一位老师让她的数学学生进行写作——在分数和余弦的世界里，她是一位人文主义者。琼·康特里曼解释说，她是这个领域里为数不多但数量不断增长的先驱者之一，经常受邀举办研讨会，向教师们介绍数学写作的理念。我给她打了个电话，问她是否愿意向我介绍一下这个理念。我的手心汗涔涔的，几乎握不住电话——AT&T的长电话线显然也影响到了我的手心。接电话的女士一眼就看出我是个数学恐惧症患者。“我知道我能帮到你，”她说。

We made a date for me to come to Philadelphia and talk to her and attend one of her classes.

我们约好时间，让我去费城和她谈谈，并旁听她的一堂课。

I put my first question to Joan Countryman as we settled down to talk in her late-Victorian house, a house I had been warmly admiring for its fanciful curves and angles and other eclectic design details.

我和琼·康特里曼在她那栋维多利亚晚期风格的房子里坐下交谈，我向她提出了我的第一个问题。我一直很欣赏这栋房子，因为它有着奇特的曲线、角度和其他兼收并蓄的设计细节。

“What is mathematics?” I asked.

“什么是数学？”我问道。

“You’ve been talking about mathematics ever since you walked into this house,” she said. “When you commented on the dormers and the staircase and the circular windows you were making mathematical points.”

“自从你走进这栋房子，你就一直在谈论数学，”她说。“当你评论老虎窗、楼梯和圆形窗户时，你其实是在阐述数学观点。”

I said I thought they were aesthetic points. Like Molière’s bourgeois gentleman, who was astonished to learn that he had been speaking prose all his life, I was surprised to learn that I had been speaking mathematics.

我说我认为它们是美学上的要点。就像莫里哀笔下的资产阶级绅士惊讶地发现自己一生都在说散文一样，我惊讶地发现自己一生都在说数学。

“Sure they’re aesthetic points,” she said, “but there are all sorts of interesting mathematics about the way the house is constructed and about the shapes you’ve been noticing. Unfortunately, most people don’t see the world that way because they’ve been alienated from mathematics and told that it’s something apart from what they’re able to do.”

“当然，这些都是美学上的亮点，”她说，“但这座房子的构造方式以及你注意到的那些形状，都蕴含着各种有趣的数学原理。可惜的是，大多数人并不这样看待世界，因为他们与数学疏远了，并且被告知数学与他们的能力无关。”

“So what is mathematics?” I asked, still hoping for a definition.

“那么，数学究竟是什么呢？”我问道，仍然希望能得到一个定义。

“What are any of the disciplines but a way in which people try to make sense of the world or the universe?” she said. “Mathematics is one way of doing that, just as literature is, or philosophy, or history. Math does it by looking for patterns and abstracting—that is, by examining a specific case and generalizing from that. But that’s not how a child would define mathematics. He’d say that math is arithmetic—adding and subtracting and multiplying and dividing—because that’s the first thing we make him do. We spend far too much time on it; today we’ve got calculators that can do the job faster and better. I don’t think we should even teach long division anymore; kids spend so much time learning to do it, and getting it wrong, that they never see the point of it—why you would want to do it. But with a calculator doing the drudgery, you can ask an interesting question, like ‘How much fabric do I need to cover this chair?’”

“所有学科不都是人们试图理解世界或宇宙的一种方式吗？”她说道，“数学是其中一种方式，就像文学、哲学和历史一样。数学通过寻找规律和抽象——也就是通过研究具体案例并从中概括——来实现这一点。但这并不是孩子对数学的定义。他会说数学就是算术——加减乘除——因为这是我们让他做的第一件事。我们在这方面花费了太多时间；如今我们有了计算器，可以更快更好地完成这些工作。我认为我们甚至不应该再教长除法了；孩子们花了太多时间学习长除法，却总是出错，以至于他们根本不明白它的意义——为什么要学习它。但有了计算器来完成这些繁琐的计算，你就可以提出一些更有趣的问题，比如‘我需要多少布料来罩住这把椅子？’”

“When you ask a question about the fabric does it become something beyond arithmetic?” I asked.

“当你问一个关于织物的问题时，它就超越了算术的范畴了吗？”我问道。

“It does, because you begin to make connections. Unless you make those connections, children will always think of mathematics as somehow ‘other than me—not part of my world.’ And that continues right through high school, where there’s a heavy emphasis on exercises and computation, with numbers as the sole language and the right answer as the sole objective.”

“的确如此，因为你会开始建立联系。除非建立这些联系，否则孩子们总会觉得数学‘与我无关——不属于我的世界’。这种情况会一直持续到高中，高中阶段非常注重练习和计算，数字是唯一的语言，正确答案是唯一的目标。”

I asked Joan Countryman when she began to think that there might be another language—writing—which could take students into the subject by a different route.

我问琼·康特里曼，她是什么时候开始认为可能存在另一种语言——写作——可以带领学生以不同的途径进入这个学科的。

“When I started teaching math I was thirty,” she recalled, “and I had been out working in the field of urban education as a program planner for the Philadelphia school district, so when I got into a classroom I had serious questions about the relationship between what one does in school and what one does in life. I didn’t like the isolation of the process of learning math: You study it alone and you take your tests alone and you don’t have much to do with other people. I immediately put the kids in groups and made them teach each other and take tests together. I was determined to get them away from the idea that their education is a private experience.

“我开始教数学的时候已经三十岁了，”她回忆道，“之前我一直在费城学区做项目规划师，从事城市教育方面的工作。所以当我真正走进教室的时候，我对学校学习和生活之间的关系产生了很深的疑问。我不喜欢学习数学的孤立性：你独自学习，独自考试，很少与其他人交流。我立刻把孩子们分组，让他们互相学习，一起考试。我决心让他们摆脱那种认为教育是私人体验的想法。”

“I also wanted them to be less passive. Math is an active process, and you’ll never know that if you sit and wait for the teacher to tell you, ‘This is how to do long division—it’s a set of specific steps.’ The action should begin long before that, with the student initiating a question like ‘I’ve got fifty-three of these things; how am I going to divide them among the people in the room?’ Most kids think that the teacher has all the information and they don’t have any. I don’t like the implications of that—that you aren’t capable of finding things out yourself.

“我还希望他们不要那么被动。数学是一个主动的过程，如果你只是坐着等老师告诉你‘长除法怎么做——它包含一系列特定的步骤’，你永远不会明白这一点。行动应该在此之前很久就开始，比如学生主动提出问题，像‘我有53个这样的东西；我该如何把它们分给教室里的人？’大多数孩子认为老师掌握了所有信息，而他们一无所知。我不喜欢这种想法——它暗示你没有能力自己去发现问题。”

“So from the start I got my students to write about what they were doing. My first idea was to ask them to write mathematics autobiographies. That’s when I realized there was some amazing stuff in their heads. They had very specific memories of their classroom experiences. It wasn’t just: ‘I don’t like math’; it was: ‘In the middle of the third grade when Miss Thompson made me do that sheet with the 100 additions I felt terrible because I couldn’t get it right.’ They conveyed a strong sense of what it was like to be in a math classroom. Many of them told wonderful stories; in fact, some of the kids who were most enthusiastic weren’t particularly good at math. What those autobiographies did was to remind me that I wasn’t teaching empty vessels—that these people had long histories of mathematics even though they were only thirteen. I saw that it was possible for me to be in touch with them.”

“所以一开始我就让学生们写下他们在学习的内容。我的第一个想法是让他们写数学自传。那时我才意识到，他们脑子里装着多么丰富的知识啊！他们对课堂经历有着非常具体的记忆。不仅仅是‘我不喜欢数学’，而是‘三年级的时候，汤普森老师让我做那张100道加法题的练习纸，我做错了，感觉糟透了。’他们生动地描述了在数学课堂上的感受。他们中的许多人都讲述了精彩的故事；事实上，一些最热情的孩子数学并不好。这些自传让我意识到，我教的不是一群空洞的容器——这些孩子虽然只有十三岁，但他们的数学之路却源远流长。我意识到，我可以和他们建立联系。”

Still, writing about math isn’t the same thing as writing math. I asked Mrs. Countryman how she made the crucial next step: from writing as recollection to writing to learn. She said she began encouraging her students to think of math topics they could explore in writing.

然而，写关于数学的文章并不等同于写数学本身。我问康特里曼夫人，她是如何完成这关键的下一步：从回忆式写作过渡到学习式写作。她说，她开始鼓励学生思考可以用文字探讨的数学主题。

“One of my favorites,” she said, “was a student who has since become a professional tennis player. He said, ‘Do you really mean I could study the geometry of the tennis court?’ He wrote a paper that analyzed the serve and discussed various issues that he discovered as he wrote about them. Mainly he was noticing that mathematics was involved in what he was doing on the tennis court—a connection he had never made before because he was math-handicapped. He was the kind of person who said, ‘Math isn’t for me.’”

“我最喜欢的学生之一，”她说，“后来成为了一名职业网球运动员。他当时问我：‘你是说我可以研究网球场的几何形状吗？’他写了一篇论文，分析了发球动作，并探讨了他在写作过程中发现的各种问题。他主要注意到，他在网球场上的动作中蕴含着数学原理——这是他以前从未意识到的，因为他的数学很差。他以前总是说：‘数学不适合我。’”

Whether the student also improved his serve I didn’t ask. A different question was on my mind: “Are there things you can find out by writing about a math problem that you can’t learn by mathematics alone? Or would a math whiz know everything he needed to know by the conventional methods?”

我没有问这位学生的发球是否也有所提高。我当时想的是另一个问题：“通过写作来分析数学问题，能否发现一些仅靠数学本身无法学到的东西？或者说，一个数学天才是否能够通过传统方法掌握他需要知道的一切？”

“That’s the question that worried me most when I started,” Mrs. Countryman said. “The students I was frightened of—wary of—were the hotshot math kids who were sure they didn’t want to do any writing or would consider it a waste of time. But even those kids are eventually saying to me, ‘This is really useful. I’m learning mathematics better because I’m writing this stuff.’”

“这正是我刚开始教这门课时最担心的问题，”康特里曼夫人说。“我最害怕——或者说最担心——的是那些数学成绩优异的学生，他们坚信自己不想写东西，或者认为写东西是浪费时间。但即使是这些孩子最终也对我说：‘这真的很有用。我写这些东西，数学学得更好了。’”

I needed to see some examples of what we were talking about. Joan Countryman began by showing me two pieces of writing elicited by the question: “Find a number with thirteen factors.” Her usual procedure, she said, is to pose a problem to the class, lead a discussion of it and ask the students to write about it in this format: (1) Describe the problem; (2) Discuss your approach; (3) Explain what you found out.

我需要看看我们正在讨论的内容的一些例子。琼·康特里曼首先给我看了两篇根据“求一个有13个因数的数”这个问题写出来的文章。她说，她通常的做法是向全班提出一个问题，引导大家讨论，然后要求学生按照以下格式写作：（1）描述问题；（2）讨论你的解题思路；（3）解释你的发现。

The first example, by a seventh-grade boy named Francis Vargas, was in the form of a letter—a device Mrs. Countryman invented because “math students often find it easier to write about their work when they’re writing to a specific person.” Francis’s letter began like this:

第一个例子是一位名叫弗朗西斯·瓦格斯的七年级男生写的，形式是一封信——这是康特里曼夫人发明的一种方式，因为“数学学生在写信给特定的人时，往往更容易表达他们的学习成果”。弗朗西斯的信是这样开头的：

Dear Jim:

亲爱的吉姆：

In math class we had a problem which was to find a number that had thirteen factors. At first we tried it by guessing, but it seemed hopeless. Then we made a list which included squares of numbers up to twenty and the factors of the numbers, and at the end we counted the factors. From that we saw that the squares that had three factors had square roots that were prime. Then we made a list like the one below…. From that list we saw that when the numbers were doubled we noticed a consecutive sequence starting from two in the column that showed the number of factors….

数学课上我们遇到一个问题：找出有十三个因数的数。一开始我们尝试靠猜，但感觉毫无希望。后来我们列了一个清单，包括20以内所有数的平方以及它们的因数，最后统计了因数的数量。我们发现，那些有三个因数的平方的平方根都是质数。然后我们又列了一个类似下面的清单……从这个清单中我们发现，当数字翻倍时，从表示因数个数的那一列中的2开始，出现了一个连续的序列……

Proceeding with narrative logic, Francis needed only a few more sentences to tell Jim how he found the missing number.

按照叙事逻辑，弗朗西斯只需要再说几句话就能告诉吉姆他是如何找到丢失的号码的。

“Writing is a way to explore a question and gain control over it,” Mrs. Countryman said. “But it also engages the imagination, the intellect and the emotions, and these are powerful aids to learning.” True enough, I thought—at least in most subjects. But could that apply to math? The next paper answered my question. Written by a seventh grader named Ian Childs, it came at the problem of the thirteen factors from a strikingly different direction:

“写作是一种探索问题并掌控问题的方式，”康特里曼夫人说。“但它也能激发想象力、智力和情感，而这些都是学习的强大助力。” 我心想，这话不假——至少在大多数学科中是如此。但这是否也适用于数学呢？下一篇作文解答了我的疑问。这篇作文出自一位名叫伊恩·查尔兹的七年级学生之手，他从一个截然不同的角度探讨了十三个因数的问题：

THE THIRTEENTH FACTOR

第十三因素

As I sat in my office on Saturday morning waiting for a case, suddenly a sharp knock came upon my door.

星期六早上，我坐在办公室里等案子，突然有人用力敲门。

“Come in,” I called.

“请进，”我喊道。

The door opened slowly and in came a man with a long overcoat and hat. A shadow was cast over his face. He walked slowly up to my desk and dropped an envelope on it.

门缓缓打开，一个身穿长外套、头戴帽子的男人走了进来。阴影笼罩着他的脸庞。他慢慢走到我的桌前，把一个信封扔在桌上。

“Read,” he said.

“读，”他说。

I read, “ TOP SECRET GOVERNMENT INFORMATION: Find a number with 13 factors or the world is…” Suddenly the paper burned up. I imagined that it was supposed to self-destruct after a certain period of time.

我读到：“绝密政府信息：找到一个有13个因数的数字，否则世界将……”突然，纸张燃烧起来。我猜想它应该是会在一段时间后自动销毁的。

“Do you accept?” he asked.

他问：“你接受吗？”

“Yes.”

“是的。”

“Good. Begin work immediately.” He turned, began to walk out the door and said, “and swiftly.”

“很好。立刻开始工作。”他转身，朝门口走去，说道：“而且要快。”

I soon realized that the number had to be a perfect square, perfect squares being the only numbers with an odd number of factors since the square root would pair off with itself. The number’s square root could not be a prime because all numbers squared from a prime would have three and only three factors.

我很快意识到这个数一定是完全平方数，因为完全平方数只有奇数个因数，它的平方根会与自身配对。这个数的平方根不可能是质数，因为质数的平方都只有三个因数。

Should I list every square number? No, too long and too much work. I’ve got it!! The perfect way! Why didn’t I think of it before? I will list all the numbers that are power of two, and the one to the twelfth power will have to have 13 factors!

我应该列出所有平方数吗？不，太长太费劲了。我想到了！！完美的办法！我之前怎么没想到呢？我列出所有2的幂，1的12次方肯定有13个因数！

Conclusion: the number 4096 was the one with 13 factors and I returned it to the government. What part it played in saving the world I don’t know, but I’m still here today. I learned many things from this case, like how to find a number with any amount of factors and how to get a number with three factors (a prime 2 ).

结论：4096 是那个有 13 个因数的数字，我已经把它交还给了政府。它在拯救世界的过程中发挥了什么作用，我不得而知，但我今天还活着。我从这个案例中学到了很多东西，比如如何找到一个有任意个因数的数字，以及如何得到一个有三个因数的数字（一个质数²）。

Another format is for students to keep a journal with a running account of their work. “In a journal,” Mrs. Countryman said, “I want them to suspend judgment—to feel free to ask questions, to experiment, to make statements about what they do and don’t understand. At first they need help to learn to write without censoring their thoughts—to feel confident that nobody will criticize what they’ve written.”

另一种形式是让学生写日记，持续记录他们的学习过程。“在日记里，”康特里曼夫人说，“我希望他们能放下成见——自由地提问、尝试，并表达他们理解和不理解的地方。一开始，他们需要帮助才能学会不加审查地写作——才能相信没有人会批评他们写的东西。”

The following entry, written by a twelfth-grade student named Neil Swenson after a month’s exposure to calculus, is typical of how the form lends itself to recording successive stages of thought:

以下这段文字是一位名叫尼尔·斯文森的十二年级学生在接触微积分一个月后写下的，它典型地体现了这种形式如何便于记录连续的思考阶段：

In my first journal entry I wrote that I believed that calculus is a way of finding solutions to problems that can’t be solved with conventional math, by using abstractions. I was partially correct in that many parts of calculus do require abstract thinking. But that’s not really what calculus is. Calculus is a way of dealing with motion. It’s a way of finding out exactly how something is moving. Without calculus it was impossible for us to know what the instantaneous velocity of something was. We could only know the actual rate of change if it was changing at a constant rate; then its derivative or the slope of its tangent line is equal to the slope of the original line. When we had something that had a variable rate of exchange we tried to find the average velocity, but this was inaccurate.

在我的第一篇日记里，我写道，我认为微积分是一种利用抽象思维来解决传统数学无法解决的问题的方法。我的说法部分正确，因为微积分的很多部分确实需要抽象思维。但这并非微积分的真正本质。微积分是一种处理运动的方法。它是一种精确计算物体运动方式的方法。如果没有微积分，我们就无法知道物体的瞬时速度。只有当物体以恒定速率变化时，我们才能知道它的实际变化率；此时，它的导数或切线的斜率等于原线的斜率。当物体的变化率是变化的时，我们试图找到平均速度，但这并不准确。

I wondered whether Neil and Ian were both versions of my own teen-age self—boys whose main aptitude was for writing—and whether I might also have been able to write my way toward the thirteen-factor number and the instantaneous velocity of a moving object. Or was the whole matter of aptitudes a myth—a cop-out used by people like me to avoid subjects that would force us to think in new and therefore threatening ways? I asked Joan Countryman how valid it is to say that most people have a bent either for words or for numbers.

我不禁思考，尼尔和伊恩是不是我少年时代的自己——两个天赋异禀的男孩，他们最擅长写作——而我是否也能通过写作推导出十三因数和运动物体的瞬时速度呢？或者，天赋论根本就是个神话——是像我这样的人用来逃避那些会迫使我们以全新、因而也更具挑战性的方式思考的课题的借口？我问琼·康特里曼，说大多数人要么擅长文字，要么擅长数字，这种说法到底有多准确。

“You could certainly divide people into those two rough categories,” she said, “but within those categories there are big differences in how people think. Last week in seventh grade we were doing an algebra problem about how much it would cost to take x number of kids to the movies. The movie tickets cost $3, it costs $28 to rent the bus, and there’s $150 to spend. The algebraic sentence we were working with was 3 x + 28 = 150. I asked the students to talk about it—to describe what the sentence meant. Their perceptions of what it meant differed a great deal. One child clearly saw a number as the solution to the sentence; he was fixed on the answer. Another child saw what I was interested in—that it doesn’t matter what x is, but that when you multiply it by 3 you can find out how much money you’ll have to spend for any number of people if the tickets cost $3. I’ve never been all that interested in the right answer; I don’t really care how many people I can take to the movies. I want students to see mathematics as a way of asking questions.”

“你当然可以把人大致分成这两类，”她说，“但即使在这两类人中，人们的思维方式也存在很大差异。上周，我们在七年级做一道代数题，题目是带x个孩子去看电影要花多少钱。电影票3美元，租车28美元，总共有150美元。我们用的代数式是3x + 28 = 150。我让学生们讨论一下——描述一下这个等式的意思。他们对等式的理解差异很大。一个孩子显然认为一个数字就是等式的答案；他执着于这个答案。另一个孩子则看到了我感兴趣的——x是多少并不重要，重要的是，当电影票3美元时，用x乘以3就能算出带任意数量的人去看电影要花多少钱。我从来都不太在意正确答案；我并不关心能带多少人去看电影。我希望学生们能理解电影的真正含义。”将数学视为提出问题的一种方式。

I was reminded of the philosophy professor at Gustavus Adolphus College who told me that many of his best student papers had been failures—papers in which the student explained why he couldn’t get where he wanted to go. I asked Mrs. Countryman if it was possible to be a good math student and still not get the right answer.

这让我想起了古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院的一位哲学教授，他告诉我，他教过的许多最好的学生论文其实都是失败之作——学生在论文中解释了自己为什么无法达到目标。我问康特里曼夫人，一个人是否有可能数学成绩很好，却仍然无法得出正确答案。

“It certainly is—up to a point,” she said. “Today the advanced placement exam in calculus has 50 percent multiple-choice questions and 50 percent ‘free-response essays,’ where the examiners give credit for the amount of information that’s given instead of worrying about what isn’t given. One of the things we keep telling the kids is: ‘You can get credit, even if you don’t know what the area under the figure is, if you give evidence that you know how to do it: how to set the problem up and what the boundaries are.’ In advanced calculus papers I’ve seen kids write, ‘I don’t know how to evaluate this integral, but if I could evaluate it I’d get the area.’ I think that’s fascinating.”

“确实如此——在某种程度上，”她说。“如今，大学先修课程的微积分考试中，50%是选择题，50%是‘简答题’，阅卷人更看重考生提供的信息量，而不是纠结于未提供的信息。我们一直告诉孩子们：‘即使你不知道图形下方的面积是多少，只要你能证明你知道如何计算，比如如何建立问题以及边界条件是什么，你也能拿到分数。’我在一些大学微积分试卷中看到学生写道：‘我不知道如何计算这个积分，但如果我能计算出来，我就能算出面积了。’我觉得这很有意思。”

Listening to these examples, I saw that many of my beliefs about writing and learning also apply to mathematics: that we write to discover what we know and don’t know; that we write more comfortably if we go exploring, free of the fear of not being on the “right” road to the right destination, and that we learn more if we feel that the work has a purpose. Motivation is as important in mathematics writing as in every other kind of writing. I asked Joan Countryman how she keeps alive the awareness that math is closely related to life.

听了这些例子，我发现我关于写作和学习的许多信念也适用于数学：我们写作是为了发现我们已知和未知的东西；如果我们勇于探索，不必担心自己是否走在通往正确目的地的“正确”道路上，写作就会更加轻松自如；如果我们感到这项工作有意义，就能学到更多。动机在数学写作中与其他任何类型的写作一样重要。我问琼·康特里曼，她是如何保持对数学与生活密切联系的认识的。

“There’s no dearth of topics for math papers,” she said, “but often students seem to be just meeting an assignment instead of pursuing a genuine interest of theirs. I’m always looking for a connection between mathematics and social questions. Recently in my twelfth-grade calculus class the lesson was on exponential functions, and I wanted to find an example of exponential growth that would make sense to the kids. One method that we have in math is to construct a mathematical model that uses exponential functions. It enables you to get at all kinds of world problems.”

“数学论文的选题从来不缺，”她说，“但学生们似乎常常只是为了完成作业而写，而不是真正出于兴趣。我一直在寻找数学与社会问题之间的联系。最近，我给十二年级学生上微积分课，讲的是指数函数，我想找一个孩子们能理解的指数增长的例子。数学中有一种方法，就是构建一个运用指数函数的数学模型。这种方法可以帮助我们解决各种各样的现实世界问题。”

The model that she found for her class began like this:

她为班级找到的模型是这样开始的：

Let’s suppose that the population of the world today is 4.7 billion and is growing at the rate of 1.64% per year, which is very close to the actual figures. This doesn’t seem like much of a growth rate, but let’s see what the implications are.

假设当今世界人口为47亿，年增长率为1.64%，这与实际数字非常接近。这个增长率看起来似乎不高，但让我们来看看这意味着什么。

Then it posed a series of numerical questions that would lead the student to some disturbing answers. Then, switching gears, it offered another example of exponential growth:

然后，它提出了一系列数值问题，这些问题会引导学生得出一些令人不安的答案。接着，它转换思路，提供了指数增长的另一个例子：

Bacteria grow by cell division. One cell divides to produce two. Two produce four, four produce eight, and so on. Suppose that we start with one bacterium in a jar, that each will divide once each minute, and that the jar is full at 12:00 noon. When is it half full?

细菌通过细胞分裂生长。一个细胞分裂产生两个细胞，两个细胞分裂产生四个细胞，四个细胞分裂产生八个细胞，以此类推。假设我们从一个装有细菌的罐子开始，每个细菌每分钟分裂一次，并且罐子在中午 12 点时装满。那么罐子什么时候半满？

Then it posed another set of numerical questions, one of which told the students to suppose that three more bottles were discovered and to calculate how long it would take to fill them also.

然后，它提出了另一组数值问题，其中一个问题要求学生假设又发现了三个瓶子，并计算将它们装满需要多长时间。

From this model Joan Countryman asked her students to write a paper that would draw an analogy between population growth and bacterial growth and to say whether they could see a “simple” solution to the problem of population growth. One of the essays she got back was this one by seventeen-year-old Hasan Mooney:

基于这个模型，琼·康特里曼要求她的学生们写一篇论文，将人口增长与细菌增长进行类比，并探讨他们是否能找到解决人口增长问题的“简单”方案。她收到的其中一篇论文是十七岁的哈桑·穆尼写的：

The examples of bacteria growth and world population are analogous in that both increase the numbers exponentially. This seems obvious but actually is intimidating when you consider that although the rate of increase is constant, the amount of increase every year (or minute) gets larger and larger without bound.

细菌增长和世界人口增长的例子具有相似之处，二者的数量都呈指数级增长。这看似显而易见，但实际上却令人望而生畏：虽然增长率是恒定的，但每年（甚至每分钟）的增长量却在无限增长。

Well, this is not entirely true. The bacteria example was simply a mathematical model, and for that it was O.K. to assume that growth could continue infinitely. That idea helped to demonstrate how quickly the bacteria would fill up three extra bottles.

嗯，这并不完全正确。细菌的例子只是一个数学模型，因此可以假设细菌的生长可以无限持续下去。这个假设有助于展示细菌如何迅速地填满另外三个瓶子。

There are a couple of problems in comparing this to the world population. First, we have no three extra bottles (extra planets?) to drop people into. Also, after a time it will become impossible for the growth rate to continue as it is, for the same reason: that there is a limited amount of space and that extra crowding will lead to disease, food shortage, war, etc.

将这种情况与世界人口进行比较存在一些问题。首先，我们没有额外的三个瓶子（或者说额外的星球？）来安置人口。其次，随着时间的推移，人口增长率将无法继续维持，原因也相同：空间有限，过度拥挤会导致疾病、粮食短缺、战争等等。

I don’t believe there is a simple solution to the population problem. Certainly it would be very useful to reduce the growth rate through mass education or birth control. But people will always have kids. It is also important to learn to conserve and maximize the resources we have.

我认为人口问题没有简单的解决办法。当然，通过普及教育或计划生育来降低人口增长率会非常有益。但人们总是会生育子女。因此，学会保护和最大化利用现有资源也至关重要。

“A problem like that one has many advantages,” Joan Countryman said. “First, for a kid who likes to write, there’s a lot to say. The math isn’t too hard, and it also suggests certain obvious techniques for producing an answer: for example, choosing a population of a certain size and making certain assumptions about childbearing age. A similar problem that I gave my class was this: Suppose every family in China was allowed to have children until they had a son. What effect would that have on population growth, and would it change the proportion of males and females in the country? The result was very surprising. The students not only wrote their way through the mathematics of exponential growth; they raised many interesting side issues of economics and agriculture and social structure. One girl pointed out that no Chinese boy would ever have a brother.”

“像这样的问题有很多优点，”琼·康特里曼说道。“首先，对于喜欢写作的孩子来说，有很多东西可以写。数学部分并不难，而且还提供了一些显而易见的解题技巧：例如，选择一个特定规模的人口，并对生育年龄做出一些假设。我给学生布置过一个类似的问题：假设中国的每个家庭都可以生育，直到生出儿子为止。这会对人口增长产生什么影响？会改变该国的男女比例吗？结果非常令人惊讶。学生们不仅用文字阐述了指数增长的数学原理，还提出了许多关于经济、农业和社会结构的有趣旁支问题。一位女生指出，中国男孩永远不会有兄弟。”

One by-product of these essays is the reminder that mathematical models are fallible; human nature will always have the last word. “Models enable us as citizens to ask, ‘Do we have control over the problem?’” Mrs. Countryman said. “In the case of the bacteria in the bottle, the model does what it’s supposed to do: It produces an answer. But the point that Hasan makes in his paper is that you have to be careful that your model relates to the world, because very often it leaves out significant problems. I don’t think these larger issues would have occurred to students who only used mathematical methods to get their answer. Writing is what forced them to think through both the math and its relationship to their own lives.”

这些文章的一个副产品提醒我们，数学模型并非完美无缺；最终决定一切的永远是人性。“模型让我们这些公民能够扪心自问：‘我们能否掌控这个问题？’”康特里曼夫人说道。“就瓶子里的细菌而言，模型发挥了它应有的作用：它给出了答案。但哈桑在他的文章中指出，你必须谨慎地选择与现实世界相关的模型，因为模型往往会忽略一些重要的问题。我认为，如果学生仅仅依靠数学方法来寻找答案，他们就不会想到这些更深层次的问题。正是写作迫使他们深入思考数学及其与自身生活的联系。”

Physiological note: I had been sitting in Joan Countryman’s living room for two hours talking about mathematics. My pulse was steady, the hand that held my note-taking pencil didn’t shake and wasn’t even clammy. Where was that old math anxiety? I hadn’t been at any loss for questions; they came to me naturally. Like the process of writing, the process of asking questions had been a form of learning, raising further questions and telling me what I wanted to know next. I was genuinely curious. It never occurred to me that this was a subject I wasn’t supposed to be any good at. What did occur to me was that mathematics was not some arcane system of numbers; it was a language, a way of putting thoughts together. I might never master the language—my checkbook might still go unbalanced—but at least I had begun to glimpse what the language was trying to say and how it could help people to understand the world around them.

生理感受：我在琼·康特里曼的客厅里坐了两个小时，和她聊数学。我的脉搏平稳，握着铅笔做笔记的手没有颤抖，甚至连汗都没出。以前那种数学焦虑哪去了？我一点问题都没有，它们自然而然地涌现出来。就像写作一样，提问的过程本身就是一种学习，它引发了更多的问题，也让我知道自己接下来想知道什么。我是真的好奇。我从没想过自己不擅长这门学科。我真正意识到的是，数学并非某种晦涩难懂的数字系统；它是一种语言，一种将思想融会贯通的方式。我或许永远无法掌握这门语言——我的支票簿或许依然会不平衡——但至少我已经开始窥见这门语言想要表达的内容，以及它如何帮助人们理解周围的世界。

By extension, I thought, this must also be true of engineering, chemistry, biology and all the other special languages that have been invented to express special ideas. They can be at least broadly apprehended. What keeps us from trying is fear; the engineer is as frightened of my language (writing) as I am of his. Scared away by the probable difficulty of learning the language, we never get to its literature—the purpose it was created for.

由此推断，工程学、化学、生物学以及所有其他为表达特定概念而发明的专门语言也必然如此。它们至少可以被大致理解。阻碍我们尝试的是恐惧；工程师们对我的语言（写作）感到恐惧，正如我对他们的语言感到恐惧一样。由于害怕学习这种语言的难度，我们永远无法接触到它的文学作品——而这正是它被创造出来的目的。

I asked Joan Countryman whether the new technology of computers could knock this barrier down.

我问琼·康特里曼，计算机这项新技术能否打破这一障碍。

“That’s one of the things that got me thinking about writing,” she said. “In the face of so much new technology, math teachers are starting to have to rethink what they do. For instance, all that algebra we used to spend weeks teaching—factoring and quadratic equations—is available today on a little piece of software that a school can buy for less than fifty dollars. I don’t think you can make a case for teaching quadratic equations anymore; 95 percent of the general population can’t solve them anyway. Instead you can give your class a problem that requires a quadratic equation and let the machine solve the equation. That liberates you to think about what makes the problem interesting and what its ramifications are. In the past, kids spent all their time figuring out how to do the equation.

“正是这件事让我开始思考写作，”她说。“面对如此多的新技术，数学老师们不得不重新思考他们的教学方式。例如，我们过去要花几周时间教授的代数知识——因式分解和二次方程——如今只需不到五十美元就能在一款小型软件上找到。我认为现在已经没有必要再教授二次方程了；反正95%的人都解不出来。你可以给学生布置一个需要用到二次方程的问题，然后让机器来求解。这样你就可以腾出时间来思考是什么让问题变得有趣，以及它会带来哪些影响。过去，孩子们把所有时间都花在了琢磨如何解方程上。”

“I made this point at a conference of math teachers a few years ago. I said that to take advantage of the computer you could have kids do some writing about the problems they’re trying to solve. In fact, you could have them write their own problems and make up their own questions. That’s totally new to students. I was surprised by the teachers’ response. There were teachers at the conference from states like Nebraska and Rhode Island and Washington, which had a mandate from the board of education to do writing across the curriculum, and the math teachers were resisting it because they didn’t know what the writing might be. So they said, ‘Tell us more—what are you doing?’ I went home and wrote a paper called ‘Writing to Learn Mathematics,’ which is just a set of ideas about the kind of things you can do, and that led to all these workshops.”

“几年前，我在一次数学教师会议上提出了这个观点。我说，为了充分利用计算机，可以让孩子们把他们正在尝试解决的问题写下来。事实上，你可以让他们自己编写问题，自己设计题目。这对学生来说是全新的。老师们的反应让我很惊讶。参加会议的老师来自内布拉斯加州、罗德岛州和华盛顿州等州，这些州的教育委员会都要求在所有课程中融入写作，而数学老师们对此持抵触态度，因为他们不知道写作具体应该是什么形式。所以他们说：‘请详细说说——你们是怎么做的？’我回家后写了一篇题为《用写作学习数学》的论文，其中列举了一些可以采用的方法，而这篇文章也促成了所有这些研讨会的举办。”

I was struck by the fact that for students to make up their own problems was something “totally new.” Only then did it come back to me from my boyhood that the math teacher not only has custody of all the right answers; the teacher (or his surrogate, the textbook) also provides all the questions. I thought of the countless hours I had spent in math classes determining how long it took those three musketeers of math pedagogy, A, B and C, rowing at different speeds, to reach a certain bend in the river. No suspense about the outcome relieved the monotony of those races, for the three rowers were as foreordained as figures in a morality play to finish in the same order. It was a matter of character. A was strong and handsome, honest and decent, patriotic and God-fearing; B was plucky but flawed, fated to catch his oar on a rock just when victory seemed possible; and C was the amiable bumbler who is every one of us, capsizing in the stream. I always hoped for an upset—for C to redeem the best dreams of life’s losers, or at least for B to redeem the best dreams of life’s runners-up. It was not to be; in algebra textbooks, life’s races were rigged.

令我震惊的是，让学生自己出题竟然是“全新的”事情。直到那时，我才想起童年时，数学老师不仅掌握着所有正确答案，老师（或者他的代理人——教科书）还提供了所有题目。我想起了无数次在数学课上花费的时间，计算着数学教学界的三位“火枪手”A、B和C，以不同的速度划桨，到达河道某个弯道需要多长时间。比赛结果毫无悬念，但这场比赛却单调乏味，因为这三位划桨者就像道德剧中的人物一样，注定要以相同的顺序到达终点。这完全取决于性格。A强壮英俊，诚实正直，爱国虔诚；B勇敢却有缺陷，注定会在看似胜利在望时，桨被石头卡住；而C就像我们每个人一样，笨手笨脚，在人生的洪流中翻了个底朝天。我一直盼望着能爆冷——希望C能为人生失败者们的梦想画上圆满的句号，或者至少希望B能为人生亚军们的梦想画上圆满的句号。然而事与愿违；在代数课本里，人生的竞赛早已被操纵。

I explained to Joan Countryman that my conception of mathematics was largely rooted in the lives and fortunes of A, B and C. “Those problems,” she said, “were the sole effort that textbooks made to establish a connection between math and the world. If your only notion of a math problem is those questions about A, B and C, or about those two trains going in opposite directions, that’s a very limited notion of the kinds of things that mathematics does. But if you encourage students to write their own questions, there’s no limit to where they can go.”

我向琼·康特里曼解释说，我对数学的理解很大程度上根植于A、B和C的生活和命运。“这些问题，”她说，“是教科书试图建立数学与世界联系的唯一尝试。如果你对数学问题的唯一理解就是关于A、B和C的问题，或者关于两列朝相反方向行驶的火车的问题，那么你对数学的理解就非常有限了。但如果你鼓励学生自己提出问题，他们的探索空间将是无限的。”

One place they can go is into other disciplines, I suggested to Joan Countryman. “Obviously one of the things you’re after is to break down the compartments between different subjects.”

我向琼·康特里曼建议，他们可以考虑进入其他学科领域。“显然，你想要达成的目标之一就是打破不同学科之间的壁垒。”

“I try to do that a lot,” she said. “The tradition is that there should be a connection between math and what we call science. Actually, in most schools, math and science teachers don’t have anything to do with each other. But in many fields there’s a natural crossover. Philosophy, for instance. I co-teach an introductory course in philosophy with the woman who’s head of our classics department. One thing I did was to read Euclid with the class, which normally isn’t part of philosophy. It turned out that it was very useful to the kids because Euclid’s style, which was to make propositions and derive theorems from them, was adopted by many later philosophers, like Spinoza. We’ve had a good time playing around with that, trying to figure out what some of the connections are. The kids were startled by it.”

“我经常这样做，”她说。“传统上认为数学和我们所说的科学之间应该有所联系。但实际上，在大多数学校，数学老师和科学老师之间没有任何交集。不过，在很多领域，两者之间存在着天然的交叉。比如哲学。我和古典学系主任共同教授一门哲学入门课程。我做的一件事就是和学生们一起阅读欧几里得的著作，这通常不属于哲学范畴。结果发现这对孩子们非常有用，因为欧几里得的论证方式——先提出命题，再从中推导出定理——被许多后来的哲学家所采用，比如斯宾诺莎。我们一直在探索其中的联系，乐在其中。孩子们对此感到非常惊讶。”

Another discipline with startling connections, I suggested, is history. From my days at the Book-of-the-Month Club I remembered when the first trickle of books of “new history” came along—books that use the new technology of numbers crunching to reconstruct the daily life of earlier eras. Two that took us by surprise with their popularity were The Structures of Everyday Life and The Wheels of Commerce , by the French historian Fernand Braudel, which were intimate accounts of how “ordinary” people lived and worked and made their money in Europe between the fifteenth and the eighteenth centuries. So strong was Braudel’s influence that the Club was soon awash in histories—about medieval England, about czarist Russia, about revolutionary America—that were grounded in population figures, agricultural records and other quantitative data that scholars had never had before the advent of computers.

我指出，历史学也是一门有着惊人联系的学科。我还记得当年在每月读书俱乐部时，第一批“新历史”书籍涌现——这些书籍运用当时新兴的数据分析技术来重构早期时代的日常生活。其中两本让我们始料未及的畅销书是法国历史学家费尔南·布罗代尔的《日常生活结构》和《商业的车轮》。这两本书生动地描绘了15至18世纪欧洲“普通”人的生活、工作和谋生之道。布罗代尔的影响力如此之大，以至于俱乐部很快就被各种历史著作所淹没——从关于中世纪英国的历史，到关于沙皇俄国的历史，再到关于美国革命的历史——这些著作都以人口统计数据、农业记录和其他量化数据为基础，而这些数据在计算机出现之前是学者们从未接触过的。

“It’s a wonderful development,” Joan Countryman agreed, “and because of it there’s far more conversation now between history teachers and math teachers. I tell our history teachers that I’ll put a history question on my test if they’ll put a math question on their test. I’m teasing, of course.”

“这真是个好兆头，”琼·康特里曼赞同道，“正因为如此，现在历史老师和数学老师之间的交流也多了很多。我跟历史老师开玩笑说，如果他们愿意在考试里出一道数学题，我就在我的考试里出一道历史题。当然，我只是开玩笑。”

It didn’t strike me as a teasing notion. On the contrary, it was a unifying idea, one that summed up much of what we had been talking about all afternoon. “Wouldn’t it be the same question?” I asked. “Wouldn’t the history question on the math test be the same as the math question on the history test?” I had in mind some question like “How can we find out what people ate in eighteenth-century France?”

我并不觉得这是个玩笑。恰恰相反，这是一个能概括我们整个下午讨论内容的统一观点。“难道问题不是一样的吗？”我问道，“数学考试中的历史题和历史考试中的数学题难道不是一模一样吗？”我脑海中浮现出一个类似“我们如何才能了解十八世纪法国人的饮食？”这样的问题。

Mrs. Countryman said it could easily be the same question, and in both cases writing would be the tool for thinking about how to find the answer. That would make for unusually interesting mathematics, I thought, and also for interesting history. At least it would be more interesting than all those trips up—or was it down?—the river with A, B and C.

康特里曼太太说，这很可能是同一个问题，而写作在两种情况下都是思考如何找到答案的工具。我想，这不仅会造就异常有趣的数学，也会造就有趣的历史。至少，这比和A、B、C一起沿河而上——或者说是顺流而下？——的那些旅行要有趣得多。

The next day I sat in on Joan Countryman’s eleventh-grade precalculus class.
