The arriving students grabbed their notebooks from her desk and began to write in them intently. “This year I got braver,” she explained to me, “and decided to have everybody just do free writing at the beginning of every class. ‘Check your editor at the door,’ I told them. ‘You can write about anything as long as you’re willing to have me see what it is.’ What they write doesn’t have to be about math, but half the time it is: ‘Why does this formula function? What does this pattern of numbers mean?’ Or it might be about one of their other subjects: ‘Here’s a physics experiment I tried that didn’t come out right.’ They seem to want to know what’s going on inside their heads—what their learning styles are—and that’s something I’m eager for them to know.

第二天，我旁听了琼·康特里曼的十一年级预备微积分课。学生们一到教室就从她桌上拿起笔记本，开始认真地写起来。“今年我更大胆了，”她向我解释道，“我决定让每个人在每节课开始前都进行自由写作。‘把你们的编辑留在门外，’我告诉他们，‘你们可以写任何东西，只要你们愿意让我看到你们写的内容。’他们写的东西不一定非得是数学，但有一半的时间都是关于数学的：‘为什么这个公式有效？这个数字模式意味着什么？’或者也可能是关于他们其他科目的：‘这是我尝试做的一个物理实验，结果失败了。’他们似乎很想知道自己脑子里在想什么——他们的学习风格是什么——而这正是我渴望他们了解的。”

“I also talk with them individually about what they’ve written. One point I make is that if you grow up to be a middle-aged engineer you’re going to need to write, and this is one way to make yourself comfortable with it. If only for that reason, keeping these notebooks is helpful. But it also turns out to do other things: it’s a way of clearing the palate. Kids come into the classroom with all this other stuff in their heads. If they write it down for ten minutes they become much more available for whatever it is we want to do in the class. One of my colleagues worries that if she does this she’ll get less teaching done because every class will be ten minutes shorter, but it doesn’t seem to work out that way.”

“我还会和他们单独谈谈他们写的东西。我强调的一点是，如果你长大后成为一名中年工程师，你就需要写作，而这正是让你适应写作的一种方式。即使仅仅出于这个原因，记笔记也很有帮助。但它还有其他作用：它能帮助你清空思绪。孩子们走进教室时脑子里装着各种各样的东西。如果他们花十分钟时间把这些东西写下来，他们就能更专注于课堂上我们要做的事情。我的一位同事担心，如果她这样做，每节课都会缩短十分钟，从而减少她的教学时间，但事实并非如此。”

When free writing ended, math began. Mrs. Countryman drew a triangle on the blackboard and told the class she wanted them to determine the size of its three angles. But she gave them none of the information they would need—for instance, the length of the sides.

自由写作结束后，数学课开始了。康特里曼老师在黑板上画了一个三角形，告诉同学们她想让他们求出三角形三个角的度数。但她没有提供任何必要的信息——例如，三角形的边长。

“I want you to write how you might go about solving this problem when you do get more information from me,” she said. The students wrote for about five minutes. They looked like writers—they were thinking hard and laboriously putting sentences on paper and crossing out sentences that obviously didn’t express what they were thinking, perhaps because their thinking kept changing as they wrote and discovered what they really thought. They even sounded like writers; I heard the scratching out of words that is the obbligato of a writer’s life.

“我希望你们写下，当你们从我这里获得更多信息后，你们会如何解决这个问题，”她说。学生们写了大约五分钟。他们看起来像作家——他们认真思考，一丝不苟地在纸上写下句子，然后划掉那些显然不能表达他们想法的句子，或许是因为随着写作的进行，他们的想法也在不断变化，最终才找到了自己真正的想法。他们的声音也像作家；我听到了他们划掉文字的声音，那是作家生活中必不可少的。

After that some of them were asked to read what they had written. The papers were all brief journeys in logic: if I knew this I’d be able to find out that ; what I need to determine is a , so the best method to use is probably x and y . Writing and thinking and learning had merged into one process. The class was off to a good start, and when it got down to actual mathematics—when the students were given the length of the sides and began to do some calculating—they were working from a common understanding of how the problem should be approached. They threw numbers and suppositions and probabilities into the room until they got the first of the three angles, and the rest was easy.

之后，一些学生被要求朗读自己写的内容。这些文章都是简短的逻辑探索：如果我知道这个，我就能推导出那个；我需要确定的是a，所以最好的方法可能是x和y。写作、思考和学习融为一体。课堂开局良好，当真正进入数学环节——学生们被告知各边的长度并开始计算时——他们对如何解决问题有着共同的理解。他们抛出各种数字、假设和概率，直到算出三个角中的第一个，剩下的就轻而易举了。

Joan Countryman’s part in all this had been to coax scraps of information out of the students until the pieces formed themselves into the right answer. I never felt that she was the owner of that answer. I almost had the feeling that she didn’t know it herself; the answer was just there waiting to be found by all of them. What I did feel was that I was watching a very good teacher.

琼·康特里曼在这一切中的作用，就是引导学生们一点一点地提供信息，直到这些碎片拼凑成正确的答案。我从未觉得她掌握了那个答案。我甚至觉得她自己也不知道；答案就在那里，等着他们所有人去发现。我当时确实觉得，我正在见证一位非常优秀的老师。

Earlier I had asked her how she happened to be at Germantown Friends. She said it was a homecoming. “The town where I spent my early childhood didn’t have good enough schools to satisfy my parents,” she explained. “At just about that time Germantown Friends decided that it wanted to integrate, but they were somewhat fearful because they didn’t know what would happen. We were a black family that the school felt it could take a chance on. I went to the school for ten years, beginning in third grade. After that I went to Sarah Lawrence, where I had a wonderful math professor named Ed Cogan, and when I became a math teacher myself it seemed natural to start where I had begun. I’ve been here ever since. In fact, my own children have also gone through the school—they’re both through Yale now—so my being here is part of a circle.”

之前我问过她为什么会来到日耳曼敦友谊学校。她说这是一次回家。“我童年早期居住的小镇没有足够好的学校，无法让我的父母满意，”她解释道。“就在那时，日耳曼敦友谊学校决定实行种族融合，但他们有些忐忑，因为他们不知道会发生什么。我们家是黑人家庭，学校觉得可以给我们一个机会。我从三年级开始在这所学校读了十年。之后我去了莎拉·劳伦斯学院，在那里我遇到了一位很棒的数学教授，名叫埃德·科根。后来我自己也成为了一名数学老师，所以很自然地就回到了我最初开始的地方。我一直在这里任教至今。事实上，我的孩子们也都曾就读于这所学校——他们现在都在耶鲁大学读书——所以，我在这里也算是一个轮回。”

Now I was in her classroom with still another generation of math students; the circle was by no means closed. Thinking about the enjoyment that the students had brought to the problem of the triangle, I asked Joan Countryman what difference it would have made if no writing had been done—if she had provided the length of the triangle’s three sides and told the class to figure it out by straight trigonometry.

现在我又回到了她的教室，面对的是另一批数学学生；这圈子远未结束。想到学生们在解决三角形问题时所展现出的乐趣，我问琼·康特里曼，如果当初没有做任何书写——如果她直接给出三角形三边的长度，让学生们用三角函数直接计算，结果会有什么不同呢？

“Two or three kids with an aptitude for numbers would probably have come up with a fairly quick answer,” she said, “but even they wouldn’t have thought about what they were doing as thoroughly as they did when they wrote about how they would do it. And the rest of the kids wouldn’t have been forced to think about it at all; they would have just waited for someone else to come up with the answer. Writing gets everybody involved.”

“两三个对数字敏感的孩子可能很快就能想出答案，”她说，“但即使是他们，也不会像写下来那样认真思考。而其他孩子则根本不会被迫思考；他们只会等着别人给出答案。写作能让每个人都参与进来。”

I wondered how sanguine Joan Countryman was about converting other math teachers to her approach. Resistance to new teaching methods usually takes one of two forms: conservatism (“We’ve always done it our way”) or inertia (“Your way is too much work”).

我很好奇琼·康特里曼对说服其他数学老师接受她的方法有多乐观。对新教学方法的抵制通常有两种形式：保守主义（“我们一直都是这么做的”）或惯性（“你的方法太麻烦了”）。

“It’s mostly inertia,” she said. “At math conferences teachers ask how much time it’s going to take to work with this kind of writing, and all of us who are doing it say it doesn’t take as much time as you’d think, especially because we’re not teaching writing; we’re teaching mathematics. I do occasionally make corrections, or comments, or tell them how to spell Pythagoras; if you’re going to write about geometry you ought to be able to spell the words that geometry mentions. But I’m not so concerned about that. And I’m not concerned about writing style at all. What happens is that you just come to celebrate those wonderful phrases and sentences that the kids write. The writing jumps out at you.”

“主要是惯性使然，”她说。“在数学研讨会上，老师们会问，指导这种写作需要多少时间，而我们这些正在这样做的人都说，其实并没有想象中那么费时，尤其因为我们教的是数学，而不是写作。我偶尔会做一些修改、评论，或者告诉他们毕达哥拉斯的拼写；如果你要写几何，就应该能拼写出几何中提到的那些词汇。但我并不太在意这些。我也完全不在意写作风格。最终的结果就是，你会不由自主地去欣赏孩子们写的那些精彩的词句。他们的文字会自然而然地吸引你的目光。”

# ↩

10. Man, Woman and Child

10. 男人、女人和孩子

One of the jobs I most enjoyed during my years at the Book-of-the-Month Club was to run an annual series of six lectures—sponsored by the Club and held at the New York Public Library—in which writers talked about a particular aspect of the art and craft of writing. The talks were taped, and at the end of each series I edited the transcripts into a book.

我在“每月一书俱乐部”工作期间最喜欢的工作之一，就是负责组织一年一度的六场系列讲座——由俱乐部赞助，在纽约公共图书馆举办——讲座中，作家们会探讨写作艺术和技巧的某个特定方面。讲座会被录音，每场讲座结束后，我都会把录音整理成书。

The first series was on the craft of biography, and the biographers included Robert A. Caro, who was then well into his three-volume life of Lyndon Johnson, and David McCullough, then in mid-pursuit of people who had known his subject, Harry Truman, in Independence, Missouri. Another year the theme was religious writing, the writers being, among others, Mary Gordon, the Catholic novelist, and Allen Ginsberg, the Buddhist poet.

第一期系列讲座的主题是传记写作技巧，主讲的传记作家包括罗伯特·A·卡罗（当时他正在撰写林登·约翰逊的三卷本传记）和大卫·麦卡洛（当时他正在密苏里州独立城寻找认识哈里·杜鲁门的人）。另一期讲座的主题是宗教写作，主讲作家包括天主教小说家玛丽·戈登和佛教诗人艾伦·金斯伯格等。

But the series that comes back to me now, as I recall literature that I’ve admired about the species called man, was on the craft of memoir. I’m a pushover for memoir; to me it’s the most powerful of nonfiction forms because it goes to the deepest roots of personal experience. Unlike autobiography, which covers an entire life, the memoirist focuses on one period that was unusually vivid or that was framed by historical events—childhood, for instance, or war. Memoir is a window into a life, and in our lecture series writers as different as Russell Baker, Annie Dillard, Alfred Kazin and Toni Morrison took us into corners of their past that had a heightened degree of emotion.

但如今，当我回想起那些我曾欣赏过的关于人类的文学作品时，脑海中浮现的却是关于回忆录写作的系列讲座。我向来对回忆录情有独钟；在我看来，它是非虚构作品中最有力量的一种，因为它直抵个人经历的最深处。与涵盖整个人生的自传不同，回忆录作家往往聚焦于一段格外生动或被历史事件所塑造的时期——例如童年或战争。回忆录是一扇通往人生的窗口，在我们举办的系列讲座中，像罗素·贝克、安妮·迪拉德、阿尔弗雷德·卡津和托妮·莫里森这样风格迥异的作家，都带领我们走进了他们过往生活中那些充满强烈情感的角落。

Lewis Thomas, however, had a different journey in mind. Dr. Thomas first served notice with Lives of a Cell , in 1974, that a cell biologist can also be a lyrical writer. But I had chosen him for the series because of a later book called The Youngest Science , which is a memoir—in fact, two memoirs. On one level it’s Dr. Thomas’s story of his own life as a doctor, starting with his boyhood when he accompanied his father, a general practitioner, on his rounds. Medicine was then “a profoundly ignorant occupation,” and his father carried only four medications in his black bag because they were the only ones that were known to do any good. On another level it’s the story of the coming of age of American medicine, starting with the wartime discovery of antibiotics, which made doctors far less ignorant and helpless. I hoped Lewis Thomas would tell us how he had gone about writing that double narrative. His talk started like this:

然而，路易斯·托马斯博士却有着不同的创作历程。早在1974年，托马斯博士就凭借《细胞的生命》一书宣告，细胞生物学家也可以是一位文笔优美的作家。但我之所以选择他作为系列访谈对象，是因为他后来出版了一本名为《最年轻的科学》的书，这是一部回忆录——实际上是两部回忆录。一方面，它讲述了托马斯博士作为一名医生的人生故事，从他童年时期跟随身为全科医生的父亲出诊开始。当时的医学被认为是“极其无知的职业”，他父亲的黑色药包里只有四种药，因为那是当时唯一被认为有效的药物。另一方面，它讲述了美国医学的成长历程，从战时抗生素的发现开始，抗生素的出现使医生们不再那么无知和束手无策。我希望路易斯·托马斯博士能告诉我们，他是如何创作出这双重叙事的。他的演讲是这样开始的：

To begin personally, on a confessional note, I was at one time, at my outset, a single cell. I have no memory of this stage of my life, but I know it to be true because everybody says so. There was a sort of half-life before that, literally half, when the two half-endowed, haploid gametes, each carrying half my chromosomes, were off on their own looking to bump into each other and did so, by random chance, sheer luck, for better or worse, richer or poorer, et cetera, and I got under way.

先坦白说，我最初只是一个单细胞。我对这段时期没有任何记忆，但我知道这是真的，因为大家都这么说。在那之前，我经历了一段类似“半衰期”的阶段，确切地说，是“半衰期”。那时，两个单倍体配子各自携带着我一半的染色体，各自游荡，寻找彼此。它们最终相遇了，纯粹是出于偶然，纯粹是运气，无论好坏、贫富等等，就这样，我的生命开始了。

I do not remember this, but I know that I began dividing. I have probably never worked so hard, and never again with such skill and certainty. At a certain stage, very young, a matter of hours of youth, I sorted myself out and became a system of cells, each labeled for what it was to become—brain cells, limbs, liver, the lot—all of them signaling to each other, calculating their territories, laying me out. At one stage I possessed an excellent kidney, good enough for any higher fish; then I thought better and destroyed it all at once, installing in its place a neater pair for living on land. I didn’t plan on this when it was going on, but my cells, with a better memory, did.

我不记得这件事了，但我知道我开始分裂。我可能从未如此努力过，也再未如此熟练而自信地工作过。在某个阶段，非常年轻，大概只有几个小时的青春，我完成了自我重组，变成了一个细胞系统，每个细胞都被贴上了标签，标明了它们将要成为什么——脑细胞、四肢、肝脏等等——它们彼此传递信号，计算着各自的领地，规划着我的身体。我曾经拥有一个非常优秀的肾脏，足以满足任何高等鱼类的需求；后来我改变了主意，一口气摧毁了它，取而代之的是一对更适合陆地生活的肾脏。我当时并没有计划这样做，但我的细胞，记忆力更好，却记住了这一切。

Thinking back, I count myself lucky that I was not in charge at the time. If it had been left to me to do the mapping of my cells I would have got it wrong, dropped something, forgotten where to assemble my neural crest, confused it. Or I might have been stopped in my tracks, panicked by the massive deaths, billions of my embryonic cells being killed off systematically to make room for their more senior successors, death on a scale so vast that I can’t think of it without wincing. By the time I was born, more of me had died than had survived. It is no wonder I can’t remember; during that time I went through brain after brain for nine months, finally contriving the one model that could be human, equipped for language.

回想起来，我庆幸当时自己并非负责人。如果让我来绘制细胞图谱，我肯定会出错，会遗漏什么，会忘记如何组装神经嵴，会搞得一团糟。或者，我可能会被大规模的细胞死亡吓得不知所措，数十亿个胚胎细胞被系统性地清除，为更成熟的细胞腾出空间——如此巨大的死亡规模，我一想到就感到不寒而栗。等我出生时，死去的细胞比存活下来的还要多。难怪我记不清了；在那九个月里，我不断地改造大脑，最终构建出一个能够成为人类、具备语言能力的模型。

This was terrific stuff, but it caught me off guard—it had never occurred to me that a memoir could be prenatal. I was reassured, however, by the word “language”; Dr. Thomas would soon get himself born and his chronology would move forward. It didn’t.

这真是精彩绝伦，却也让我措手不及——我从未想过回忆录竟然可以以孕育为主题。不过，“语言”这个词让我稍稍安心；托马斯博士很快就会“出生”，他的叙述也会继续向前推进。然而，事实并非如此。

It is because of language that I am able now to think farther back into my lineage. By myself, I can only remember two parents, one grandmother and the family stories of Welshmen, back into the shadows when all the Welsh were kings, but no farther. From there on I must rely on reading the texts.

正是因为语言，我才能追溯到更远的家族历史。仅凭我自己，我只能记起两位父母、一位祖母，以及威尔士人的家族故事，那些故事仿佛都发生在遥远的过去，那时威尔士人都是国王，仅此而已。从那以后，我只能依靠阅读文献来了解家族历史。

They instruct me that I go back to the first of my immediate line, the beginner, the earliest Homo sapiens , human all the way through, or not quite human if you measure humanness as I do by the property of language and its property, the consciousness of an indisputably singular, unique self. I’m not sure how far back that takes me, and no one has yet told me about this convincingly. When did my relations begin speaking?

他们指示我追溯到我的直系祖先，追溯到始祖，追溯到最早的智人，追溯到完全意义上的人类，或者，如果你像我一样，以语言及其特质——无可争议的独特自我意识——来衡量人类，那么他/她就不完全是人类。我不确定这能追溯到多久以前，而且至今无人能令人信服地告诉我答案。我的祖先究竟何时开始说话？

Writing is easier to trace, having started not more than a few years back, maybe 10,000 years, not much more. Tracking speech requires guesswork. If we were slow learners, as slow as we seem to be in solving today’s hard problems, my guess is that we didn’t begin talking until sometime within the last 100,000 years, give or take 50,000. That’s what’s called a rough scientific guess. But no matter, it is an exceedingly short time ago, and I am embarrassed at the thought that so many of my ancestors, generations of them—all the way back to the very first ones a million-odd years ago—may have been speechless. I am modestly proud to have come from a family of toolmakers, bone scratchers, grave diggers, cave painters. Humans all. But it hurts to think of them as so literally dumb, living out their lives without metaphors, deprived of conversation, even small talk. I would prefer to have had them arrive fully endowed, talking their heads off, the moment evolution provided them with braincases large enough to contain words, so to speak. But it was not so, I must guess, and language came late.

文字的起源更容易追溯，它出现的时间不过几年，也许只有一万年，不会更久。而语言的起源则需要推测。如果我们学习能力很慢，就像我们解决当今难题的速度一样慢，那么我猜测我们开始说话的时间大概在过去十万年左右，上下浮动五万年。这只是一个粗略的科学推测。但无论如何，那都是非常短暂的过去，想到我的许多祖先，一代又一代——一直追溯到一百万多年前的第一批人——可能都无法说话，我就感到羞愧。我为自己来自一个制造工具、雕刻骨头、挖掘坟墓、绘制洞穴壁画的家族而感到自豪。他们都是人类。但想到他们真的如此愚钝，一生没有比喻，没有对话，甚至连闲聊都没有，我就感到难过。我更希望他们一出生就天赋异禀，能言善辩，仿佛进化赋予了他们足够大的脑容量来容纳语言。但我想事实并非如此，语言出现得比较晚。

By now it was dawning on me that this was no ordinary excursion into the past. It was the story of what it means to be human. Still, something in me continued to want Lewis Thomas to get to his own humanity: How did this twentieth-century descendant of toolmakers and bone scratchers learn to use so compellingly the language that all those generations of his forebears never possessed at all? To be human is to want a tidy conclusion. Dr. Thomas pressed on:

这时我才意识到，这并非一次普通的追溯历史之旅。它讲述的是人性的意义。然而，我内心深处仍然渴望路易斯·托马斯能够探寻他自身的人性：这位二十世纪的工具制造者和骨匠的后裔，是如何学会如此生动地运用他的祖辈从未拥有过的语言的？人之常情就是渴望一个圆满的结局。托马斯博士继续说道：

What sticks in my mind is another, unavoidable aspect of my genealogy, far beyond my memory, but remembered still, I suspect, by all my cells. It is a difficult and delicate fact to mention. To face it squarely, I come from a line that can be traced straight back, with some accuracy, into a near-infinity of years before my first humanoid ancestors turned up. I go back, and so do you, like it or not, to a single Ur-ancestor whose remains are on display in rocks dated approximately 3.5 thousand million years ago, born a billion or so years after the earth itself took shape and began cooling down. That first of the line, our n-granduncle, was unmistakably a bacterial cell.

真正让我难以忘怀的，是我家谱中另一个无法回避的方面，它远远超出了我的记忆，但我怀疑，我体内的每一个细胞都仍然记得它。这是一个难以启齿且敏感的事实。坦白地说，我的血脉可以追溯到近乎无限的远古时期，远在我最早的人类祖先出现之前。无论你是否愿意，我都可以追溯到一位始祖，他的遗骸保存在距今约350亿年的岩石中，诞生于地球形成并开始冷却后约10亿年。这条血脉的始祖，我们的n祖叔，毫无疑问是一个细菌细胞。

I cannot get this out of my head. It has become the most important thing I know, the obligatory beginning of any memoir, the long-buried source of language. We derive from a lineage of bacteria, and a very long line at that. Never mind our embarrassed indignation when we were first told, last century, that we came from a family of apes and had chimps as near-cousins. That was relatively easy to accommodate, having at least the distant look of a set of relatives. But this new connection, already fixed by recent science beyond any hope of disowning the parentage, is something else again. At first the encounter must come as a kind of humiliation. Humble origins indeed.

这件事一直萦绕在我心头，挥之不去。它成了我所知的最重要的事，是任何回忆录的必写开篇，是语言深埋心底的源泉。我们起源于细菌谱系，而且谱系非常悠久。别忘了，上个世纪我们第一次得知自己来自猿类家族，与黑猩猩是近亲时，我们是多么尴尬和愤慨。毕竟，我们之间至少存在着某种远亲关系，所以这种说法还算容易接受。但如今，科学已经证实了我们与猿类的血缘关系，让我们再也无法否认，这又是另一回事了。起初，这种认知必然会让我们感到某种屈辱。我们的出身真是卑微啊。

Around here I finally told myself to relax and enjoy the trip, wherever it was going. Ask a cell biologist to talk about memoir and he won’t be satisfied until he gets back to the original cell. Only once did the collection of cells known as Lewis Thomas enter his own narrative. “I do have a few memories,” he said, “of studying to read and write, age four or five, I think, but I have no earlier recollection at all of learning speech. This surprises me. You’d think that the first word, the first triumphant finished sentence, would have been such a stunning landmark to remain fixed in memory forever, the biggest moment in life. But I have forgotten.” His brief appearance over, Dr. Thomas plunged back into the abyss, taking us on a voyage of unimaginable length—nothing less than a memoir of life on earth. “We are all,” he said, “in the same family—grasses, seagulls, fishes, fleas and voting citizens of the republic.”

在这里，我终于告诉自己要放松，享受这段旅程，无论它将带我去向何方。你问一位细胞生物学家关于回忆录的话题，他非得回到最初的细胞才肯罢休。路易斯·托马斯博士的叙述中，只提到过一次他那被称为“细胞集合”的个体。“我确实有一些记忆，”他说，“记得四五岁的时候学习读写，但我完全不记得更早的时候学习说话的事。这让我很惊讶。你会觉得，第一个词，第一个完整的句子，应该是一个令人难忘的里程碑，永远铭刻在记忆中，是人生中最伟大的时刻。但我却忘记了。” 托马斯博士短暂的露面结束后，他又一头扎进了茫茫的海洋，带领我们踏上了一段难以想象的漫长旅程——这简直就是一部关于地球生命的回忆录。“我们都是，”他说，“属于同一个大家庭——草、海鸥、鱼、跳蚤，以及共和国的公民。”

I’ve slightly bent the rules of this book by presenting a talk instead of a piece of writing. Obviously, however, this is a piece of writing—nobody could improvise such a graceful chain of sentences—and by now it has properly found its way into a book. But mainly I’m using it to make a point about unexpectedness. I had a preconceived notion of what Lewis Thomas was going to say. More presumptuously, I had a notion of what I wanted him to say. What he did say was vastly more exciting than anything I could have conceived of. I loved how thoroughly he smashed my pious expectations. Originality and surprise are the most refreshing elements in nonfiction writing. There’s no “right” way to approach the subject of memoir, or the subject of man, or any other subject. A writer who comes at his discipline from an oblique angle is almost always more fun to travel with. Risk gives writing an edge.

我稍微打破了本书的规则，用演讲而非文章的形式呈现。当然，这显然也是一篇文字作品——没人能即兴创作出如此优美流畅的句子——而且它现在已经正式收录到书中了。但我主要想借此说明“出乎意料”的重要性。我原本对路易斯·托马斯要讲的内容有所预想。更确切地说，我甚至预设了自己希望他讲什么。但他实际讲的内容远比我所能想象的精彩得多。我喜欢他彻底颠覆我那些自以为是的预期。原创性和惊喜是非虚构写作中最令人耳目一新的元素。无论是回忆录、人性，还是其他任何主题，都没有所谓的“正确”写作方法。一位以独特视角切入主题的作家，其作品往往更引人入胜。冒险赋予写作独特的魅力。

Of the many disciplines that deal with the study of man, one that appeals to me is anthropology. I can trace the seeds of my interest to a night on Broadway in 1952. In those years journalistic duty required me to attend every opening, and so it happened that I found myself in the Fulton Theater waiting for a show called Dancers of Bali to begin. The troupe was from the Balinese village of Pliatan, and I had no idea what I was in for. Nowhere had my life or my education been touched by the culture of Southeast Asia.

在众多研究人类的学科中，我尤其钟情于人类学。我对人类学的兴趣可以追溯到1952年百老汇的一个夜晚。那时，记者的职责要求我必须出席每一场新剧的首演，于是，我碰巧来到了富尔顿剧院，等待一场名为《巴厘岛舞者》的演出开始。这个舞团来自巴厘岛的普利亚坦村，而我当时对即将发生的一切一无所知。我的生活和教育从未接触过东南亚文化。

The curtain went up and the gamelan orchestra on the stage struck a note that went through me like an electrical current. It was a tremendous CLANG! that reverberated through the theater. Then the gamelan began to play, and I was an instant convert. What wonderful combination of instruments was making this wonderful sound? I saw that about twenty-five Balinese men, sitting cross-legged on the stage, were striking an array of gongs, cymbals, drums and metallophones with a rhythmical intricacy that was like nothing I had ever heard. No visible signal passed among them, but the precision was absolute, and although the Balinese scale contained only five notes, it seemed to keep renewing itself and to have unending variety because the percussion instruments were so alive.

幕布拉开，舞台上的加麦兰乐团奏响了一个音符，那音符如同电流般贯穿我的全身。一声震耳欲聋的巨响，响彻整个剧院。随后，加麦兰开始演奏，我瞬间被它征服。究竟是怎样的乐器组合，才能奏出如此美妙的乐章？我看到大约二十五位巴厘岛男子盘腿坐在舞台上，敲击着一排锣、钹、鼓和金属琴，节奏之精妙，是我前所未闻的。他们之间没有传递任何可见的信号，但演奏却精准无比。尽管巴厘岛音阶只有五个音符，但由于打击乐器如此鲜活灵动，它仿佛不断自我更新，变化无穷。

Next the actors began to appear, some of them costumed as witches and dragons, performing Balinese dances that enacted the island’s legends and religious beliefs, including the potent kris dance, in which the men went into a deep and ominous trance. The beauty and intensity of the dancers was joined with the beauty and intensity of the music—a perfect fusion of art and ritual. Yet we were told that this troupe, though probably Bali’s best, was not untypical of what might be found in almost any Balinese village. That would be worth testing, I thought, and on my next summer vacation I took off for Indonesia.

随后，演员们开始登场，其中一些人装扮成女巫和龙，表演巴厘岛舞蹈，演绎着岛上的传说和宗教信仰，包括气势磅礴的克里斯舞。在克里斯舞中，男舞者会进入一种深沉而神秘的恍惚状态。舞者们优美而充满力量的表演与音乐的优美和震撼相得益彰——艺术与仪式完美融合。然而，我们被告知，这支舞团虽然可能是巴厘岛最好的，但在几乎任何一个巴厘岛村庄都能找到类似的表演团体。我想，这值得一试，于是，在下一个暑假，我启程前往印度尼西亚。

First I went to Jogjakarta, in central Java, to see the ancient shadow plays of the Javanese court, which also had a gamelan accompaniment. Those stylized dramas put me in the mood for Bali, and when I got there I made my way up into the hills to the village of Pliatan. The musicians and dancers who had conquered Broadway had long since come home and were back at their everyday jobs in the rice fields. That’s how I found out that the Balinese have almost no concept of “art.” What I had assumed was their art turned out to be organic to their life. Night after night, standing in the dirt temple courtyard in Pliatan, Ubud and other villages, I watched the same dances that I had seen on Broadway, performed by men and women who during the day had been working. Art, life and religion were intertwined. Children and chickens were everywhere. Mothers holding their babies stood in a circle around the dancers; the delicate movements of the dancers and the clinking sounds of the gamelan got absorbed almost from birth.

我先去了爪哇岛中部的日惹，观看爪哇宫廷的古老皮影戏，这些戏还有加麦兰音乐伴奏。这些风格化的戏剧让我对巴厘岛充满了向往，抵达巴厘岛后，我便驱车前往山上的普利亚坦村。那些征服百老汇的音乐家和舞者早已回到家乡，在稻田里继续着他们日常的劳作。正是在那里，我发现巴厘岛人几乎没有“艺术”的概念。我原以为的艺术，其实早已融入他们的生活。夜复一夜，我站在普利亚坦、乌布和其他村庄的泥土寺庙庭院里，观看着与我在百老汇看到的同样的舞蹈，表演者是白天辛勤劳作的男男女女。艺术、生活和宗教交织在一起。到处都是孩子和鸡。抱着婴儿的母亲们围成一圈，围绕着舞者；舞者轻柔的动作和加麦兰乐器清脆的叮当声，几乎从出生起就被深深地吸引住了。

That was my first view of a unified culture, and I remember how resentful I felt that my own culture didn’t have such an enviable wholeness. I thought of how American schools treat the arts as frills—a detour off the main road of education—and how religion is something that’s done on Sunday morning. I wondered how often in my earlier travels I had patronized as “quaint” some entirely sensible custom of another country. Bali was the beginning of my treatment—still far from over—for the disease of ethnocentricity. Since then I’ve been impatient with travel pieces that rhapsodize over quaint Dutch farmers wearing wooden shoes or picturesque muezzins calling the Muslim faithful to prayer. We have plenty of quaint customs of our own; recently I saw a Japanese tourist taking a snapshot of a Park Avenue matron who was scooping the droppings of her poodle into a bag, as required by our New York “leash law.”

那是我第一次见到如此统一的文化，我至今仍记得当时我有多么愤懑，因为我自己的文化并没有如此令人艳羡的完整性。我想到美国学校是如何把艺术当作点缀——教育主干道上的岔路——以及宗教活动只是星期天早上才有的事。我不禁反思，在我早年的旅行中，我曾多少次把其他国家一些完全合理的习俗贬低为“古雅”。巴厘岛之行开启了我治疗民族中心主义的征程——至今仍远未结束。从那时起，我就对那些对穿着木鞋的古雅荷兰农民或召唤穆斯林信徒祈祷的英姿飒爽的宣礼员大加赞赏的旅行文章感到不耐烦。我们自己也有许多古雅的习俗；最近，我看到一位日本游客正在给一位住在公园大道上的贵妇拍照，这位贵妇正按照纽约的“牵狗绳法”规定，把她家贵宾犬的粪便装进袋子里。

Hence my admiration for the writing of anthropologists, who bring to each culture an austere objectivity, free of prior judgment, unlike sociologists, who come bearing certitudes about how everybody should behave. Anthropologists also tend, unlike sociologists, to write well; they disdain slippery language and easy escapes. You can open Margaret Mead’s books to any page and find yourself in the company of a careful observer describing an alien society with rigorous clarity, detail and respect. Here’s a page from her Growing Up in New Guinea:

因此，我十分钦佩人类学家的写作。他们以一种严谨客观的态度审视每一种文化，不带任何先入为主的观念，这与社会学家截然不同，后者总是带着一套关于所有人应该如何行事的确定性论断而来。此外，与社会学家不同，人类学家往往文笔流畅；他们不屑于使用含糊不清的语言，也不轻易逃避问题。你随便翻开玛格丽特·米德的任何一本书，都会发现自己仿佛置身于一位细致观察者的笔下，她以严谨的清晰度、丰富的细节和高度的尊重，描绘着一个陌生的社会。以下摘自她的《在新几内亚长大》：

In Manus there is neither heaven nor hell; there are simply two levels of existence. On one level live the mortals, all of whose acts, each of whose words, are known to the spirits, provided the spirit is present and paying attention. The spirit is not conceived as omniscient. He, like a living man, can only see and hear within the range of his senses. A spirit will disclaim knowledge of what went on in a house during his absence. Spirits are invisible, only rarely are they seen by mortals, but they occasionally make their presence manifest by whistling in the night. They are more powerful than mortals, being less dependent upon time and space and having the power to translate material objects into their own sphere of invisibility.

在马努斯，既无天堂也无地狱；存在着两个层面。凡人生活在一个层面，凡人的所有行为、每一句话，只要灵体在场并留意，都会被灵体知晓。灵体并非全知全能。如同活人一般，他只能在感官范围内视听。灵体会否认知晓在他不在时屋内发生的一切。灵体是无形的，凡人极少能看见他，但他偶尔会在夜里吹口哨，以此显现自身。他比凡人更强大，不受时间和空间的限制，并且拥有将物质转化为自身无形领域的能力。

They act upon mortals by extracting bits of the soul stuff. If all of a mortal’s soul stuff is taken by a spirit or spirits the mortal will die. Spirits can also hide things, steal things, throw stones, and otherwise manipulate the material world in a capricious, unaccountable fashion. This, however, they very seldom do. In spite of their greater powers they are conceived very humanly. So a man will beseech his spirit to drive an expected school of fish into a particular lagoon. He will not ask his spirit to multiply the fish, only to herd them. The chief duties of a spirit are to prosper the fishing of his wards and to preserve their lives and limbs against the machinations of hostile spirits.

它们通过抽取凡人的灵魂碎片来影响他们。如果凡人的所有灵魂碎片都被一个或多个灵体夺走，那么凡人就会死亡。灵体还可以藏匿物品、偷窃物品、投掷石块，并以反复无常、难以解释的方式操纵物质世界。然而，它们很少这样做。尽管它们拥有强大的力量，但它们的本质却非常人性化。因此，一个人会祈求自己的灵体将一群鱼赶入特定的泻湖。他不会祈求灵体让鱼的数量增加，而只会祈求它们被驱赶。灵体的主要职责是保佑其守护之人捕鱼丰收，并保护他们的生命和肢体免受敌对灵体的阴谋诡计的侵害。

It is the spirits’ privilege to demand in return the exercise of certain restraints and virtues. In the first place, the living must commit no sex offenses which interfere with the Manus social order (i.e.: a spirit will not object to an intrigue with a woman of another tribe). This is a rigorous prohibition; light words, chance physical contacts, evil plans, careless jests, non-observance of the proper avoidance reactions toward relatives-in-law, all these may bring down the spirits’ righteous wrath, either upon the sinner or upon some one of his relatives—perhaps pushing a decrepit old man from his lingering bed into death, perhaps afflicting a newborn baby with the colic.

神灵有权要求生者遵守某些戒律和美德。首先，生者不得犯下任何扰乱马努斯社会秩序的性罪行（例如：神灵不会反对与异族女子发生关系）。这是一条严苛的禁令；轻率的言语、偶然的身体接触、邪恶的计划、不谨慎的玩笑、对姻亲疏远、不遵守应有的规矩，所有这些都可能招致神灵的义愤，惩罚对象可能是罪人本人，也可能是他的亲属——或许会将卧床不起的老人推下病床，致其死亡；或许会让新生儿患上绞痛。

Additionally, the spirits abhor economic laxity of any sort: failure to pay debts, careless manipulation of family properties, economic procrastination, and unfair allotment of funds among the needs of several relatives, as when a man uses all the wealth which comes into the family to make spectacular payments for his wife and fails to make betrothal payments for his younger brothers. Insubordination within a family, quarrels between in-laws also stir their wrath. And bad housing annoys the critical spirits, who object to presiding over unsafe floors, sagging piles, and leaky thatch.

此外，神灵憎恶任何形式的经济懈怠：不偿还债务、随意处置家产、拖延理财，以及在满足多位亲属的需求之间不公平地分配资金，例如，一个男人将所有家产都用于为妻子支付巨额聘金，却不支付弟弟们的聘金。家庭内部的不服从行为，以及姻亲之间的争吵也会激怒他们。糟糕的居住环境也会惹恼这些挑剔的神灵，他们不愿守护不安全的地板、摇摇欲坠的屋顶和漏水的茅草屋。

What an amazing wealth of information Margaret Mead packs into that one passage. She is truly a recording angel. Her scholarly pleasure is to get it right and get it down for the use of other scholars.

玛格丽特·米德在这短短一段文字中蕴含了多么丰富的信息啊！她真是一位记录天使。她学术上的乐趣就在于力求准确无误地记录下来，供其他学者使用。

Beneath all such research, of course, is a staggering amount of work on the part of the anthropologist to become accepted by the people of the community as an observer in their midst, to learn their language, and to record and transcribe endless notes—an effort measured in years, not months. Even a nonfiction writer who conducts extensive interviews for an article or a book has no conception of such labor. The reader can only guess at the magnitude of the feat from the meticulous detail of the results.

当然，所有这些研究背后，都凝聚着人类学家的大量心血：他们需要被当地社区接纳，成为他们生活中的观察者；学习他们的语言；记录并整理数不胜数的笔记——这项工作以年而非月来计算。即使是为文章或书籍进行大量访谈的非虚构作家，也无法想象这种艰辛。读者只能从研究成果的详尽细节中，窥见这项工作的艰巨程度。

What often does get described, however, is the process of acceptance by the local culture—the anthropologist walking the thin line of approval. An engaging example is Clifford Geertz’s preamble to his famous essay “Deep Play: Notes on the Balinese Cockfight.”

然而，人们经常描述的是融入当地文化的过程——人类学家如履薄冰地游走在认可的边缘。克利福德·格尔茨在其著名论文《深度游戏：巴厘岛斗鸡笔记》的序言就是一个引人入胜的例子。

That Geertz was drawn to Bali during his illustrious career is hardly a coincidence; no piece of land on the face of the earth has been so anthropologized. The music and dance that captivated me are only two of many strands in a web of identifying traits found nowhere else. Equally distinctive to Bali, Geertz points out, are its mythology, art, ritual, social organization, patterns of child rearing, forms of law and even styles of trance. But the cockfight, he says, “has barely been noticed, although as a popular obsession of consuming power it is at least as important a revelation of what being Balinese ‘is really like’ as these more celebrated phenomena. As much of America surfaces in a ball park, on a golf links, at a race track, or around a poker table, much of Bali surfaces in a cock ring.”

吉尔茨在其辉煌的职业生涯中被巴厘岛深深吸引，这绝非偶然；地球上没有任何一块土地像巴厘岛一样被如此深入地研究过。令我着迷的音乐和舞蹈只是众多独特特征中的两个，这些特征构成了一张独一无二的网。吉尔茨指出，巴厘岛同样独具特色的还有它的神话、艺术、仪式、社会组织、育儿模式、法律形式，甚至还有独特的冥想方式。但他表示，斗鸡“几乎无人问津，尽管作为一种追求权力的流行方式，它至少与那些更广为人知的现象一样，揭示了巴厘岛人‘真实面貌’的本质。正如美国人常常在棒球场、高尔夫球场、赛马场或扑克桌旁展现自我一样，巴厘岛人也常常在斗鸡场上展现自我。”

This is how Geertz’s classic study of that popular obsession got off to its highly unscientific start:

这就是格尔茨对这种流行现象的经典研究是如何以高度不科学的方式开始的：

Early in April of 1958, my wife and I arrived, malarial and diffident, in a Balinese village we intended, as anthropologists, to study. A small place, about five hundred people, and relatively remote, it was its own world. We were intruders, professional ones, and the villagers dealt with us as Balinese seem always to deal with people not part of their life who yet press themselves upon them: as though we were not there. For them, and to a degree for ourselves, we were nonpersons, specters, invisible men….

1958年4月初，我和妻子带着疟疾和羞怯，抵达巴厘岛的一个村庄。作为人类学家，我们此行的目的是研究这个村庄。村庄很小，大约只有五百人，位置也比较偏远，仿佛自成一个世界。我们是闯入者，而且是专业的闯入者。村民们对待我们的方式，似乎总是巴厘岛人对待那些与他们生活无关却又强行闯入的人的方式：仿佛我们根本不存在。对他们来说，某种程度上对我们自己来说也是如此，我们如同非人，如同幽灵，如同隐形人……

When you first meet a Balinese, he seems virtually not to relate to you at all; he is, in the term Gregory Bateson and Margaret Mead made famous, “away.” Then—in a day, a week, a month (with some people the magic moment never comes)—he decides, for reasons I have never quite been able to fathom, that you are real, and then he becomes a warm, gay, sensitive, sympathetic, though, being Balinese, always precisely controlled, person. You have crossed, somehow, some moral or metaphysical shadow line. Though you are not exactly taken as a Balinese (one has to be born to that), you are at least regarded as a human being rather than a cloud or a gust of wind. The whole complexion of your relationship changes to, in the majority of cases, a gentle, almost affectionate one—a low-keyed, rather playful, rather mannered, rather bemused geniality.

初次与巴厘岛人见面时，他似乎对你漠不关心；用格雷戈里·贝特森和玛格丽特·米德的名言来说，他“心不在焉”。然后——或许一天，一周，一个月（有些人，这种神奇的时刻永远不会到来）——他出于我至今也无法完全理解的原因，认定你是真实存在的，然后他变成了一个热情、快乐、敏感、富有同情心的人，尽管作为巴厘岛人，他总是保持着一丝不苟的克制。你不知何故跨越了某种道德或形而上的界限。虽然你并不完全被视为巴厘岛人（巴厘岛人的身份必须与生俱来），但至少你被视为一个活生生的人，而不是一朵云或一阵风。你们之间的关系也随之改变，在大多数情况下，变得温柔而亲切——一种低调、略带玩味、略显拘谨、略带困惑的友善。

Geertz explains that he and his wife were still “very much in the gust-of-wind stage” when a large cockfight was held to raise money for a new school. Though such fights were illegal, the villagers thought that because their cause was worthy and “the necessary bribes had been paid” they could safely hold the fight in a relatively public part of the village.

格尔茨解释说，他和妻子当时还处于“懵懂无知”的阶段，就发生了一场大型斗鸡比赛，目的是为新建学校筹款。尽管这种斗鸡活动是非法的，但村民们认为，既然他们的理由正当，“必要的贿赂也已经支付”，那么他们就可以在村里相对公共的区域安全地举行比赛。

They were wrong. In the midst of the third match, with hundreds of people, including, still transparent, myself and my wife, fused into a single body around the ring, a superorganism in the literal sense, a truck full of policemen armed with machine guns roared up. Amid great screeching cries of “pulisi! pulisi!” from the crowd, the policemen jumped out, and, springing into the center of the ring, began to swing their guns around like gangsters in a motion picture, though not going so far as actually to fire them. The superorganism came instantly apart as its components scattered in all directions. People raced down the road, disappeared headfirst over walls, scrambled under platforms, folded themselves behind wicker screens, scuttled up coconut trees. Cocks armed with steel spurs sharp enough to cut off a finger or run a hole through a foot were running wildly around. Everything was dust and panic.

他们错了。第三场比赛正酣，数百人——包括我和我妻子，我们当时还处于透明状态——围绕着擂台融为一体，形成一个名副其实的超级有机体。这时，一辆满载警察、配备机枪的卡车呼啸而至。人群中爆发出震耳欲聋的“警察！警察！”的喊声，警察跳下车，冲进擂台中央，像电影里的黑帮一样挥舞着枪，但并没有真的开枪。超级有机体瞬间瓦解，成员四散奔逃。人们沿着马路奔跑，一头栽进墙里，钻进平台下，躲在藤编屏风后面，爬上椰子树。一些公鸡身上装着锋利的钢爪，足以切断手指或刺穿脚掌，它们在周围疯狂乱窜。一切都化为尘土和恐慌。

Even in the dust and panic the anthropologist had his eyes open for the human details of flight. His paragraph has the comic exactitude of a Keystone Cops movie script.

即使在尘土飞扬、惊慌失措之中，这位人类学家依然睁大眼睛，捕捉着逃亡过程中人类的种种细节。他这段文字的精准程度，简直就像一部基斯顿警察电影的剧本，充满了滑稽的讽刺。

On the established anthropological principle, “When in Rome,” my wife and I decided, only slightly less instantaneously than everyone else, that the thing to do was run too. We ran down the main village street, northward, away from where we were living, for we were on that side of the ring. About halfway down another fugitive ducked suddenly into a compound—his own, it turned out—and we, seeing nothing ahead of us but rice fields, open country, and a very high volcano, followed him. As the three of us came tumbling into the courtyard, his wife, who had apparently been through this sort of thing before, whipped out a table, a tablecloth, three chairs, and three cups of tea, and we all, without any explicit communication whatsoever, sat down, commenced to sip tea, and sought to compose ourselves.

遵循着“入乡随俗”的人类学原则，我和妻子也决定，不出所料，我们也得跑。我们沿着村里的主街一路向北，远离我们居住的地方，因为我们住在环城公路的另一侧。跑到一半的时候，另一个逃犯突然钻进了一个院子——后来才知道是他自己的——我们眼前除了稻田、开阔的乡村和一座高耸的火山什么也看不到，只好跟着他跑了进去。我们三个跌跌撞撞地冲进院子时，他的妻子——显然她以前也遇到过这种情况——迅速拿出一张桌子、一块桌布、三把椅子和三杯茶，我们三个人一句话也没说，就都坐了下来，开始喝茶，努力让自己镇定下来。

Still no letup. Mack Sennett couldn’t have contrived a more enjoyable chase.

依然没有丝毫喘息之机。麦克·塞内特也想不出比这更精彩的追逐戏了。

A few moments later, one of the policemen marched importantly into the yard, looking for the village chief. (The chief had not only been at the fight, he had arranged it. When the truck drove up he ran to the river, stripped off his sarong, and plunged in so he could say, when at length they found him sitting there pouring water over his head, that he had been away bathing when the whole affair had occurred and was ignorant of it. They did not believe him and fined him three hundred rupiah, which the village raised collectively.) Seeing me and my wife, “White Men,” there in the yard, the policeman performed a classic double take. When he found his voice again he asked, approximately, what in the devil did we think we were doing there. Our host of five minutes leaped instantly to our defense, producing an impassioned description of who and what we were, so detailed and so accurate that it was my turn, having barely communicated with a living human being save my landlord and the village chief for more than a week, to be astonished. We had a perfect right to be there, he said. We were American professors; the government had cleared us; we were there to study culture; we were going to write a book to tell Americans about Bali. And we had all been there drinking tea and talking about cultural matters all afternoon and did not know anything about any cockfight. Moreover, we had not seen the village chief all day; he must have gone to town. The policeman retreated in rather total disarray. And, after a decent interval, bewildered but relieved to have survived and stayed out of jail, so did we.

片刻之后，一名警察大摇大摆地走进院子，寻找村长。（村长不仅参与了打架，还是他一手策划的。卡车开过来时，他跑到河边，脱下纱笼，跳进水里，等他们找到他时，他正坐在那里往头上浇水，这样他就可以辩解说，事发时他正在洗澡，对这一切毫不知情。警察不相信他，罚了他三百印尼盾，这笔钱是全村人凑的。）看到我和妻子——“白人”——站在院子里，警察愣了一下。等他再次开口，他大概是这么问的：我们到底在干什么？我们这位只住了五分钟的房东立刻跳出来为我们辩护，滔滔不绝地描述了我们是谁，是什么人，描述得如此详细准确，以至于轮到我了——我已经一个多星期没跟任何人说过话了，除了房东和村长——我当时也感到十分惊讶。他说，我们完全有权利待在那里。我们是美国教授；政府已经批准了我们的入境；我们是来研究文化的；我们打算写一本书，向美国人介绍巴厘岛。而且，我们整个下午都在喝茶、谈论文化，对什么斗鸡一无所知。此外，我们一整天都没见到村长；他肯定进城了。警察慌忙逃走了。过了一会儿，我们也同样感到困惑，但庆幸自己活了下来，没有被关进监狱。

The paragraph has a double-take quality of its own. Beneath a veneer of knockabout farce Geertz has given us a striking fact about the Balinese character, as impressive as any that he will discover by more orthodox methods during the remainder of his stay. Here’s the payoff:

这段文字本身就具有一种令人深思的特质。在看似滑稽闹剧的表象之下，格尔茨向我们揭示了巴厘岛人性格中一个惊人的事实，其震撼力丝毫不亚于他在接下来的旅程中通过更为正统的方法所发现的任何其他事实。以下是关键所在：

The next morning the village was a completely different world for us. Not only were we no longer invisible, we were suddenly the center of all attention, the object of a great outpouring of warmth, interest, and, most especially, amusement. Everyone in the village knew we had fled like everyone else. They asked us about it again and again (I must have told the story, small detail by small detail, fifty times by the end of the day), gently, affectionately, but quite insistently teasing us: “Why didn’t you just stand there and tell the police who you were?” “Why didn’t you just say you were only watching and not betting?” “Were you really afraid of those little guns?” As always, kinesthetically minded and, even when fleeing for their lives, the world’s most poised people, they gleefully mimicked, also over and over again, our graceless style of running and what they claimed were our panic-stricken facial expressions. But above all, everyone was extremely pleased and even more surprised that we had not simply “pulled out our papers” (they knew about those too) and asserted our Distinguished Visitor status, but had instead demonstrated our solidarity with what were now our co-villagers. (What we had actually demonstrated was our cowardice, but there is fellowship in that too.)

第二天早上，村子对我们来说就像另一个世界。我们不仅不再是隐形人，反而成了所有人关注的焦点，大家对我们表现出极大的热情、兴趣，尤其是好笑。村里每个人都知道我们和其他人一样逃了出来。他们一遍又一遍地问起这件事（到一天结束的时候，我大概把事情的来龙去脉都讲了五十遍），语气温柔、亲切，却又执拗地逗弄着我们：“你们为什么不站在那里告诉警察你们是谁？”“你们为什么不说你们只是在旁观，没有参与赌博？”“你们真的害怕那些小枪吗？”他们一如既往地肢体语言丰富，即便在逃命之际，也依然保持着世界上最沉着冷静的姿态，兴高采烈地一遍又一遍地模仿着我们笨拙的奔跑姿势，以及他们所谓的我们惊恐万状的表情。但最重要的是，大家都非常高兴，也更加惊讶于我们并没有简单地“掏出证件”（他们也知道这些），然后宣称自己是杰出访客，而是展现了我们与如今的村民们的团结。（我们实际上展现的是我们的怯懦，但这其中也蕴含着友谊。）

In Bali, to be teased is to be accepted. It was the turning point so far as our relationship to the community was concerned, and we were quite literally “in.” The whole village opened up to us, probably more than it ever would have otherwise, and certainly very much faster. Getting caught, or almost caught, in a vice raid is perhaps not a very generalizable recipe for achieving that mysterious necessity of anthropological field work, rapport, but for me it worked very well. It led to a sudden and unusually complete acceptance into a society extremely difficult for outsiders to penetrate. It gave me the kind of immediate, inside-view grasp of an aspect of “peasant mentality” that anthropologists not fortunate enough to flee headlong with their subjects from armed authorities normally do not get. And, perhaps most important of all, for the other things might have come in other ways, it put me very quickly on to a combination emotional explosion, status war, and philosophical drama of central significance to the society whose inner nature I desired to understand. By the time I left I had spent about as much time looking into cockfights as into witchcraft, irrigation, caste, or marriage.

在巴厘岛，被戏弄反而意味着被接纳。就我们与当地社群的关系而言，这成为了一个转折点，我们算是真正“融入”了其中。整个村庄向我们敞开了大门，或许比以往任何时候都更加开放，速度也更快。在一次缉毒行动中被抓获（或者差点被抓获）或许并非建立人类学田野调查中那种神秘的必要关系——融洽关系——的通用方法，但对我而言却非常有效。它让我突然且异常彻底地融入了这个外人极难渗透的社会。它让我对“农民心态”的某个方面有了直接而深刻的理解，而这种理解是那些没有幸带着研究对象逃离武装当局的人类学家通常无法获得的。而且，或许最重要的是，尽管其他方面可能以其他方式获得，但它让我迅速地感受到了一种情感爆发、地位之争和哲学思辨交织的复杂局面，而这正是我渴望了解的这个社会的核心所在。到我离开的时候，我花在研究斗鸡上的时间，几乎和花在研究巫术、灌溉、种姓制度或婚姻上的时间一样多。

In all of Geertz’s essays I feel that he thinks of himself as a writer. He is personal and spontaneous—having a good time and writing above all for himself. Such humanity is so rare in the prose of academics that it glitters when it appears, especially because, as in this case, Professor Geertz has abdicated none of his professional stature by writing in clear, robust English. On the contrary, through his writing he has become not only a giant of his own discipline, but an intellectual prophet to scholars in other fields. A recent article about Princeton’s “hot history department” in the New York Times Magazine , for instance, noted his impact on a whole generation of historians.

在格尔茨的所有文章中，我都能感受到他把自己视为一名作家。他的文风真挚而随性——他享受写作的过程，并且写作首先是为了自己。这种人文情怀在学术散文中极为罕见，因此一旦出现便熠熠生辉，尤其像格尔茨教授这样，他并没有因为使用清晰流畅的英语而降低自己的专业水准。相反，他的写作不仅使他成为自己学科的泰斗，也使他成为其他领域学者的思想先知。例如，《纽约时报杂志》最近一篇关于普林斯顿“炙手可热的历史系”的文章就指出了他对整整一代历史学家的影响。

“In the early 1970s,” the article said, “it was not only at Princeton that historians were beginning to read Geertz. In universities around the country, graduate students and some of their teachers could be heard wondering about how to ‘make use of the insights of anthropology,’ and if there was a single text that best conveyed those insights it was Geertz’s essay, ‘Deep Play: Notes on the Balinese Cockfight.’” What Geertz did, as one Princeton historian put it, was to “provide what he calls local knowledge, a way of finding deep human meaning in small sets of relationships, creating a significance which didn’t rely on transcendental expectations about change.”

文章指出：“20世纪70年代初，不仅是普林斯顿大学的历史学家开始研读格尔茨的作品。在全国各地的大学里，研究生和一些教师都在思考如何‘运用人类学的洞见’，而如果说有一本书最能传达这些洞见，那就是格尔茨的散文《深度游戏：巴厘岛斗鸡札记》。”正如一位普林斯顿大学的历史学家所说，格尔茨所做的是“提供他所谓的‘地方知识’，一种在小规模的人际关系中发现深刻的人类意义的方法，这种意义并不依赖于对变革的超验预期。”

I wish more academics could present the fruits of their considerable knowledge and research in writing as broadly accessible as Geertz’s books are, or as Lewis Thomas’s books are. But I’m not waiting for that millennium. It’s a fact of the publishing industry that at least 90 percent of the manuscripts that academics submit for general publication are too poorly written to be considered. Their style is one that has been decreed by other academics—gatekeepers of the lodge—as the passport to a Ph.D., to tenure and to the approval of their peers. It’s a language squeezed dry of human juices—a Sargasso Sea of passive verbs, long and generalized nouns, pompous locutions and unnecessary jargon. “I can’t help it—I’ve got to play by the rules,” the perpetrators explain when they ask why they can’t get a certain book or article published and are told the horrid truth. I find it hard to sympathize. Other people’s rules are shackles on the mind. Timidity never produced a good piece of writing.

我希望更多学者能像吉尔茨或刘易斯·托马斯那样，将他们渊博的知识和研究成果以通俗易懂的方式呈现出来。但我并不指望等到下一个千年。出版业的现实是，至少有90%的学者投稿到大众出版物的稿件质量太差，根本无法被考虑。他们的写作风格是由其他学者——也就是学术圈的守门人——所规定的，是获得博士学位、终身教职和同行认可的通行证。这种语言枯燥乏味，如同马尾藻海一般，充斥着被动语态、冗长空泛的名词、浮夸的措辞和不必要的术语。“我没办法——我必须遵守规则，”当被问及为何某些书籍或文章无法出版，并被告知残酷的真相时，这些作者总是这样解释。我很难对他们产生同情。别人的规则就像思想的枷锁。胆怯从来都写不出好文章。

If the proper study of mankind is man, as Alexander Pope so self-evidently reminded us, one of the vital roles an anthropologist can play is to tell us who we are and what makes every race peculiarly different. One stimulating example is a book by the anthropologist Edward T. Hall, called The Hidden Dimension , that dimension being the “bubble” of personal space that surrounds every man, woman and child. How we feel about that bubble is how we define ourselves, Professor Hall says, pointing out that many well-meant works of architecture and city planning have come to grief over their failure to recognize this inexorable law of biology.

如果说研究人类的真正对象是人本身，正如亚历山大·蒲柏不言而喻地提醒我们的那样，那么人类学家最重要的职责之一就是告诉我们自己是谁，以及是什么造就了每个种族的独特差异。人类学家爱德华·T·霍尔的著作《隐藏的维度》便是一个引人入胜的例子。他所说的“隐藏的维度”指的是环绕着每个人（无论男女老幼）的“个人空间泡泡”。霍尔教授指出，我们如何看待这个泡泡，就决定了我们如何定义自己。他还强调，许多出于好意的建筑和城市规划作品，最终都因为未能认识到这条不可抗拒的生物学规律而遭遇失败。

“Architects,” Hall writes, “are traditionally preoccupied with the visual patterns of structures—what one sees. They are almost totally unaware of the fact that people carry around with them internalizations of fixed-feature space learned early in life.” Man, he says, like other members of the animal kingdom, “is first, last and always a prisoner of his biological organism. No matter how hard he tries, it is impossible for him to divest himself of his own culture, for it has penetrated to the roots of his nervous system and determines how he perceives the world.”

霍尔写道：“建筑师传统上过于关注建筑的视觉模式——也就是人们所看到的。他们几乎完全没有意识到，人们会将早期生活中习得的固定空间特征内化于心。” 他说，人和其他动物一样，“从始至终都是其生物机体的囚徒。无论他多么努力，都无法摆脱自身的文化，因为文化已经渗透到他神经系统的根源，并决定了他如何感知世界。”

Thinking about that nervous system, Hall considers the fact that after two thousand years of contact, Westerners and Arabs still don’t understand each other. Each is discomfited by the other’s “sensory world.” Why do Americans in the Middle East, for instance, feel so claustrophobic when they encounter Arabs in public places? Hall recalls how he stumbled on the answer:

霍尔思考着这种神经系统，想到两千年来西方人和阿拉伯人接触不断，却仍然无法互相理解。双方都对对方的“感官世界”感到不自在。例如，为什么身处中东的美国人在公共场所遇到阿拉伯人时会感到如此压抑？霍尔回忆起他偶然发现答案的过程：

Pushing and shoving in public places is characteristic of Middle Eastern culture. Yet it is not entirely what Americans think it is (being pushy and rude) but stems from a different set of assumptions concerning not only the relations between people but how one experiences the body as well…. After repeated unsuccessful attempts to gain insight into the cognitive world of the Arab on this particular point, I filed it away as a question that only time would answer. When the answer came, it was because of a seemingly inconsequential annoyance.

在公共场所推搡是中东文化的一个特征。然而，它并不完全像美国人所认为的那样（咄咄逼人、粗鲁无礼），而是源于一套不同的假设，这不仅关乎人际关系，也关乎人们对身体的体验……在多次尝试了解阿拉伯人在这方面的认知世界无果后，我便将这个问题搁置一旁，希望时间能给出答案。而答案的到来，竟源于一件看似无关紧要的小事。

The last sentence piques our curiosity. We absolutely must continue. Professor Hall maintains contact with the reader as biological organism, one that craves a story.

最后一句话激起了我们的好奇心。我们必须继续读下去。霍尔教授与读者保持着一种如同生物体般的联系，一种对故事充满渴望的联系。

While waiting for a friend in a Washington, D.C., hotel lobby and wanting to be both visible and alone, I had seated myself in a solitary chair outside the normal stream of traffic. In such a setting most Americans follow a rule, which is all the more binding because we seldom think about it, that can be stated as follows: as soon as a person stops or is seated in a public place, there balloons around him a small sphere of privacy which is considered inviolate. The size of the sphere varies with the degree of crowding, the age, sex, and the importance of the person, as well as the general surroundings. Anyone who enters this zone and stays there is intruding. In fact, a stranger who intrudes, even for a specific purpose, acknowledges the fact that he has intruded by beginning his request with, “Pardon me, but can you tell me…?”

在华盛顿特区一家酒店的大堂里等朋友时，我既想引人注目又想独处，于是找了个远离人流的单人椅子坐下。在这种情况下，大多数美国人都会遵循一条规则，这条规则之所以如此有效，是因为我们很少会意识到它的存在。这条规则可以概括如下：一旦一个人在公共场所停留或坐下，他周围就会形成一个小小的隐私空间，这片空间被认为是不可侵犯的。这个空间的大小取决于人流的拥挤程度、年龄、性别、身份地位以及周围环境。任何进入并停留在这个空间的人都是在打扰别人。事实上，即使是出于特定目的的陌生人，在提出请求时也会以“打扰一下，请问……？”开头，以此来表明自己已经闯入了别人的私人空间。

As I waited in the deserted lobby, a stranger walked up to where I was sitting and stood close enough so that not only could I easily touch him but I could even hear him breathing. In addition, the dark mass of his body filled the peripheral field of vision on my left side. If the lobby had been crowded with people, I would have understood his behavior, but in an empty lobby his presence made me exceedingly uncomfortable. Feeling annoyed by this intrusion, I moved my body in such a way as to communicate annoyance. Strangely enough, instead of moving away, my actions seemed only to encourage him, because he moved closer.

我在空荡荡的大厅里等候时，一个陌生人走到我坐的地方，站得离我非常近，近到我不仅能轻易碰到他，甚至能听到他的呼吸声。此外，他那身影占据了我左侧视野的余光。如果大厅里人来人往，我或许还能理解他的行为，但在空无一人的大厅里，他的出现让我感到极度不适。我感到恼火，于是挪动了一下身体，以示不满。奇怪的是，我的举动非但没有让他走开，反而似乎更加激怒了他，因为他反而靠得更近了。

By now we are caught up in the anthropologist’s sensory gavotte. He has put us into his own chair, one that we realize we have often occupied—in the subway or some other public space—and always with mounting squeamishness.

现在我们已经完全沉浸在人类学家的感官之旅中。他把我们放在了他的椅子上，我们意识到自己也经常坐在那把椅子上——在地铁或其他公共场所——而且总是伴随着越来越强烈的不安。

In spite of the temptation to escape the annoyance, I put aside thoughts of abandoning my post, thinking, “To hell with it. Why should I move? I was here first and I’m not going to let this fellow drive me out even if he is a boor.” Fortunately, a group of people soon arrived whom my tormentor immediately joined. Their mannerisms explained his behavior, for I knew from both speech and gestures that they were Arabs. I had not been able to make this crucial identification by looking at my subject when he was alone because he wasn’t talking and he was wearing American clothes.

尽管很想逃离这令人厌烦的局面，但我还是打消了放弃岗位的念头，心想：“管他呢。我为什么要走？我先来的，就算这家伙是个粗人，我也不会让他把我赶走。”幸运的是，很快来了一群人，我的骚扰者立刻加入了他们。他们的举止解释了他的行为，因为我从他们的言谈举止中就能看出他们是阿拉伯人。之前他独自一人时，我没能通过观察他来做出这个关键的判断，因为他一言不发，而且穿着美国人的衣服。

In describing the scene later to an Arab colleague, two contrasting patterns emerged. My concept and my feelings about my own circle of privacy in a “public” place immediately struck my Arab friend as strange and puzzling. He said, “After all, it’s a public place, isn’t it?” Pursuing this line of inquiry, I found that in Arab thought I had no rights whatsoever by virtue of occupying a given spot; neither my place nor my body was inviolate. For the Arab, there is no such thing as an intrusion in public. Public means public.

后来我向一位阿拉伯同事描述当时的情景时，两种截然不同的模式浮现出来。我对在“公共”场所拥有个人隐私的概念和感受，立刻让我的阿拉伯朋友感到既奇怪又困惑。他说：“毕竟，这是个公共场所，不是吗？” 顺着这个思路探究下去，我发现，在阿拉伯人的思维模式中，我占据某个位置并不意味着我拥有任何权利；我的位置和我的身体都不是不可侵犯的。对阿拉伯人来说，公共场所不存在侵犯的概念。公共场所就是公共场所。

With this insight, a great range of Arab behavior that had been puzzling, annoying, and sometimes even frightening began to make sense. I learned, for example, that if A is standing on a street corner and B wants his spot, B is within his rights if he does what he can to make A uncomfortable enough to move. In Beirut only the hardy sit in the last row in a movie theater, because there are usually standees who want seats and who push and shove and make such a nuisance that most people give up and leave. Seen in this light, the Arab who “intruded” on my space in the hotel lobby had apparently selected it for the very reasons I had: it was a good place to watch two doors and the elevator. My show of annoyance, instead of driving him away, had only encouraged him. He thought he was about to get me to move.

有了这个认识，许多之前令我困惑、恼火，甚至有时令人恐惧的阿拉伯人行为开始变得合情合理。例如，我了解到，如果A站在街角，B想要占他的位置，那么B有权采取任何措施让A感到不舒服，迫使他让路。在贝鲁特，只有胆大的人才敢坐在电影院的最后一排，因为通常会有站着的人想要座位，他们会推推搡搡，制造各种麻烦，以至于大多数人都会放弃离开。从这个角度来看，那个在酒店大堂“闯入”我空间的阿拉伯人显然和我一样，选择这个位置也是出于同样的原因：这是一个可以观察两扇门和电梯的好地方。我的恼怒并没有让他离开，反而让他更加肆无忌惮。他以为他能让我让路。

This chance encounter in a hotel lobby prompts Professor Hall to ask himself whether Arabs have wholly different assumptions about the human body and the rights that are associated with it. In answering his own question he gives us, as always, specific examples. We never think: I get the general point, but what exactly does he mean?

在酒店大堂的这次偶遇促使霍尔教授思考，阿拉伯人对人体及其相关权利的看法是否与我们截然不同。在回答这个问题时，他一如既往地举出了具体的例子。我们从来不会想：我明白他的意思，但他究竟是什么意思？

Certainly the Arab tendency to shove and push each other in public and to feel and pinch women in public conveyances would not be tolerated by Westerners. It appeared to me that Arabs must not have any concept of a private zone outside the body. This proved to be precisely the case.

当然，阿拉伯人在公共场合互相推搡、在公共交通工具上摸女性、掐女性的习性，西方人是绝对无法容忍的。在我看来，阿拉伯人似乎根本没有身体以外的隐私概念。事实证明，我的想法完全正确。

In the Western world, the person is synonymous with an individual inside a skin. And in northern Europe generally, the skin and even the clothes may be inviolate. You need permission to touch either if you are a stranger. This rule applies in some parts of France, where the mere touching of another person during an argument used to be legally defined as assault. For the Arab the relation of the person in relation to the body is quite different. The person exists somewhere down inside the body. The ego is not completely hidden, however, because it can be reached very easily with an insult. It is protected from touch but not from words.

在西方世界，“人”等同于拥有肉身的个体。在北欧，人们普遍认为皮肤乃至衣物都是不可侵犯的。如果你是陌生人，触摸它们都需要得到允许。这条规则在法国部分地区仍然适用，在争吵中仅仅是触碰他人，过去都会被法律定义为攻击。而对于阿拉伯人来说，“人”与身体的关系则截然不同。他们认为“人”存在于身体深处。然而，自我并非完全隐藏，因为一句侮辱就能轻易触及它。自我受到保护，免受触碰，但却无法免受言语的伤害。

Of course it’s not necessary to go outside the United States, or even outside your hometown, to find a culture idiosyncratic enough to be worth writing about. Any enclosed clan will give an anthropologist ample food for thought about society as a whole, and today much good writing in the discipline is minutely local.

当然，不必非得去美国以外的地方，甚至不必离开家乡，就能找到足够独特的文化，值得深入研究。任何一个封闭的氏族都能为人类学家提供丰富的素材，让他们思考整个社会，而如今，该领域许多优秀的著作都聚焦于细致入微的地域性问题。

Nor does the anthropologist have a monopoly on helpful truth; other disciplines yield other insights. I think instantly—inevitably—of Robert Coles, a doctor and a child psychiatrist by training but also a fine writer. Coles has taken children as his constituency and their survival under stress as his passionate concern. It’s hard to imagine any chronicle of our times more important or more impressive than his Children of Crisis .

人类学家并非唯一掌握有用真理的人；其他学科也能提供不同的见解。我立刻——不出所料地——想到了罗伯特·科尔斯，他是一位受过专业训练的医生和儿童精神科医生，同时也是一位优秀的作家。科尔斯将儿童视为他的研究对象，并将他们在压力下的生存视为他毕生关注的焦点。很难想象还有哪部时代纪实作品比他的《危机中的儿童》更重要、更令人印象深刻。

A born-and-bred New Englander, Coles was sent in 1958 as an air force physician to Mississippi, a region that he “cared little to know.” But the South at that moment happened to be poised on the edge of a traumatic decade, one whose civil rights struggles would inflict harsh pressures on black children, and when Coles’s two-year service was over he found that the South had become a place, as he later wrote, “whose continuing pull on my mind and heart prevents me from staying away very long.” That pull fixed the course of his life and produced Children of Crisis .

科尔斯生于新英格兰，长于新英格兰，1958年被派往密西西比州担任空军医生，他对这个地区“几乎不感兴趣”。然而，当时的南方正处于一个充满创伤的十年前夕，民权运动给黑人儿童带来了沉重的压力。科尔斯两年的服役期满后，发现南方已成为一个地方，正如他后来所写，“它持续地吸引着我的思想和心灵，让我无法长时间远离。”这种吸引力改变了他的人生轨迹，并最终促成了《危机中的孩子们》的诞生。

The following passage is from his introduction to Volume I. I’ve chosen it for several reasons. It’s well and warmly written. It’s also a good example of writing about three subjects that I wanted to include in this book—medicine, psychiatry and children. It’s also a prime example of the writer as citizen. In a society whose priorities flagrantly favor the privileged, Coles refuses to doze off. “Something’s wrong here,” Children of Crisis keeps telling us, but never in a voice that’s didactic or political. Clinical detail is Coles’s truth; the evidence that he accumulates with the tools of his discipline is corrosive enough.

以下段落摘自他为第一卷所作的引言。我选择这段文字有几个原因。首先，它文笔优美，充满温情。其次，它很好地展现了本书想要涵盖的三个主题——医学、精神病学和儿童。最后，它也是作者作为公民的绝佳例证。在一个社会中，特权阶层的利益被公然凌驾于一切之上，科尔斯却从未袖手旁观。《危机中的儿童》一书不断地告诉我们：“这里出了问题”，但他的语气从不说教，也不政治化。临床细节是科尔斯的真理；他运用专业知识积累的证据足以令人警醒。

Finally, it may be worth asking—since this is a book about writing in different disciplines—exactly what a discipline is. How loosely or narrowly should we think about these arbitrary containers of knowledge? How usefully can scholars define the boundaries of their scholarship? Here’s Robert Coles explaining how he applied his discipline to the writing of Children of Crisis:

最后，既然这是一本探讨不同学科写作的书，或许值得一提的是，学科究竟是什么？我们应该如何看待这些知识的框架？学者们又该如何有效地界定其学术研究的边界？以下是罗伯特·科尔斯阐述他如何将自己的学科应用于《危机中的孩子们》一书的写作：

What I am trying to do is describe certain lives; specifically, describe the way those lives have come to terms with the political and social changes that have taken place in a particular region of this country. If the book concerns itself with adults as well as children, its title accurately reflects my chief professional interest—though obviously no one can study children too long without taking a look at the people who nurture them, teach them, and on occasion fail them terribly….

我试图描绘某些人的生活；具体来说，是描绘这些人如何适应这个国家特定地区发生的政治和社会变革。如果说这本书既关注儿童也关注成人，那么它的书名就准确地反映了我的主要研究兴趣——当然，研究儿童不可能太久而不去关注那些养育他们、教育他们，以及偶尔让他们失望的人……

I am working under the assumption that there still is room—maybe a corner here and there—for direct, sustained observation of individual human beings living in a significant and critical period of history. By direct observation I mean talking with people, listening to them, watching them—and being watched by them. By sustained observation I mean taking a long time: enough time to be confused, then absolutely certain and confident, then not so sure but a little more aware of why one or another conclusion seems the best that can be argued, or at least better than any other available.

我秉持着这样的假设：在历史的这一重要且关键时期，我们仍然有机会——或许只是零星的角落——对个体人类进行直接、持续的观察。所谓直接观察，是指与人交谈，倾听他们，观察他们——同时也被他们观察。所谓持续观察，是指投入大量的时间：足够长的时间，让我们先感到困惑，然后确信无疑，最后不再那么确定，但却更加清楚地意识到，为什么某个结论似乎是最佳选择，或者至少比其他任何现有结论都要好。

There is another qualifying word to the kind of observation I have attempted. It has been clinical, in the twin sense that I am a clinician and that I was looking at how children (or their parents and teachers) managed under stress; that is, abnormal and dangerous circumstances. The people I met had discernible cause to feel nervous, to develop a variety of symptoms in both mind and body. Whether they did so, and if they did how and when they did—such questions are reasonably the doctor’s; while the psychiatrist, at least in this century, traditionally wants to know who chooses which kind of danger, and for what reason, known or unknown.

我尝试进行的这种观察还有另一个限定词。它是临床性的，这体现在两个方面：一是我作为一名临床医生，二是我观察的是儿童（或他们的父母和老师）在压力下——也就是在异常和危险的情况下——是如何应对的。我遇到的这些人都有明显的理由感到紧张，并在身心两方面出现各种症状。他们是否真的出现了这些症状，以及如果出现，又是如何、何时出现的——这些问题理应由医生来解答；而精神科医生，至少在本世纪，传统上更想知道的是谁选择了哪种危险，以及出于何种原因，无论这些原因是否已知。

Even as a writer Coles is a clinician; that last sentence analyzes in the briefest space how the primary concern of the doctor differs from the primary concern of the psychiatrist. Having stated it, Coles explains how his own work, though he is both a doctor and a psychiatrist, doesn’t quite fall in either camp:

即使作为一名作家，科尔斯也是一名临床医生；这句话以最简洁的语言分析了医生和精神科医生的主要关注点有何不同。阐明这一点后，科尔斯解释说，尽管他既是医生又是精神科医生，但他自己的工作却并不完全属于任何一方：

What doctors and psychiatrists usually do not do is work with people who have no particular reason, interest or desire to see them—perhaps quite the opposite inclination. Medical students and psychiatrists in training are taught to understand the ways of disease, and then to heal pragmatically the illnesses that so often fail to follow the descriptions textbooks give to them. As a result, little if any medical or psychiatric attention is directed toward asking what exactly makes for survival under stress, for endurance, for courage against grim odds; indeed, for plain good health in contrast, say, to bad health and perhaps even bad “mental health,” whatever that is.

医生和精神科医生通常不会接诊那些没有特定理由、兴趣或意愿就诊的人——或许恰恰相反。医学生和精神科住院医师接受的培训是了解疾病的运作方式，然后务实地治疗那些往往不符合教科书描述的疾病。因此，医学界或精神病学界很少关注究竟是什么造就了人们在压力下生存的能力、忍耐力和在逆境中保持勇气的能力；实际上，也很少有人关注如何才能拥有良好的健康状态，从而避免出现不良健康状况，甚至包括糟糕的“心理健康”（无论其定义如何）。

Who is the “ordinary man,” if he exists, and what does the word “normal” mean, if anything? What makes for persistence and stability in ordinary people (not patients)? What really does bring about the mind’s collapse? A threshold of suffering passed? A long-standing weakness finally exposed, or given a decisive chance to do its bad work? Should we in medicine consider the economic indices or environmental settings that are sometimes summoned in the abstract as “causes” of this problem, or “factors” in that? What does the child’s mind make of the world—of politics, race and the facts of money? Why does one person make satisfied peace with the world, while another takes the world on and tries to change it in any number of ways?

如果存在“普通人”，那么他/她究竟是谁？“正常”一词又意味着什么？是什么造就了普通人（而非病人）的坚持和稳定？究竟是什么导致了精神崩溃？是痛苦的阈值被突破？是长期存在的弱点最终暴露出来，还是获得了决定性的机会来发挥其破坏作用？在医学领域，我们是否应该将那些有时被抽象地提及为这一问题的“原因”或“因素”的经济指标或环境因素纳入考量？孩童的思维如何看待这个世界——政治、种族和金钱的真相？为什么有些人能够与世界和平相处，而另一些人却要与世界抗争，并试图以各种方式改变它？

These are lovely questions, beautifully phrased. Can they be answered? Coles tells us whose job it is to try:

这些问题问得真好，措辞也很优美。它们能得到解答吗？科尔斯告诉我们，究竟是谁的责任来尝试解答这些问题：

Social scientists have the job, the very necessary job, of documenting exactly what “outside” world it is—the time, the place, the culture and the society—that a particular child finds at birth and learns about as he grows. The clinician has always been interested in what goes on “inside” others—he himself being part of their “outside,” their world. Presumably he is as qualified as anyone to go back and forth, to see how the two worlds (outside, inside) connect, blend, engage—words and images fail to describe the continuity between man’s thinking and the world’s state of affairs. So, what I have tried to pursue is a method of study (the clinical) and what I have tried to do is locate my body and mind where certain citizens are up against difficult times, so that their lives, like those of the sick, may have something to teach the rest of us.

社会科学家肩负着一项至关重要的职责：记录一个特定儿童出生时所处的“外部”世界——时间、地点、文化和社会——以及他成长过程中所了解的一切。临床医生一直对他人“内在”的体验充满兴趣——他自身也是他人“外部”世界的一部分。想必他与任何人一样，都有资格在内外之间穿梭，观察这两个世界（外部与内部）如何连接、融合、互动——语言和图像都难以描述人类思维与世界现状之间的连续性。因此，我一直尝试探索一种研究方法（临床方法），我尝试将我的身心置于某些身处困境的人们身边，让他们的生活，如同病患的生活一样，或许能给我们其他人带来一些启示。

Coles concludes by explaining that the process of writing Volume I of Children of Crisis made him realize that his labors, far from being over on the last page, were just starting. His foreword should therefore be viewed, he says, as the introduction to a work in progress, not just to one book. He saw as he wrote Volume I that the problems he had found in the South were “shared in one way or another by many other Americans.” To pursue that discovery would ultimately require four more volumes:

科尔斯在结尾解释说，撰写《危机中的孩子们》第一卷的过程让他意识到，他的工作远未在最后一页结束，而仅仅才刚刚开始。因此，他认为，他的序言应该被视为一部正在进行中的著作的引言，而不仅仅是一本书的引言。他在撰写第一卷的过程中发现，他在南方发现的问题“以某种方式存在于许多其他美国人身上”。为了进一步探究这一发现，他最终需要再写四卷：

What I learned as I came to know one family after another was that individual families share problems, just as regions and nations do. Many of the children I observed in Southern cities have cousins whose parents are migrant farmers, or sharecroppers, or “mountain folk” from the Appalachian hills of Virginia, North Carolina or Tennessee. Then, there are the cousins—not only Negroes, either—“abroad,” in Chicago, New York or on the West Coast. When I finished the main, everyday part of my work with Southern children attending desegregated schools, I moved my concern to some of those cousins. I started looking further into the lives of migrant children, tenant farm and mountain children, and eventually the children of Northern cities who must also face social isolation, segregation, desegregation—in brief, the dislocated, hard living that is still America’s gift to some of its young, regardless of race or ancestry. In future volumes—there seems no end to crisis in this world—I hope to tell of them and have them speak their own thoughts.

随着我逐渐了解一个又一个家庭，我发现，正如地区和国家一样，各个家庭也面临着共同的问题。我在南方城市观察到的许多孩子，他们的表兄弟姐妹的父母是流动农民、佃农，或是来自弗吉尼亚州、北卡罗来纳州或田纳西州阿巴拉契亚山区的“山民”。此外，还有一些表兄弟姐妹——他们并非全是黑人——生活在“国外”，比如芝加哥、纽约或西海岸。当我结束了在南方非种族隔离学校与孩子们朝夕相处的主要工作后，我的关注点转移到了这些表兄弟姐妹身上。我开始深入探究流动儿童、佃农和山民儿童的生活，最终也关注到了北方城市的孩子们。他们同样面临着社会孤立、种族隔离、种族融合——简而言之，无论种族或出身如何，这种颠沛流离、艰辛的生活仍然是美国部分年轻人不得不面对的现实。在未来的书中——这个世界似乎危机永无止境——我希望讲述他们的故事，让他们表达自己的想法。

# ↩

11. Writing Physics and Chemistry

11. 物理和化学写作

Albert Einstein gazes out at me from the cover of a small paperback book called Relativity: The Special and the General Theory , looking not at all scary—looking, in fact, like a benign uncle who is about to tell me a story. The blurb on the cover says: A CLEAR EXPLANATION THAT ANYONE CAN UNDERSTAND . Albert Einstein is going to explain the theory of relativity to me. To me? That’s what it says.

阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦的头像出现在一本名为《相对论：狭义相对论与广义相对论》的小册子封面上，他看起来一点也不吓人——事实上，他看起来就像一位慈祥的叔叔，正准备给我讲故事。封面上的简介写着：任何人都能理解的清晰解释。阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦要给我解释相对论。给我？简介上是这么写的。

I’ve wanted to get the book ever since two science professors at Gustavus Adolphus College mentioned that it was a model of clear linear writing. At first that surprised me; I hadn’t expected Einstein’s theory to be reducible to plain English. But on second thought it made sense. If clear writing is clear thinking, a mind clear enough to think of the theory of relativity would be likely to express itself simply and well. The burden was therefore on me. Could a lifelong science boob follow Einstein’s train of thought?

自从古斯塔夫·阿道夫学院的两位科学教授提到这本书是清晰线性写作的典范之后，我就一直想买它。起初我对此感到惊讶；我没想到爱因斯坦的理论竟然可以用浅显易懂的英语表达出来。但仔细想想，这倒也说得通。如果清晰的写作代表清晰的思考，那么一个头脑清晰到足以构思相对论的人，很可能也能用简洁明了的方式表达出来。因此，重担就落在了我身上。一个毕生对科学一窍不通的人，能跟上爱因斯坦的思路吗？

The only way to find out was to find out. I opened the book, which Einstein wrote, incidentally, in 1916, and plunged in:

唯一的办法就是去读。我打开那本书——顺便一提，这本书是爱因斯坦在1916年写的——然后一头扎了进去：

In your schooldays most of you who read this book made acquaintance with the noble building of Euclid’s geometry, and you remember—perhaps with more respect than love—the magnificent structure, on the lofty staircase of which you were chased about for uncounted hours by conscientious teachers. By reason of your past experience, you would certainly regard everyone with disdain who should pronounce even the most out-of-the-way proposition of this science to be untrue. But perhaps this feeling of proud certainty would leave you immediately if someone were to ask you: “What, then, do you mean by the assertion that these propositions are true?” Let us proceed to give this question a little consideration.

在你们求学时期，读过这本书的大多数人都接触过欧几里得几何这座宏伟的体系，你们或许怀着敬畏而非热爱之情，还记得那些尽职尽责的老师们曾无数次追着你们，沿着它高耸的阶梯讲解。基于过去的经验，你们肯定会对任何胆敢断言这门学科中最离经叛道的命题是错误的人的蔑视。但是，如果有人问你们：“那么，你们断言这些命题是正确的，究竟是什么意思呢？”或许你们这种引以为傲的自信会立刻消失。让我们来仔细思考一下这个问题。

I hesitate to call that a good “lead”—to cling to the lingo of journalism while scaling the higher slopes of theoretical science. But it is in fact a delightful lead. In one paragraph Einstein reminds us of one of the great temples in intellectual history—Euclid’s geometry—but also raises some doubts about how solid its foundations are today.

我犹豫是否该称之为“好的导语”——毕竟，在攀登理论科学高山的同时，还要拘泥于新闻报道的语言。但事实上，这的确是一个引人入胜的导语。爱因斯坦仅用一段话就让我们想起了思想史上的一座伟大殿堂——欧几里得几何——但同时也对它如今的根基是否稳固提出了质疑。

In paragraph two he tells us more about Euclid’s “noble building”:

在第二段中，他进一步向我们介绍了欧几里得的“宏伟建筑”：

Geometry sets out from certain conceptions such as “plane,” “point” and “straight line,” with which we are able to associate more or less definite ideas, and from certain simple propositions (axioms) which, by virtue of these ideas, we are inclined to accept as “true.” Then, on the basis of a logical process, the justification of which we feel ourselves compelled to admit, all remaining propositions are shown to follow from those axioms, i.e . they are proven. A proposition is then correct (“true”) when it has been derived in the recognized manner from the axioms. The question of the “truth” of the individual geometric propositions is thus reduced to one of the “truth” of the axioms.

几何学从“平面”、“点”和“直线”等概念出发，这些概念可以与我们或多或少确定的想法联系起来；它也从一些简单的命题（公理）出发，基于这些概念，我们倾向于接受这些命题为“真”。然后，基于一个我们不得不承认其合理性的逻辑过程，所有其他命题都被证明是由这些公理推导出来的，也就是说，它们被证明了。当一个命题以公认的方式从公理推导出来时，它就是正确的（“真”的）。因此，单个几何命题的“真”的问题就简化为公理的“真”的问题。

Now it has long been known that the last question is not only unanswerable by the methods of geometry, but that it is in itself entirely without meaning. We cannot ask whether it is true that only one straight line goes through two points. We can only say that Euclidean geometry deals with things called “straight lines,” to each of which is ascribed the property of being uniquely determined by two points situated on it. The concept “true” does not tally with the assertions of pure geometry, because by the word “true” we are eventually in the habit of designating always the correspondence with a “real” object; geometry, however, is not concerned with the relation of the ideas involved in it to objects of experience, but only with the logical connection of these ideas within themselves.

现在人们早已知道，最后一个问题不仅无法用几何学的方法回答，而且它本身也毫无意义。我们不能问“只有一条直线经过两点”是否属实。我们只能说，欧几里得几何研究的是所谓的“直线”，每条直线都被赋予了由其上的两个点唯一确定的属性。“真”的概念与纯粹几何学的断言不符，因为我们最终习惯于用“真”来指代与“真实”对象的对应关系；然而，几何学关注的并非其中涉及的观念与经验对象之间的关系，而仅仅是这些观念自身内部的逻辑联系。

Still so far so good. If I understand Einstein—always a possibility—he’s saying that Euclid’s geometry is an abstract exercise that falls short of being applicable to the real world.

目前为止一切顺利。如果我理解爱因斯坦的意思没错——当然，这也并非不可能——他的意思是欧几里得几何是一种抽象的理论，难以应用于现实世界。

It is not difficult to understand why, in spite of this, we feel constrained to call the propositions of geometry “true.” Geometrical ideas correspond to more or less exact objects in nature, and these last are undoubtedly the exclusive cause of the genesis of those ideas. Geometry ought to refrain from such a course, in order to give to its structure the largest possible logical unity. The practice, for example, of seeing in a “distance” two marked positions on a relatively rigid body is something which is lodged deeply in our habit of thought. We are accustomed further to regard these points as being situated on a straight line, if their apparent positions can be made to coincide for observation with one eye, under suitable choice of our place of observation.

不难理解，尽管如此，我们为何仍然觉得有必要称几何命题为“真”。几何概念与自然界中或多或少精确的物体相对应，而这些自然物体无疑是这些概念产生的唯一原因。几何学应当避免这种做法，以使其结构具有尽可能大的逻辑统一性。例如，在相对刚体上“远距离”观察两个标记点的做法，已经深深植根于我们的思维习惯之中。此外，如果通过适当选择观察位置，使这两个点的视觉位置能够用一只眼睛同时观察到，我们就习惯于认为它们位于一条直线上。

If, in pursuance of our habit of thought, we now supplement the proposition of Euclidean geometry by the single proposition that two points on a practically rigid body always correspond to the same distance (line-interval), independently of any changes in position to which we may subject the body, the propositions of Euclidean geometry then resolve themselves into propositions on the possible relative position of practically rigid bodies. Geometry which has been supplemented in this way is then to be treated as a branch of physics. We can now legitimately ask as to the “truth” of geometrical propositions interpreted in this way, since we are justified in asking whether these propositions are satisfied for those real things we have associated with the geometrical ideas. In less exact terms we can express this by saying that by the “truth” of a geometrical proposition in this sense we understand its validity for a construction with ruler and compasses.

如果按照我们惯常的思维方式，我们现在在欧几里得几何的命题之外，补充一个命题：一个实际刚体上的两点始终对应着相同的距离（线段-区间），无论该刚体的位置如何变化，那么欧几里得几何的命题就转化为关于实际刚体可能相对位置的命题。如此补充后的几何学便可被视为物理学的一个分支。现在，我们可以合理地询问以这种方式解释的几何命题的“真值”，因为我们有理由询问这些命题是否适用于我们与几何概念联系起来的那些真实事物。更通俗地说，我们可以这样表达：在这个意义上，几何命题的“真值”是指它对于用直尺和圆规作图的有效性。

Of course the conviction of the “truth” of geometrical propositions in this sense is founded exclusively on rather incomplete experience. For the present we shall assume the “truth” of the geometrical propositions, then at a later stage (in the general theory of relativity) we shall see that this “truth” is limited.

当然，这种意义上的几何命题“真理”信念完全建立在相当不完整的经验之上。目前我们暂且假定几何命题为“真理”，然后在后续阶段（在广义相对论中）我们将看到这种“真理”是有限的。

That’s Chapter 1 in its entirety. If the style is slightly rotund, remember that it was written in 1916, in German, a language of some rotundity. But there’s nothing circular about the reasoning; Einstein’s sentences move as sequentially as his mind evidently did in considering the problem in the first place. We are left with the idea that classical geometry has limitations but that modern physics can transcend them.

以上便是第一章的全部内容。如果文风略显圆润，请记住，它写于1916年，是用德语——一种本身就略显圆润的语言——写成的。但论证本身并无循环论证之嫌；爱因斯坦的语句行文清晰连贯，正如他最初思考这个问题时的思路一样。最终，我们得出的结论是：经典几何学存在局限性，而现代物理学可以超越这些局限性。

Next Einstein gives us a brief chapter called “The System of Co-ordinates,” knowing that we won’t understand how physics has pushed beyond geometry unless we first understand geometry’s working principle: that it enables us “to establish the distance between two points on a rigid body by means of measurements”:

接下来，爱因斯坦用一个简短的章节，题为“坐标系”，他知道，除非我们首先理解几何学的工作原理，否则我们将无法理解物理学是如何超越几何学的：几何学使我们能够“通过测量来确定刚体上两点之间的距离”：

Every description of the scene of an event or of the position of an object in space is based on the specification of the point on a rigid body (body of reference) with which that event or object coincides. This applies not only to scientific description, but also to everyday life. If I analyze the place specification “Trafalgar Square, London,” I arrive at the following result. The earth is the rigid body to which the specification of place refers; “Trafalgar Square, London” is a well-defined point to which a name has been assigned and with which the event coincides in space.

对事件场景或物体空间位置的任何描述，都基于对刚体（参考体）上与该事件或物体重合的点的指定。这不仅适用于科学描述，也适用于日常生活。如果我分析“伦敦特拉法加广场”这一地点描述，我会得出以下结论：地球是该地点描述所指的刚体；“伦敦特拉法加广场”是一个被赋予名称且在空间中与事件重合的明确定义的点。

This primitive method of place specification deals only with places on the surface of rigid bodies and is dependent on the existence of points on this surface which are distinguishable from each other. But we can free ourselves from these limitations without altering the nature of our specification of position.

这种原始的位置指定方法仅适用于刚体表面上的位置，并且依赖于表面上存在彼此可区分的点。但是，我们可以在不改变位置指定本质的前提下，摆脱这些限制。

How can we do that? “It should be possible by means of numerical measures,” Einstein tells us, “to make ourselves independent of the existence of marked positions (possessing names) on the rigid body of reference.” This brings him, in Chapter 3, into physics—specifically, into the question of “how bodies change their position in space with ‘time.’”

我们该如何做到这一点呢？爱因斯坦告诉我们：“通过数值测量，我们应该能够摆脱对刚体参考系上标记位置（具有名称）的依赖。” 这就引出了他在第三章中探讨的物理学问题——具体来说，是“物体如何随‘时间’改变其在空间中的位置”这个问题。

With the mention of time, Einstein’s story quickens; even I know that the theory of relativity deals with how moving objects are perceived in relation to both their own motion and the motion of the person observing them. Here’s how Einstein introduces the principle:

提到时间，爱因斯坦的叙述节奏加快；即使是我也知道，相对论研究的是运动物体相对于其自身运动以及观察者运动的感知关系。以下是爱因斯坦介绍这一原理的方式：

I stand at the window of a railway carriage which is traveling uniformly, and drop a stone on the embankment without throwing it. Then, disregarding the influence of the air resistance, I see the stone descend in a straight line. A pedestrian who observes the misdeed from the footpath notices that the stone falls to the ground in a parabolic curve. I now ask: Do the “positions” traversed by the stone lie “in reality” on a straight line or on a parabola? Moreover, what is meant here by motion “in space”? The answer is self-evident. In the first place we entirely shun the vague word “space,” of which, we must honestly acknowledge, we cannot form the slightest conception, and we replace it by “motion relative to a practically rigid body of reference.” The positions relative to the body of reference (railway carriage or embankment) have already been defined in the preceding section. If instead of “body of reference” we insert “system of mathematical co-ordinates,” which is a useful idea for mathematical description, we are in a position to say: The stone traverses a straight line relative to a system of co-ordinates rigidly attached to the carriage, but relative to a system of co-ordinates rigidly attached to the ground (embankment) it describes a parabola. With the aid of this example it is clearly seen that there is no such thing as an independently existing trajectory (or “path-curve”), but only a trajectory relative to a particular body of reference.

我站在一节匀速行驶的火车车厢的窗边，不经意地将一块石头扔到路堤上。然后，忽略空气阻力的影响，我看到石头沿直线下落。一位在人行道上目睹这一幕的行人注意到，石头的下落轨迹呈抛物线。现在我问：石头运动的“位置”实际上位于一条直线上还是一条抛物线上？此外，这里所说的“空间运动”指的是什么？答案显而易见。首先，我们完全摒弃了模糊的“空间”一词，因为我们必须坦诚地承认，我们对它根本无法形成任何概念，我们用“相对于一个近乎刚体的参考系的运动”来代替它。相对于参考系（火车车厢或路堤）的位置已经在前一节中定义过了。如果用“数学坐标系”代替“参考体”（这对于数学描述来说是一个很有用的概念），我们就可以这样说：相对于与车厢刚性连接的坐标系，石头沿直线运动；但相对于与地面（堤岸）刚性连接的坐标系，它则沿抛物线运动。通过这个例子可以清楚地看出，并不存在独立存在的轨迹（或“路径曲线”），而只有相对于特定参考体的轨迹。

That’s important information about the trajectory of the stone. It’s not, however, information enough. We still need one more piece:

这是关于石块运动轨迹的重要信息。然而，这些信息还不够。我们还需要最后一个信息：
